h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 3 – Valuing banks > 3.4 Value creation and the implied P/BV ratio
x:
The value creation rule
A bank creates value for shareholders when it earns more on their equity than they require: ROE > ke. It destroys value when ROE < ke, even if it is profitable. Comparing ROE with the cost of equity is the most direct test of value creation.
Deriving the implied (target) P/BV
Net income = BV × ROE and dividends = net income × payout, so dividends = BV × ROE × payout.
Gordon terminal value = BV × ROE × payout × (1+g)/(k_e-g) , with g = net income growth rate.
For a mature bank growing at a stable rate forever, this terminal value is the whole equity value. Divide by BV: P/BV = ROE × (1 + g) × (payout)/(k_e-g) .
ROE × (1 + g) is next year's ROE (ROE1), so P/BV = ROE1 × (payout)/(k_e-g) .
From the SGR, g = ROE × (1 − payout), so ROE × payout = ROE − g.
Substitute into the numerator:
Implied (target) P/BV = (ROE_1-g)/(k_e-g) ROE1 = next year's (expected, sustainable) ROE · g = net income growth rate in perpetuity · ke = cost of equityFair price per share = implied P/BV × current BV per share
Getting the inputs right
ROE1 must be next year's ROE. If you are given the latest historical ROE, grow it: ROE1 = ROE0 × (1 + g). If you are given a forecast ROE ("next year", "going forward", "in perpetuity"), use it as it is: do not grow it again.
g = net income growth. If you are given ROE and equity but not net income, calculate net income = ROE × equity for each year, then g = (NI_t)/(NI_t-1) − 1.
The formula needs ke > g.
In practice analysts often use tangible book value (equity less goodwill and other intangibles) and return on tangible common equity (equity less preference shares, goodwill and other intangibles).
Interpretation
P/BV | Means | Value
> 1× | ROE > ke | The bank is creating value: each rand of equity is worth more than a rand.
= 1× | ROE = ke | Neither creating nor destroying value: each rand of equity earns exactly what shareholders require, so it is worth exactly one rand.
< 1× | ROE < ke | The bank is destroying value: shareholders pay less than book value.
Why P/BV ≈ 1 is the natural anchor for a bank: assets are marked to market, so book value is roughly what the assets are worth. Any premium or discount to book reflects the market's view of whether the bank will earn more or less than its cost of equity.
Comparing the market P/BV with ROE (over- and undervaluation)
High ROE | Low ROE
High market P/BV | Potentially correctly valued | Potentially overvalued
Low market P/BV | Potentially undervalued | Potentially correctly valued
The slide labels the rows "implied P/BV", but the matrix only works with the observed market P/BV: an implied P/BV is calculated from ROE, so it cannot disagree with ROE. Equivalently, compare the market P/BV with the implied P/BV: market > implied suggests overvalued; market < implied suggests undervalued.
How to write up a value creation question
Compare ROE with ke in each year and state which years created or destroyed value.
Comment on the trend in the gap (ROE − ke): is it widening or narrowing? Is ke rising or falling (a falling ke makes value creation easier)?
Explain what drives ROE using the decomposition: is ROE coming from margins and efficiency, or propped up by high leverage (more risk, and possibly a rising ke)?
Bring in the market P/BV: P/BV > 1 is the market's verdict of value creation. If P/BV > 1 while ROE < ke, the market is pricing in expected recovery (optimism), not current performance. A declining P/BV signals diminishing value creation.
For an implied P/BV answer, state the number, whether it is above or below 1 and what that means, and compare it with the market P/BV (over- or undervalued). If future ROE is expected to fall or ke to rise, a high current market P/BV may be too high.
Worked example: implied P/BV from historical data (illustration: a large Chinese bank)
Latest ROE 11.15%, perpetual net income growth 5.8%, ke = 12.55%, BV per share RMB5.86, market P/BV 0.51.
ROE1 = 11.15% × 1.058 = 11.80% (the given ROE is historical, so grow it).
Implied P/BV = (0.1180-0.058)/(0.1255-0.058) = (0.0600)/(0.0675) = 0.89×.
Below 1, as it must be when ROE < ke: the bank is expected to destroy value. Fair price = 0.89 × 5.86 = RMB5.21. The market P/BV of 0.51 is far below 0.89, so on these inputs the market is more pessimistic than the formula (the bank looks undervalued), or the market expects ROE to keep falling.
Advantages and disadvantages of the implied P/BV
Advantages | Disadvantages
Uses the most critical drivers of bank performance: ROE, ke, g and BV. Focuses on shareholder value. Includes risk (through ke). Includes expected growth in earnings and dividends. Widely used in industry; the fair price is usually shown as a sensitivity table over a range of g and ROE. | Biased to short- and medium-term profitability: short-term estimates of g tend to be high, which inflates the value (when ROE > ke). Poorly suited to emerging markets or short data histories: inputs such as Rf or beta may be hard to estimate or meaningless. Values tend to come out larger because the formula adjusts for g (when ROE > ke).
Case: Standard Bank
Standard Bank targets an ROE of 18–20%, and recent results showed ROE of about 20% (inside target), CET1 of about 13.5% (far above the minimum), a cost-to-income ratio just under 50%, a credit loss ratio under 1% and positive jaws, with Rest of Africa providing roughly 40% of group revenue (a growth engine while SA banking is saturated). An ROE near 20%, well above any reasonable bank cost of equity, means value creation and a P/BV above 1.
Exam focus: value creation (ROE vs ke, trend in the gap, link to market P/BV) is tested in almost every mid-term and make-up test (2021–2025). Implied P/BV calculations: 2020 Final (historical ROE grown by 1 + g, with g from net income = ROE × equity), 2021 Mid-Term (forecast ROE given, not grown), 2024 Mid-Term (forward ROE given, plus over/undervaluation comment). 2026 Mid-Term MCQ: expected ROE below ke → trades below book; above → trades above book.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 3 – Valuing banks > 3.5 Excess return models
x:
Value of equity = equity capital currently invested + PV of expected excess returns to equityExcess equity return (each year) = (ROE − ke) × equity capital investedOver time: Equity value0 = BV0 + Σt=1→∞ (ROEt − ke) × (BV_t-1)/((1+k_e)^t)
A bank earning exactly a fair return (ROE = ke) should have a market value equal to the equity invested (P/BV → 1). Below-market returns push market value below book; above-market returns push it above.
Only two inputs: (A) equity capital currently invested; (B) expected excess returns on current and future equity investments. So the analyst must forecast where the bank will invest and what it will earn.
(A) is usually the book value of equity. Market value would normally be preferred, but (1) banks mark to market, so book and market values are close, and (2) depreciation, which distorts non-financial firms' book values, is negligible for banks.
Share buybacks reduce (A), so take care with banks that have bought back shares.
The ROE used is the expected future ROE, not the historical one. It depends on the bank's strengths, weaknesses and competition: banks with strong competitive advantages earn higher ROEs.
A bank expected to earn less than its cost of equity destroys value: the same message as P/BV < 1.
Link to the implied P/BV. If ROE is constant and book value (and therefore the excess return) grows at g, the excess returns form a growing perpetuity: Equity value = BV × [1 + (ROE-k_e)/(k_e-g) ] = BV × (ROE-g)/(k_e-g) . Dividing by BV gives exactly the implied P/BV formula. The two methods are the same idea.
Worked example: excess return model (illustration)
A bank has book equity of R100 million. It is expected to earn an ROE of 15% forever, with ke = 12% and no growth.
Excess return per year = (0.15 − 0.12) × R100m = R3m. PV (perpetuity) = (3)/(0.12) = R25m.
Equity value = 100 + 25 = R125m, so P/BV = 1.25. Check: (ROE-g)/(k_e-g) = (0.15)/(0.12) = 1.25. ROE > ke, so the bank creates value and trades above book.
Exam focus: 2024 Mid-Term asked for the market value of equity with the excess return model, given current equity, a further amount of new equity to be invested, an expected ROE and ke. Start from current book equity and add the excess return on the new equity, (ROE − ke) × new equity. The memo added this as a single amount without discounting it; show the formula so the method is clear.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 3 – Valuing banks > 3.6 Relative valuation (multiples)
x:
How a multiple valuation works: find a listed company that is comparable (same line of business, similar size, market and risk), take its multiple (e.g. P/E = (price)/(earnings) , both observable), and apply it to your company's figure (your earnings × comparable P/E = your implied price). The answer is only as good as the comparable, so most of the work is justifying the choice of comparable. The second choice is which multiple: for ordinary companies P/E (and price-to-sales) work well because price and earnings are strongly related, while P/BV works poorly because book values are historical. For banks it is the other way round.
EBITDA and enterprise value multiples are inappropriate: operating income and enterprise value cannot be properly measured for banks.
Use equity multiples:
P/E (price-to-earnings): usable, with two caveats. (1) Banks provide for bad loans with judgement, so conservative banks report lower earnings and higher P/Es (and vice versa): earnings can be smoothed or manipulated through credit impairments. (2) Investors may pay different multiples for earnings from different divisions, so one P/E for the whole bank may not fit.
P/BV (price-to-book): preferred for banks. Daily marking to market keeps book value close to market value, so there is a strong link between price and book value. Research shows a very strong relationship between P/BV and ROE for US banks, even during the financial crisis.
Using the methods together
The market P/BV is a sense check: look at it before valuing (P/BV > 1 implies ROE > ke); if your valuation contradicts it, either you have made a mistake or the market is badly wrong (usually the former).
Use several methods (implied P/BV, excess return, multiples): if they converge on a similar value you can have more confidence. Analysts therefore quote a range, not a single price.
Keep the model simple. Every input is an assumption, and small changes in inputs move the value a lot; adding complexity adds uncertainty and more assumptions to justify, not accuracy.
You do not need to reproduce the algebraic derivation of the implied P/BV formula; you need to use and interpret it.
Exam focus: "P/BV or P/E for a bank, and why?" (2022 Mid-Term 2nd paper, 5 marks): P/BV, because of mark-to-market book values; P/E is weakened by earnings smoothing through impairments.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 4 – Corporate treasury management
x: This part moves from running a bank to running the treasury of an ordinary company. The treasury is the department, usually reporting to the chief financial officer (CFO), that manages the company's cash. The core ideas are: what treasury does, how cash is managed and concentrated (sweeping and notional pooling), the trade-off in working capital, the operating cycle and cash conversion cycle (CCC), how much cash can be released from debtors and inventory, and supply chain finance.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 4 – Corporate treasury management > 4.1 What treasury management is
x:
Treasury management is managing a business's cash and liquidity needs so that it runs efficiently. It focuses on cash inflows and outflows, funding and investments, which are the traditional corporate finance activities.
In larger firms it can also include trading securities (bonds, currencies, derivatives) and managing the risks that come with them.
Treasury functions fall into three groups:
Core functions: typical for most companies.
Marginal functions: specific to a company or industry.
Ancillary functions: critical to the treasury function but not part of the treasurer's own role.
The four areas of treasury work
Area | What the treasurer does
1. Cash and liquidity management – the "navigator" for day-to-day cash | Cash-flow tracking: monitor exactly how much comes in and goes out.Liquidity forecasting: predict future cash needs so the company never runs out of money.Process optimisation: make sure cash moves efficiently through the business.
2. Financial risk management – protect against unexpected financial losses | Risk assessment: how could market changes hurt the business?Hedging: use financial instruments to lock in prices or exchange rates, protecting against currency swings or sudden interest-rate rises.
3. Investment and capital management – manage the company's surplus cash and borrowing | Investing surplus funds: place extra cash in safe, interest-earning investments.Funding strategy: decide how and when to borrow or issue bonds to fund large projects.
4. Bank relationship management – the main link to financial institutions | Negotiation: bank fees, loan terms and interest rates.Banking partnerships: manage bank relationships to keep the firm financially stable.
Which tasks are core? (2008 treasurer survey)
Task | % saying it is core to treasury
Cash management | 95%
Procurement of finance and financial instruments | 93%
Contacts with banks and rating agencies | 93%
Liquidity planning and control | 91%
Management of interest, currency and commodity risks | 89%
Corporate finance | 78%
The two cash tasks (cash management and liquidity planning) are grouped as cash and liquidity management, the heart of treasury.
What is not a treasury function: evaluating long-term capital projects (for example, NPV project appraisal) is a capital budgeting decision. Treasury's job is to fund such decisions and manage the cash, short-term funding, liquidity and financial risk around them.
Exam focus: 2023 final MCQ – identifying which item is not a treasury function (cash flow management, short-term funding and risk management are treasury functions).

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 4 – Corporate treasury management > 4.2 Cash management
x:
Cash management is the most fundamental treasury function. It covers the efficient use of current assets and liabilities; systematic planning, monitoring and management of collections, payments (disbursements) and account balances; and collecting the information needed to use available funds most effectively.
In short: active management of a company's short-term cash resources to keep operations going and optimise liquidity.
"Cash" means more than notes and coins: it includes cheques, deposits and short-term liquid securities.
Area | Key points
Short-term liquidity | Keep enough liquidity to meet short-term obligations on time. The trade-off: being able to pay when due versus holding idle cash, which earns little and drags down return on assets (ROA). Surplus funds should be invested where they can be turned back into cash quickly and easily.
Cash flows and cash positioning | Manage daily cash flows. Which payments have been received or paid? Which are due in future? Are any departments or group companies short of cash? Do the timings of inflows and outflows match? For a group, what is the consolidated cash position?
Managing surplus cash | Invest excess cash for an adequate return while keeping liquidity risk low. A key issue is concentration risk: spread deposits across several banks in case one fails (corporate treasuries did exactly this after the 2023 Silicon Valley Bank collapse).
Procuring financing | Keep enough short- and long-term borrowing capacity to get affordable finance when needed. Internal financing is generally preferred to external financing, so the treasurer must know the cash position of the whole group: funding may be available internally, for example through cash pooling.
These tasks are especially hard for large groups spread across continents. Treasury needs real-time information, but if each company uses a different local bank with different software, collecting and reporting that information is very difficult.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 4 – Corporate treasury management > 4.3 Cash concentration: physical pooling and notional pooling
x:
Cash concentration matters most for large companies with many subsidiaries, each with its own bank accounts. It brings the balances (debit and credit) of many accounts together into one central master account, improving control and visibility of the group's cash.
Benefits: treasury sees all available funds in one place, earns more interest on the combined credit balance, and pays less interest because overdrawn accounts are offset against accounts in credit.
Two types: physical pooling (sweeping) and notional pooling.
Physical pooling (sweeping)
The bank actually moves money between accounts. Each sub-account ends at zero and the net balance sits in the master account. It is usually done daily, as part of the bank's electronic end-of-day processing.
Worked example: before and after sweeping
Account | Before sweeping | After sweeping
Master account | R0 | R200
Sub-account 1 | −R250 | R0
Sub-account 2 | R300 | R0
Sub-account 3 | R150 | R0
Net balance = −250 + 300 + 150 = R200, all in the master account. Without the sweep the group pays overdraft interest (a high rate) on −R250 while earning credit interest (a lower rate) on R450. After the sweep it earns interest on one R200 balance and pays no overdraft interest.
Variants of sweeping (only these three are taught)
One-way sweeping: usually only credit balances are swept to the master account, and they are not returned to the sub-accounts the next morning.
Target balance sweeping: leaves a small balance in each sub-account, set by treasury; the rest is swept.
Reverse sweep: funds are returned to the sub-accounts the next morning so the operating entities have money for daily operations. This is hard across different time zones.
Exam focus: 2021 final MCQ asked which option is not a sweeping variant. Know the three exact definitions above, so that a made-up variant stands out.
Practical issues with sweeping
Tax and intercompany loans: a physical sweep moves real money from one group company to another, so legally it creates an intercompany loan. Some countries (for example China) tax intercompany loans and the interest on them, so sweeps should be designed to avoid unnecessary transfers.
One bank works best: sweeping is most efficient with a single bank (domestic branches in different places).
Several banks: true end-of-day sweeping usually cannot be achieved. Time differences and execution delays mean some sub-accounts may not be zero at day end.
Two-stage sweeping for groups spread across countries: sweep all accounts in a country into one regional master account in that country, then sweep that total to the global master account. This cuts fees and shows treasury each country's position.
Cross-currency sweeping is usually costly. Instead, funds are swept by currency, and notional pooling then links the currency pools to one global master account.
Notional pooling
The bank offsets the company's balances held with it, to maximise interest earned or minimise interest paid.
No money moves between accounts. The bank simply adds up (nets) the balances and treats the net amount as the company's balance when calculating interest.
The interest result is the same as sweeping, but there are regulatory challenges. Most regulators require a cross-guarantee: each participant is jointly and severally liable (each can be held responsible) for the debit balances of the other participants, up to the amount of its own credit balances.
In practice this usually means all accounts must be with the same bank in a single jurisdiction (one country's legal system).
Physical pooling (sweeping) | Notional pooling
Does money move? | Yes – sub-accounts are zeroed into the master account | No – the bank nets balances only to calculate interest
Interest result | Interest on the net balance | Same: interest on the net balance
Main problems | Creates intercompany loans (tax, for example in China); hard across banks and time zones; cross-currency sweeps are costly | Regulators require joint and several cross-guarantees; usually one bank in one jurisdiction
Typical use | Daily end-of-day sweeps, ideally with one bank; two-stage sweeps by country | Linking currency pools to one global master account
Model answer: what problems does a large multinational face in setting up cash pooling?
Many countries: different currencies (cross-currency sweeps are costly and add exchange-rate complications), and different laws and regulations.
Tax: physical sweeps create intercompany loans, which some countries (for example China) tax.
Many banks: pooling is normally done with one bank; across banks, time-zone and execution delays stop true end-of-day sweeping, and banks may be unwilling to offer the service.
Notional pooling limits: regulators demand joint and several cross-guarantees, so notional pooling usually works only within one bank and one jurisdiction.
Likely structure: physical (two-stage) pooling within each country, then notional pooling across currencies; but because notional pooling is usually confined to one bank, a firm with several banking relationships may struggle to achieve even this.
Exam focus: 2021 MT 2.1 (explain cash concentration, physical vs notional pooling, 8 marks); 2023 MT Q2 (physical pooling, the three sweep options, challenges for multinationals, 9 marks); 2024 MT 2.2 (how pooling works and the challenges for a large multinational with several banks, 8 marks).

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 4 – Corporate treasury management > 4.4 Working capital: risk, cost and the trade-off
x:
Liquidity management covers the activities that optimise working capital, plus bank services that help customers earn more interest and pay less. It can unlock large amounts of cash without raising sales or cutting costs. Example: Alcoa made working capital a priority in 2009 and by 2013 had cut its cash conversion cycle by 23 days, releasing $1.4bn of cash.
Definitions
Gross working capital = current assetsNet working capital (NWC) = current assets − current liabilitiesOperating working capital = operating current assets − operating current liabilities
Working capital risk
Risk here means: to what extent can the firm meet its short-term obligations? The cycle runs raw materials bought (accounts payable) → inventory → credit sales (accounts receivable) → cash.
The timing of cash outflows for current liabilities is easy to predict; cash inflows from current assets are not. That mismatch is the risk.
Firms manage it by holding extra liquid current assets so that current liabilities are covered.
Measuring working capital
Metric | What it measures | Type
Current ratio, quick ratio | Liquidity: amounts at one date | Broad measures
Cash conversion cycle (DSO, DIO, DPO) | How long cash is tied up in working capital | Linked to the supply chain
Relying on the current ratio alone is a trap: it compares static amounts at one date and ignores the timing of cash flows. Large retailers (for example Shoprite, Pick n Pay) safely run current ratios below 1, because fast-selling inventory brings in cash every day to pay suppliers who give long credit terms.
The cost of working capital
Could this cash be used more productively elsewhere? A firm's productive assets are its long-term assets.
So there is a trade-off between risk and profitability:
Higher net working capital → lower risk but lower profitability.
Lower net working capital → higher profitability but higher risk.
Working capital and ROA
ROA = (Net profit)/(Total assets) = (Net profit)/(Current assets+Fixed assets)
For the same profit and fixed assets, holding fewer current assets raises ROA, because the denominator is smaller. Plotting current assets against output shows three policies:
Policy A – high working capital at every output level → lowest ROA, lowest risk.
Policy B – average working capital → average ROA.
Policy C – low working capital → highest ROA, but highest risk.
Working capital and firm value
Free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) is the cash a business generates after the investment needed to maintain its operations: the cash that could be paid to all capital providers without harming the business.
FCFF = EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CapEx − ΔNWCD&A = depreciation and amortisation (non-cash) · CapEx = capital expenditure · ΔNWC = change in net working capital
An increase in NWC reduces FCFF. A decrease in NWC (releasing cash from working capital) increases FCFF and therefore firm value. So better working capital management raises value through two channels: higher ROA and higher free cash flow.
Positive or negative working capital?
Benefits | Costs
Positive working capital | Lower risk; stronger liquidity | Lower profitability; lower value; higher costs; trapped cash
Negative working capital | Higher value; higher profitability | Stock shortages; lower creditworthiness; risky
Neither is inherently optimal.
Negative working capital suits businesses with fast inventory turnover and strong bargaining power over suppliers (for example large retailers).
Positive working capital may be needed in businesses with long production cycles, uncertain cash flows or large inventory needs.
The goal is optimal working capital, not the lowest possible level.
Reducing working capital increases risk
Lever | Risk
Hold less cash | May not meet obligations on time
Stricter credit terms to customers (lower DSO) | May lose sales and customers to competitors
Lower inventory (lower DIO) | May not have enough stock (stock-outs)
Pay suppliers later (higher DPO) | Suppliers raise prices; damaged relationships
Working capital management is a constant tension between liquidity, risk and profitability.
Every firm wants to avoid both excess working capital (an opportunity cost: lost returns) and a shortage (risk). Both are dangerous, but a shortage is potentially more damaging.
The aim is just enough working capital to meet operating needs, with no excess.
The inventory trade-off in particular: too much inventory brings opportunity costs (cash tied up), holding costs (storage, insurance, security, transport) and contingent costs (obsolescence, losses from changes in customer demand or new production methods). Too little inventory brings stock-outs, with customers buying from competitors.
Exam focus: 2022 MT 2.1 (risk–profitability trade-off, 5 marks); 2021 MT 2.2c and 2022 MT 2.3 (inventory trade-off and the costs of holding too much stock); 2026 MT MCQ (why minimising the CCC is not the goal: too-aggressive cuts raise risk).

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 4 – Corporate treasury management > 4.5 The operating cycle and the cash conversion cycle
x:
Operating cycle: the time from receiving raw materials or inventory to receiving cash from selling the product.
Timeline: delivery from supplier → payment to supplier (cash out) → delivery to customer → payment from customer (cash in).
DIO (days inventory outstanding) runs from delivery from the supplier to delivery to the customer: time in inventory.
DSO (days sales outstanding) runs from delivery to the customer to payment by the customer: time to collect debtors.
DPO (days payables outstanding) runs from delivery from the supplier to payment of the supplier: the part of the cycle the supplier finances.
The cash conversion cycle is the gap between cash out (paying the supplier) and cash in (customer pays): how long the firm's own cash is tied up, and therefore how long it must finance its working capital.
Operating cycle = DIO + DSO (DPO is not part of it)Cash conversion cycle (CCC) = DSO + DIO − DPO = Operating cycle − DPO
DSO = (Average accounts receivable)/(Credit sales) × days in periodDIO = (Average inventory)/(Cost of sales) × days in periodDPO = (Average accounts payable)/(Cost of sales) × days in period
Method rules
Denominators: DSO uses (credit) sales, because receivables are recorded at selling price. DIO and DPO use cost of sales, because inventory and payables are recorded at cost. If a question gives purchases separately, use purchases for DPO (payables arise from purchases).
Averages: use (opening+closing)/(2) . With two years of balance sheets you can only calculate the ratios for the later year, because the earlier year has no opening balance.
Credit sales are rarely disclosed. In practice you usually divide by total sales, because financial statements do not split cash and credit sales. If some sales are for cash, the denominator is too big, so the DSO is understated: treat it as a best-case figure.
Days: use 365 unless told otherwise.
Operating cycle vs CCC: read the question. An operating-cycle question needs only DSO and DIO; improvements must therefore target DSO or DIO, not DPO.
From days to rands: rearrange the formula. Balance = ( (annual sales or cost of sales)/(365) ) × days. Rands invested in the CCC = receivables + inventory − payables.
Direction of each change
Change | Effect on CCC | Cash effect
DSO falls (collect faster) | Shorter | Cash released
DIO falls (hold less stock) | Shorter | Cash released
DPO rises (pay suppliers later) | Shorter | Cash retained (short-term supplier financing)
DSO or DIO rises | Longer | More cash needed
DPO falls (pay suppliers sooner) | Longer | More cash needed: (old DPO - new DPO)/(365) × cost of sales
Worked example: from days to rands
A firm has credit sales of R730m and cost of sales of R438m. DSO = 40 days, DIO = 50 days, DPO = 30 days.
CCC = 40 + 50 − 30 = 60 days; operating cycle = 40 + 50 = 90 days.
Daily sales = (730)/(365) = R2m; daily cost of sales = (438)/(365) = R1.2m.
Receivables = R2m × 40 = R80m; inventory = R1.2m × 50 = R60m; payables = R1.2m × 30 = R36m.
Cash invested in the cycle = 80 + 60 − 36 = R104m.
If DPO fell to 20 days, payables would drop to R1.2m × 20 = R24m, so the firm would need R12m more cash, and the CCC would lengthen to 70 days.
Exam focus: CCC or operating cycle calculations appear almost every year – 2019 final Q2 (CCC and rands invested), 2021 final MCQ (CCC from raw figures), 2021 MT 2.2, 2022 MT (2nd paper) 2.1, 2023 final Q2a, 2025 MT 2.1, 2025 make-up 2.1, 2026 MT MCQs (effect of DSO/DIO/DPO changes on the CCC and on cash).

Cash conversion cycle, 2016
Dis-Chem | Clicks
DSO | (687 745)/(15 061 293) × 365 = 16.7 days | (1 942 000)/(24 170 879) × 365 = 29.3 days
DIO | (2 570 304)/(11 534 533) × 365 = 81.3 days | (3 364 316)/(19 156 612) × 365 = 64.1 days
DPO | (1 529 667)/(11 534 533) × 365 = 48.4 days | (5 023 500)/(19 156 612) × 365 = 95.7 days

Interpretation. Dis-Chem's own cash is tied up for about 50 days between paying suppliers and collecting from customers, so it must fund that gap (it relies on bank borrowing facilities). Clicks has a negative CCC: it collects from customers about 2 days before it pays suppliers, so its suppliers finance its operations.

Lesson: on the current ratio Dis-Chem looks more liquid, but on the cash cycle Clicks is far stronger. Liquidity ratios measure amounts at a date; the CCC measures timing.
What explains the difference between two firms' cash cycles?
Bargaining power over suppliers (drives DPO)
Supplier financing
Inventory turnover
Business model
Model answer: how to write up a CCC comparison between a client and a competitor
Calculate the CCC for both (DSO + DIO − DPO) and, for a retailer, the excess days (DIO − DPO). A similar CCC can hide very different components.
Compare each component and say which one drives the difference. A DSO close to the competitor's is probably the industry norm; tightening it risks losing customers to the competitor.
Judge DIO: a high DIO is a concern in seasonal or fashion businesses (obsolescence, markdowns) and signals cash trapped in stock.
Judge DPO: a DPO already well above the competitor's is unlikely to stretch further without damaging supplier relationships or prompting price rises. A rising DPO can also mean the firm is struggling to pay.
Recommend levers aimed at the weak component (see 4.8), for example transferring inventory risk to suppliers via just-in-time (JIT), consignment stock or direct delivery.
Link to value: working capital is in both ROA (lower current assets → higher ROA) and FCFF (lower ΔNWC → higher free cash flow → higher firm value). Released cash also reduces borrowing needs.
Exam focus: 2024 make-up Q2 (Workshop 2): advise a retail client on its cash cycle versus a competitor's, suggest improvements and explain the link to firm value.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 4 – Corporate treasury management > 4.7 Unlocking cash from working capital
x:
Cash freed = Current balance − Target balance, where Target balance = ( (Annual sales or cost of sales)/(365) ) × target daysShortcut: Cash freed = (Old days-New days)/(365) × annual sales (for DSO) or cost of sales (for DIO)For DPO, the direction reverses: Extra cash retained = (NewDPO-OldDPO)/(365) × cost of sales
Worked example: unlocking cash in debtors
Annual sales R80m, average accounts receivable R16m. How much cash is freed if DSO falls by 13 days?
Current DSO = (16)/(80) × 365 = 73 days.
Target DSO = 73 − 13 = 60 days.
Target receivables = ( (R80m)/(365) ) × 60 = R219 178 a day × 60 = R13.15m.
Cash freed = R16m − R13.15m = R2.85m.
Check: (13)/(365) × R80m = R2 849 315 ≈ R2.85m.
Worked example: unlocking cash in inventory
Cost of goods sold R45m, average inventory R10m. How much cash is freed if DIO falls to 60 days?
Current DIO = (10)/(45) × 365 = 81.1 days.
Target inventory at 60 days = ( (R45m)/(365) ) × 60 = R7.40m.
Cash freed = R10m − R7.40m = R2.60m (R2 602 740).
If one firm achieved both improvements it would release R2.85m + R2.60m ≈ R5.45m, with no change in sales or costs.
Method: use sales for DSO and cost of sales for DIO and DPO; state the current days, the target days and the target balance before subtracting. If the target is "the industry average", the target days are the industry figure.
Exam focus: cash freed by a lower DIO – 2019 final Q2c, 2021 MT 2.2b, 2022 MT 2.2, 2023 final Q2b; cash freed by matching an industry DSO – 2025 MT 2.2; cash needed when DPO falls – 2026 MT MCQ.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 4 – Corporate treasury management > 4.8 Ways to improve the cash cycle
x:
Component | Levers | Watch out for
DSO (collect faster) | Tighter credit terms and credit vetting; active collection; early-settlement discounts; pre-authorised debit orders; selling receivables to a bank (factoring, invoice discounting) | Losing sales and customers to competitors with easier terms
DIO (hold less stock) | Better forecasting and inventory control; shorter lead times; just-in-time (JIT) delivery, consignment stock and direct delivery or drop shipping (the customer orders through the firm, the supplier ships straight to the customer, so the firm holds no stock and its DIO is zero; the risk moves fully to suppliers, who may respond by raising prices); sales and specials to move stock faster (a cost: discounts); sharing forecasts with supply-chain partners | Stock-outs, especially in seasonal peaks
DPO (pay later) | Negotiate longer terms; supply chain finance, so suppliers are paid early by a bank while the firm pays later | Suppliers raising prices; damaged relationships; a rising DPO can signal distress
Lower DSO and DIO release cash; higher DPO provides short-term financing.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 4 – Corporate treasury management > 4.9 Working capital across industries
x:
Industry | Main working capital challenge
Construction | Long project cycles and delayed collections
Retail | Inventory and supplier financing
Technology hardware | Complex supply chains and inventory
Software/services | Low inventory; often negative working capital
Construction
Low-margin, highly competitive, capital- and cash-intensive. Contracts are won by sealed tender: each contractor bids without knowing competitors' prices, so bids are pushed as low as possible and margins are often only 3–5%, acceptable only because contracts run to hundreds of millions of rand.
Payment pattern: typically a deposit of about 50% of contract value up front (to fund materials and rented equipment), with the rest paid as milestones are completed.
Suppliers are often paid twice as fast as cash is collected. Trade credit is inflexible because supply is essential to meet deadlines: suppliers hold the bargaining power (any delay costs the contractor) and demand payment in about 14 days, while the contractor waits for milestones. DPO < DSO, so the contractor must finance the gap.
Large labour commitments mean regular cash outflows with no timing flexibility.
Change: complex projects face design changes and cost and time overruns.
Change: disputes over who bears overruns (unexpected ground conditions, sub-standard materials) often end up in court for years; while the project stalls, no milestone cash comes in.
Retentions: the client holds back 5–10% of each milestone payment in case defects appear, and keeps it for up to 12 months after completion, because defects often show only later.
Fragmentation: control is decentralised, often to project level.
Sub-contractors pay for materials and labour first, then invoice the main contractor on completion, who waits for the project owner to approve invoices. So the working capital gap for sub-contractors is expensive to fill, especially as many are small and cannot get cheap finance.
Sub-contractors are often small independents (an experienced foreman with a crew) who must pay workers in cash weekly or fortnightly and have no credit history, so a bank lends to them only at a high rate, if at all. The listed main contractor has cash, facilities and bank relationships. Solution: the main contractor uses its credit standing to support its sub-contractors (supply-chain-style finance), because if a sub-contractor cannot pay its workers and stops work, the whole project is delayed.
Retail
Heavy investment in inventory, the retailer's biggest risk and cost; lead times are a key focus. Accurate forecasting by product line (trends, regions, lead times) reduces excess stock and obsolescence.
Most retailers sell for cash, so DSO is close to zero and the cycle reduces to DIO − DPO (excess days, below).
Seasonality: needs vary through the year (for example the festive season).
Customers expect integrated payment and service across channels (smartphone, tablet, in-store).
Retailers transfer risk to suppliers through JIT delivery, consignment stock and direct delivery.
Large retailers can negotiate very favourable terms with suppliers.
Excess days = DIO − DPO: the days of inventory the retailer funds itself after supplier credit. This is the key retail indicator (Dis-Chem +32.9 days, Clicks −31.6 days).
Cash handling: cash can sit idle in tills; manual counting, securing and transport to the bank are costly. Cash recycling (re-using till cash rather than banking it and withdrawing it again) helps.
Technology
Distinguish hardware manufacturers from software firms.
More examples of negative working capital than in any other industry. Telecoms (and internet service providers) have the most negative CCC of all, often −20 days or lower: customers pay up front (airtime, monthly subscriptions) for a service delivered later, and there is no inventory.
Highly competitive, with complex supply chains that rely on sub-tier suppliers that are less well capitalised than tier-1 suppliers.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 4 – Corporate treasury management > 4.10 Supply chain solutions and supply chain finance
x:
Solo initiatives push the cost onto suppliers
A 2010 Grant Thornton study (316 respondents): 90% had taken steps to improve working capital (78% in 2009), mostly by renegotiating prices with suppliers (short-term) rather than building infrastructure (long-term). Only 33% shared forecasts with supply-chain partners. Firms delayed payments to suppliers, and suppliers responded by raising prices.
US food stores cut their CCC from 1.5 days (1995) to −11.5 days (2004), while their suppliers' CCC rose from 51.9 to 53.3 days.
Model answer: what was the net impact? The stores gained 13 days, but their suppliers lost 1.4 days. Much of the retailers' gain came from pushing the financing burden onto suppliers rather than from making the chain more efficient. Suppliers usually have a higher cost of capital and pass the cost back through higher prices, so the chain as a whole gains less than the retailers' figures suggest.
Optimising across the whole supply chain
Many companies still focus on solo initiatives (a 2005 study of the 300 largest US and European firms found most focused only on their own operations).
Treat a rising DPO with caution: is it a deliberate tactic, or is the company struggling to pay on time?
Whole-chain view: add up all the CCCs in the chain and optimise the total.
One firm's lower DSO is its customer's lower DPO, so DSO and DPO changes just move cash between chain members. Only a lower DIO benefits everyone in the chain: less inventory anywhere releases cash for the chain as a whole.
Example: Unilever
In 2001 Unilever had a cost of capital of 5%. Through its financial service providers it used this to finance its suppliers in countries such as Kenya, Indonesia and Sri Lanka, whose cost of capital was 11% or more.
Net working capital in the chain fell 40% over three years, freeing $2 billion (so chain NWC was about $ (2bn)/(0.40) = $5bn before).
Why it works: suppliers can borrow on the strength of Unilever's credit, at a rate close to 5% rather than 11%+. Unilever can pay later without squeezing its suppliers, and the chain as a whole carries cheaper working capital.
How supply chain finance (reverse factoring) works
Supply chain finance (SCF), also called reverse factoring, is a facility that the buyer (the large, creditworthy customer) arranges with a bank. The buyer is not arranging a loan for the supplier.
The supplier delivers goods and sends the invoice; the buyer approves it.
The bank (funder) pays the supplier directly, soon after invoicing, less a small discount priced on the buyer's credit rating.
The buyer repays the bank in full on the original (or an extended) due date.
Party | Benefit
Supplier | Paid early (DSO close to zero); cheaper finance based on the buyer's credit rating
Funder (bank) | A diversified pool of short-term assets with an attractive risk–return profile, backed by a strong buyer
Buyer | Longer payment terms (higher DPO) without hurting suppliers; releases working capital; a healthier, more stable supply chain
Exam focus: 2024 MT 2.1 (what SCF is, how it works with an example, benefits to participants, 6 marks). Marks depend on the mechanism: the bank pays the supplier on the invoice and the buyer repays the bank later. Describing a basic loan to the supplier earns little.
Typical bank working capital solutions
Working capital loans, usually a facility: the bank sets a limit (e.g. R1m) and the client draws on it when a payment is due before cash comes in, then repays when the cash arrives, within days or weeks. A facility that is drawn and left outstanding for months is being misused as cheap long-term funding; the bank spots this in the account's usage pattern.
Receivables purchases (factoring, invoice discounting): the firm sells its invoices to a bank or lender at a discount, usually receiving 85–95% of face value now; the buyer of the invoice takes the collection risk and earns the difference.
Asset financing: a loan secured on an asset, or a lease/hire-purchase where the lender buys the asset and the firm pays for it over time.
Supply chain finance (above).
Worked example: supply chain finance
A small supplier in Kenya invoices Unilever R1m on 60-day terms but needs cash now. Under Unilever's SCF programme the bank buys the approved invoice for 98%: the supplier receives R980 000 immediately (its DSO falls to zero, at a cost of 2%, priced on Unilever's credit, not the supplier's). On day 60 (or a longer agreed date) Unilever pays the bank the full R1m; the bank earns R20 000 for low risk because the debtor is Unilever. Unilever keeps (or lengthens) its DPO without squeezing the supplier.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 4 – Corporate treasury management > 4.11 Key takeaways
x:
Treasury is about liquidity and the efficient use of cash.
Working capital is a major driver of short-term liquidity.
Reducing DSO and DIO releases cash; increasing DPO provides short-term financing.
Lower working capital is not automatically better: it is a trade-off with risk.
Working capital should be optimised across the entire supply chain.
Banks provide specialised solutions (pooling, SCF, factoring, working capital loans) where operational improvements are not enough.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management
x: This part asks what changes once a firm trades and operates across borders: why firms become multinational corporations (MNCs) and how, the new risks (foreign exchange transaction exposure, political risk, credit risk), how an MNC moves money between its units and what blocks it, international working capital, cash-flow techniques (central cash management, leading and lagging, netting), in-house banks, and trade finance. Most examples use Trident, a hypothetical South African firm that grows from a local business into an MNC.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.1 Why international finance matters
x:
The world is far more integrated and globalised. Investors diversify internationally, and companies cross-list their shares on foreign exchanges to gain liquidity and access foreign capital.
Consumption, production and investment are all highly globalised.
MNCs make business more complex: funds, resources, knowledge and technology move freely, and supply chains and stakeholders span continents.
An MNC's finance function has two roles:
Treasury: financial planning and analysis, sourcing funds, cash and liquidity management, short-term investment decisions and risk management.
Control: external reporting, tax planning and management, budget planning and control.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.2 Why firms become multinational
x:
Motive | Meaning | Example
Market seekers | Produce abroad to meet local demand, or to export to markets other than the home market. | US car makers manufacturing in Europe for European buyers.
Raw material seekers | Extract raw materials where they are found, to export or to process and sell in the host country. | Oil, mining, plantation and forestry firms.
Production efficiency seekers | Produce where factors of production are cheap relative to their productivity. | Electronics assembly in Taiwan, Malaysia and Mexico; the iPhone.
Knowledge seekers | Operate abroad to gain technology or managerial expertise. | German, Dutch and Japanese firms buying US electronics firms for their technology.
Political safety seekers | Invest in countries unlikely to expropriate assets or interfere with private business. | Hong Kong firms investing in the US, UK, Canada and Australia before China's 1997 takeover of Hong Kong.
The motives are not mutually exclusive. They can be proactive (to grow the firm's own profits) or defensive (to deny competitors growth and profits).
Production efficiency: the iPhone
The iPhone's supply chain spans more than 60 countries. Apple designs in California and outsources components: processors (TSMC, Taiwan), displays (Samsung, LG Display, South Korea), cameras and LiDAR (mainly Sony, Japan), memory (Kioxia, Samsung), glass (Corning, US/Taiwan/Japan) and final assembly (China, India, Vietnam, through partners such as Foxconn).
US labour can cost more than four times Chinese labour. A fully US-made iPhone could cost over 90% more to make, pushing the retail price as high as $3 500.
Knowledge seekers and government push-back
Governments increasingly protect technologies they see as competitive advantages or national-security issues. In the US this is done by the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS). In 2020 the Chinese-backed Suirui International bought Jupiter Systems, a US maker of high-end LED displays, without filing for CFIUS review. Regulators later opened a retroactive review and went to court to force a sale; Suirui must find a buyer and get CFIUS clearance.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.3 From domestic firm to MNC: the new risks
x:
At first Trident sells in rands to SA customers and buys from SA suppliers in rands, so it is easy to judge the creditworthiness of its suppliers and buyers.
It then sees advantages in importing raw materials from China and exporting to markets such as the UK. Going global also allows it to raise funds where the cost of capital is lowest and to gain economies of scale.
Importing and exporting bring four new problems:
Risk | What it means
Direct foreign exchange (FX) risk | The firm now quotes prices, accepts payment or pays suppliers in foreign currencies. The international monetary system mixes floating and managed exchange rates, and rate swings affect profitability. MNCs must understand FX risk to anticipate competition from imports or opportunities from exports.
Political risk | Risk of loss (or gain) from unforeseen government actions or political events (see 5.5).
Credit risk of foreign buyers and sellers | The firm must reduce the chance of non-payment for exports and non-delivery of imports, and it is harder to judge foreign counterparties (see 5.6).
Market imperfections | Large differences in laws, tax systems, business practices and culture. These create risks and costs, but also opportunities.
Exam focus: 2025 MT 3.1 – the three biggest risks of expanding a supply chain overseas, covering both supplier and customer sides (FX risk, political risk, credit risk; market imperfections also accepted), 3 marks each.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.4 Foreign exchange transaction exposure
x:
Transaction exposure = the gains or losses that arise when existing financial obligations whose terms are stated in a foreign currency are settled.
It arises from:
buying or selling goods or services on credit when prices are in foreign currency (the most common case: a foreign-currency receivable or payable);
borrowing or lending with repayment in foreign currency;
being party to an unperformed FX forward contract;
otherwise acquiring foreign-currency assets or liabilities.
The life of a transaction exposure
Time | Event | Exposure that starts | Length
t1 | Seller quotes a price in foreign currency (verbally or in writing) | Quotation exposure (potential) | Until a contract is signed
t2 | Buyer places a firm order at the quoted price | Backlog exposure (actual, but nothing shipped or billed) | Time to fill the order
t3 | Seller ships and invoices (a receivable is created) | Billing exposure | Time until the cash is received
t4 | Buyer pays the foreign-currency amount quoted at t1 | Exposure ends | –
Key point: exposure starts the moment a foreign-currency price is quoted, not when the invoice is raised.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.5 Political risk
x:
Political risk is the risk of loss (or gain) from unforeseen government actions or other political events.
MNCs must assess it both where they already operate and where they plan to set up subsidiaries.
It is often greater in emerging economies, whose higher growth and untapped markets must be traded off against higher risks.
Bolivia's energy sector (expropriation)
European energy groups such as Repsol and BG Group invested billions in Bolivia's gas reserves. In 2006 the newly elected president nationalised the oil and gas industry by decree. Soldiers occupied foreign-owned refineries, and the MNCs had to hand over majority control (50% + 1 share) and up to 82% of production to the state. Projected profits disappeared overnight.
Airlines in Venezuela (blocked funds)
Foreign airlines (American, Lufthansa, Delta, United and others) operated in Venezuela. As instability grew, the government imposed strict capital controls that legally blocked airlines from converting bolívars into US dollars. About $4 billion of airline cash was trapped; carriers stopped flying there and wrote off about $3.8 billion. This is overt blockage of funds (5.9): the profit exists but cannot be converted and taken home.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.6 Credit risk and market imperfections
x:
Assessing the credit risk of foreign buyers and sellers becomes key.
It is harder because of market imperfections: differences in laws, tax systems, business practices and culture.
Example: an unpaid export
A UK electronics firm sells GBP 500 000 of parts to a new buyer in an emerging market. The buyer takes the parts and refuses to pay. In the UK the seller could sue easily; in the buyer's country foreign firms have almost no legal rights and courts protect local businesses, so the UK firm faces a total loss of GBP 500 000. A letter of credit (5.15) would have protected it.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.7 How firms operate abroad
x:
If trade succeeds, the firm sets up foreign sales and service affiliates, then often manufactures abroad or licenses foreign firms. The routes form a decision tree; moving down it means a greater foreign presence and greater foreign investment:
Start: the firm and its competitive advantage. It can change its competitive advantage or exploit it abroad:
Production at home: exporting.
Production abroad:
Licensing / management contract (no ownership of foreign assets);
Control assets abroad: a joint venture, or a wholly owned subsidiary built as a greenfield investment (from scratch) or by acquiring a foreign enterprise.
Mode | Description
Licensing | Licensing intellectual property (patents, trademarks, copyrights, brand names) to a foreign firm for fees or royalties. Uses the firm's technology abroad without a large investment.
Franchising | Letting a foreign firm use brand names and logos for royalties; unlike licensing, the franchisor also provides know-how and a business system.
Management contracts | Operating facilities or providing management services to a foreign firm for a fee.
Joint ventures | An entity jointly owned and run by two or more firms, each applying its comparative advantage.
New foreign subsidiaries | Setting up new operations abroad: greater control, but usually a large investment.
Management contracts in hotels
A South African investor builds a hotel abroad and contracts Marriott International to run it. The investor owns the hotel and supplies the capital; Marriott supplies management, operating systems, marketing and reservations. Marriott earns a management fee, possibly plus a performance-based incentive fee.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.8 Goals and agency conflicts
x:
The MNC's objective is to maximise shareholder wealth, which is harder when shareholders are spread worldwide.
Managers of foreign operations often focus on their own subsidiary's performance rather than its value to the group, acting as if it were a separate entity. This creates agency problems, handled in the usual ways (monitoring and aligned incentives).

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.9 Repositioning (moving) funds within an MNC
x:
Why not just transfer cash between bank accounts?
Separate legal persons. Parent and subsidiary are legally separate companies, even at 100% ownership. The subsidiary has its own financial statements, tax obligations, bank accounts and creditors. Cash in its account belongs to the subsidiary.
Tax. Every country protects its tax base. The subsidiary must declare its profit and pay local corporate income tax before sending cash home, and the host government often levies a withholding tax on dividends paid to a foreign parent. A plain transfer would bypass both.
Local creditors. The subsidiary owes local suppliers, banks and employees. If the parent could empty its account, the subsidiary could fail to pay them. Formal transactions such as dividends make sure it meets its own obligations first.
Unbundling: separate conduits for moving funds
MNCs unbundle transfers into separate flows for specific purposes.
Host countries are then more likely to see part of a "remittance of profits" as payment for specific benefits that also help the host country.
This recovers funds without irritating the host country with large dividend outflows ("dividend drains").
Line in the subsidiary's income statement | Payment to the parent | Host-country tax timing
Cost of goods sold | Payments for goods or services (transfer prices) | Before tax – deductible expenses that reduce host-country taxable income
Licence fees, royalties, management fees (operating expenses, above EBITDA) | Payments for technology, trademarks, copyrights, management or shared services
Interest expense (below EBIT) | Interest on intrafirm debt
Dividends (out of net income) | Dividends to the parent | After tax
Income statement order: Sales − COGS = gross profit; − operating expenses, licence fees, royalties, management fees = EBITDA; − depreciation and amortisation = EBIT; ± FX gains/losses − interest = EBT; − corporate income tax = net income, split into dividends and retained earnings.
International dividend remittances
Tax: some countries tax retained earnings at one rate and distributed earnings at a lower rate. Most countries levy withholding taxes on dividends to foreign parents. Most (not all) parent countries tax foreign dividends received but give a tax credit for foreign tax already paid. Dividends are the most tax-inefficient way to repatriate funds, because they are paid after tax.
Political risk: may lead the parent to require subsidiaries to remit all locally generated funds beyond what is needed for working capital growth and planned capital expenditure.
FX risk: if a currency loss is expected, the MNC may speed up (lead) dividends out of the weak currency, as part of moving funds from weak to strong currencies (which can include speeding up intrafirm receivables and payables). It must weigh interest rate differences and damage to host-country relations.
Earnings vs cash: a subsidiary can have earnings without cash. Fast-growing subsidiaries often have profits tied up in rising receivables and inventory, so dividend policy must consider both earnings and available cash.
Correct position for South Africa: SA does not tax retained and distributed company profits at different corporate rates; it levies a dividends withholding tax when dividends are paid (slide shows South Africa as the split-rate example; the source textbook uses Germany). The general point about split rates is what earns marks.
Constraints on moving funds
Constraint | Detail
Political | Overt blockage: the currency becomes inconvertible, or exchange controls prevent transfer at reasonable rates. Covert blockage: dividends and other remittances are severely limited, heavily taxed or delayed by bureaucratic approval.
Tax | National tax systems are complex and may contradict each other. The firm does not want funds in transit eroded by "a sequence of nibbling tax collectors" in every jurisdiction they pass through.
Transaction costs | FX conversion costs (fees and the bid–offer spread) are a small percentage per deal but significant for large or frequent transfers. Netting (5.12) is simple but saves a lot.
Liquidity | The subsidiary may be profitable in local currency but unable to convert profits into USD/EUR/GBP and send them to head office, because hard currency is not available.
Dollar droughts and trapped cash (Ghana)
Several African markets have had "dollar droughts": USD shortages that limit banks' ability to supply dollars to corporates. A US retailer in Ghana earns GHS 100 million and wants to pay it as a dividend to its US parent, which wants dollars. If the local FX market cannot supply them, the cash is trapped: earned economically but not realisable at parent level. Three risks occur together:
Repatriation risk: profits cannot be converted or sent home. IATA reported blocked airline funds at end-March 2026 of about $73m in Angola, $65m in Zimbabwe, $40m in Ethiopia and $23m in Malawi, among others.
Currency depreciation: while cash is stuck, the local currency may fall, so it buys fewer dollars when it finally comes out.
Import constraints: the subsidiary may need dollars to import machinery or parts, causing production delays, stock shortages and lost sales.
Exam focus: 2025 make-up Q3 – challenges in repositioning funds back to South Africa (political, tax, transaction-cost constraints, 8 marks) and the issues with paying dividends from foreign subsidiaries (after-tax, withholding tax, tax credits, 5 marks).

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.10 MNCs and working capital
x:
The domestic approach to working capital management manages individual assets: cash, receivables, payables and inventory.
The dynamic approach of international working capital management focuses on moving liquid funds between locations and currencies.
Main differences from domestic management: currency fluctuations, different inflation rates, exchange controls, delays in moving funds between countries, and different financing and investing options in each country.
Trident SA's operating cycle and cash conversion cycle
Point | Event | Period that follows
t0 | Price quote | Quotation period (t0–t1)
t1 | Order placed | Input sourcing period (t1–t2)
t2 | Inputs received | Inventory period (t2–t3); accounts payable period (t2–t4)
t3 | Order shipped | Accounts receivable period (t3–t5)
t4 | Cash paid for inputs (cash outflow) | –
t5 | Cash received from the customer (cash inflow) | –
Operating cycle = t0 (price quote) to t5 (payment received)Cash conversion cycle = t4 (cash paid for inputs) to t5 (cash received)
Quotation period: a quote in a foreign currency (say Chilean pesos) creates a potential but uncertain FX transaction exposure.
Input sourcing period: a contract fixes the product, delivery, price and financing terms; inputs are ordered. A deposit from the buyer would be the first actual cash flow (an inflow).
Inventory period: assembly and manufacture; length depends on the product, supply-chain integration and technology.
Accounts payable period: inputs are recorded as inventory with matching payables. Inputs invoiced in foreign currency, whether by a sister subsidiary (Trident USA) or outside suppliers, are FX transaction exposures. Paying them is a cash outflow.
Accounts receivable period: the sale is recorded at the spot rate on the sale (shipment) date; the spot rate on the settlement date (t5) determines the FX gain or loss. Length depends on credit terms and country and industry payment practices. At t5 cash comes in and the related balances are cleared.
Correct timing: the inventory period runs t2–t3 and the sale is recorded at the shipment date t3 (slides show "t1 to t2" and "t4"; the timeline diagram has the correct labels).
Intrafirm working capital
Many MNCs manufacture in a few countries and ship intermediate products to other units for completion and distribution. Each unit's payables, receivables and inventory mix intrafirm (within the group) and interfirm (with outsiders) balances, and different payment practices (days and discounts) across countries can create severe mismatches.
Managing international receivables
Currency of invoice: exporter's currency, buyer's currency or a third currency? The seller prefers the strongest currency; an informed buyer prefers the weakest.
Payment terms: collect weak-currency receivables as soon as possible to limit the loss in value between sale and collection. Hard-currency receivables can stay outstanding longer. If the seller expects its own currency to be devalued, it may even encourage slow payment of hard-currency receivables, as they will be worth more later.
Self-liquidating bills are common in Europe. A bill is a written instruction from the drawer to the drawee to pay a set sum to the bearer or a named person. It is negotiable, so it can be discounted (sold) for cash before maturity.
In many European countries (commercial law based on the Code Napoléon) it is easier to borrow against bills than against inventory: the buyer's complaints about the goods do not affect the bill holder's claim, and defaulted bills are collected through a fast court process.
Managing international inventory
Inventory is usually the largest and least liquid current asset. For an MNC the extra factors are: stock held in several countries at once, longer transit times, lengthy customs procedures, and constant political and exchange-rate risk.
The main drivers of inventory investment are the level of sales, the length of the production cycle and the durability of the product.
A domestic firm minimises carrying costs plus stock-out costs. An MNC has more flexibility: it can move production or storage to countries where it is cheaper.
Inflation and devaluation: buy inventory in advance, or when needed? Buying early costs carrying costs, insurance, storage and taxes. Buying later risks higher costs, because inflation raises local prices and devaluation raises the cost of imports.
Import-reliant firms often over-stock because of fears of inflation, raw-material shortages, import bans, delivery delays from strikes, weak inventory control and difficulty getting foreign exchange.
Exam focus: 2019 final Q3 – the extra challenges MNCs face in managing receivables and inventory across borders (8 marks).

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.11 International cash management
x:
The principles are the same as domestic cash management. Cash (including marketable securities) is held for two motives:
Transaction motive: normal day-to-day payments.
Precautionary motive: protection against unexpected deviations from budgeted cash flows.
Cash comes from (1) internal working capital turnover (the cash-to-cash cycle) or (2) short-term borrowing to fund shortfalls.
Goal: reduce cash tied up unnecessarily, without cutting profit or raising risk, so as to raise return on capital employed (less capital employed for the same profit). Better collections and payments and good cash flow forecasts keep required balances low.
Centralised cash management: centralise information, reports and decisions on moving and investing cash. All surplus funds go to a central cash depository, where one authority invests them in the currencies and money-market instruments that best serve the whole group.
Advantages of a central depository
Better information: a specialised office handling larger sums gets better information and service from banks, brokers and other financial institutions.
Lower interest costs: the pool manager finds the cheapest borrowing and the best returns, and no subsidiary borrows at more than the group's minimum available rate. For a worldwide surplus, the manager compares returns, transaction costs, FX risk and tax across markets.
Smaller precautionary balances: the centre holds one buffer for all subsidiaries. Since they are unlikely all to need emergency cash at once, the total can be smaller with no loss of protection.
Limits and risks of centralising cash
Moving the cash is not free: each subsidiary is a separate legal entity, so cash reaches the centre only through legitimate channels (intercompany loans, payments for goods and services, fees, dividends), each with tax and regulatory consequences (see 5.9).
Several currencies: the centre ends up holding dollars, euros, rand and so on. Converting everything into one currency on every transfer adds conversion costs and FX risk, so groups often pool by region or by currency and convert only when needed.
Concentration risk: all the group's surplus cash sits in one place (and often with one bank); a problem there affects the whole group rather than one subsidiary.
Operational risk: an error or a fraud at the central treasury hits the entire group's cash, whereas a mistake at one subsidiary is contained to that unit.
Hedging is imperfect: a forward contract fixes the rate only for a known date and amount. Shipping and customs delays make the timing of international payments uncertain, so hedges rarely match exactly, and hedging has a cost. Large unhedged currency movements can turn an operating profit into a loss through foreign exchange losses.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.12 Techniques to optimise cash flow
x:
1. Accelerating cash inflows
Collecting early ensures cash is there when payments fall due.
Pre-authorised payments: the company may debit a customer's bank account up to a set limit.
Same-day-value facilities: some multinational banks credit a deposit made at any branch, in any country, to the firm's account on the same day.
2. Leading and lagging
Leading = shortening credit terms (paying or collecting early). Lagging = extending credit terms (paying or collecting late).
MNCs lead or lag foreign-currency payments by changing the credit terms one unit gives another. The aim is to reduce transaction exposure.
Currency | Meaning | Payables | Receivables
Hard | Expected to stay strong or appreciate | Lead (pay early, before it gets dearer) | Lag (let them run; they will be worth more)
Soft | Expected to weaken or depreciate | Lag (pay late, when it is cheaper) | Lead (collect early, before value is lost)
Worked example: Trident leads a USD payable
Trident owes a US supplier $1 000 000 in 3 months. Today $1 = R18; management expects $1 = R20 in 3 months (USD is the hard currency).
Pay today: $1 000 000 × R18 = R18 000 000.
Pay in 3 months (if the forecast is right): $1 000 000 × R20 = R20 000 000.
Expected saving from leading: R20m − R18m = R2 000 000 ( (2)/(18) = 11.1% of today's cost).
Decision: lead (pay early), because it is a hard-currency payable. Caveats: (1) the saving is only expected; if the rand strengthens instead, leading loses. (2) Finding R18m three months early has a funding or opportunity cost, so interest rate differences must be weighed against the expected currency gain.
3. Netting
Netting eliminates counter-payments between group companies so that only the net amount is paid. It cuts administration and currency-conversion costs.
Simple case: the parent is owed R6m by a subsidiary and owes the same subsidiary R2m. Net: R6m − R2m = R4m, paid by the subsidiary to the parent, in one payment instead of two. If the amounts were equal, no money would move.
Bilateral netting: between two units (parent and one subsidiary, or two subsidiaries). Example: a US parent is owed $40 000 by its German affiliate and owes it $30 000, so the German affiliate pays the parent $10 000 in one payment.
Multilateral netting: among the parent and several affiliates. Each unit nets all its intra-group receipts against all its payments and pays or receives only the balance. It saves considerably on exchange and transfer costs, but needs a centralised communication system and discipline from subsidiaries.
Worked example: multilateral netting among four Trident companies (US$ thousands)
Before netting there are 12 separate intra-group payments, each with transfer charges.
Payer ↓ / Receiver → | USA | Europe | South Africa | China | Total paid
USA | – | 4 000 | 5 000 | 6 000 | 15 000
Europe | 3 000 | – | 3 000 | 5 000 | 11 000
South Africa | 4 000 | 2 000 | – | 2 000 | 8 000
China | 5 000 | 3 000 | 1 000 | – | 9 000
Total received | 12 000 | 9 000 | 9 000 | 13 000 | 43 000
Step 1: net position of each company (received − paid):
Company | Receives | Pays | Net | Position
USA | 12 000 | 15 000 | −3 000 | Net payer
Europe | 9 000 | 11 000 | −2 000 | Net payer
South Africa | 9 000 | 8 000 | +1 000 | Net receiver
China | 13 000 | 9 000 | +4 000 | Net receiver
Check | 0 | Net payments 5 000 = net receipts 5 000
Step 2: settle the balances. Net payers pay net receivers:
USA pays China $3 000.
Europe pays South Africa $1 000.
Europe pays China $1 000.
Check: USA −3 000 ✓; Europe −2 000 ✓; SA +1 000 ✓; China +3 000 + 1 000 = +4 000 ✓.
Approach | Number of payments | Total value moved ($000)
No netting | 12 | 43 000
Bilateral netting only (each pair nets) | 6 | 7 000
Multilateral netting | 3 | 5 000
Bilateral pairs: USA→Europe 1 000, USA→SA 1 000, USA→China 1 000, Europe→SA 1 000, Europe→China 2 000, SA→China 1 000 (total 7 000). Multilateral netting moves $38m less than gross settlement (43 000 − 5 000, an 88% cut) with 9 fewer transfers.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.14 Financing working capital: in-house banks
x:
Some MNCs' financing needs are too large or sophisticated for local banks. One solution is an in-house (internal) bank.
It is not a separate company: it is a set of functions performed by the existing treasury department.
Acting as an independent entity, central treasury deals with business units at arm's length, providing bank-like services to them.
Worked example: the in-house bank's spread
Trident Europe has surplus cash; Trident SA needs working capital.
Via an outside bank | Via the in-house bank | Gain to the unit
Trident Europe deposits surplus cash | earns 4% | earns 5% | +1%
Trident SA borrows | pays 7% | pays 6% | 1% saved
Bank's spread | 7% − 4% = 3% | 6% − 5% = 1% | –
Both units are 1% better off and the in-house bank still earns a 1% spread. Of the 3% an outside bank would take, 2% goes to the units and 1% to the in-house bank, so the whole 3% stays in the group.
Why an in-house bank can run on a smaller spread
It does not have to meet commercial banks' strict capital requirements.
No overheads of dealing rooms, branch networks and other services commercial banks need to compete.
It need not assess the creditworthiness of the units, as they are all part of the same company, so it does not provide for credit losses.
In-house banks and currency risk
When Trident SA sells its foreign-currency receivables to the in-house bank, the transaction exposure moves to the bank.
The in-house bank is better equipped to manage currency exposures and sees more international cash flows, so the group gains from more effective netting and matching.
Business units no longer manage transaction exposures and can focus on their main business.

h: Intro to Banking & Treasury > Part 5 – Multinational treasury management > 5.15 International trade finance
x:
The trust problem
Importer's preference | Exporter's preference
1. Exporter ships the goods.2. Importer pays after receiving them. | 1. Importer pays.2. Exporter ships after being paid.
Each side wants the other to move first, because neither fully trusts a foreign counterparty. The solution is a bank as intermediary:
The importer obtains the bank's promise to pay on its behalf: the letter of credit.
The bank promises the exporter to pay on behalf of the importer.
The exporter ships "to the bank", trusting the bank's promise; title passes to the bank on an order bill of lading.
The exporter claims payment with a sight draft, and the bank pays.
The bank passes title to the importer, whom it trusts.
The importer pays the bank, then or later as agreed.
Benefits of the system
The letter of credit, sight draft and bill of lading together assure both parties that the other will perform.
Hedging FX risk only works if the timing and amount of payments are certain; these documents provide that certainty.
Banks are more willing to finance goods in transit once non-completion risk and FX risk are dealt with.
Letters of credit
A letter of credit (L/C) is issued by a bank at the importer's request, promising to pay the exporter when the documents specified in the L/C are presented.
It is issued on the importer's creditworthiness, or against a cash deposit or other collateral.
The bank pays against specified documents, not the goods themselves.
For a true L/C, the issuing bank:
must receive a fee or other valid business consideration;
must state an expiry date or definite maturity;
must state a maximum amount;
must pay only on presentation of specific documents, and must not have to decide disputed questions of fact or law;
must have a customer with an unqualified obligation to reimburse the bank on the same terms as the bank paid.
Drafts (bills of exchange)
A draft (bill of exchange) is an order written by the exporter telling the importer or its agent to pay a set amount at a set time.
The writer (normally the exporter) is the maker, drawer or originator; the party it is addressed to is the drawee.
Drawee = buyer → trade draft. Drawee = buyer's bank → bank draft.
Sight draft: payable on presentation (pay immediately or dishonour). Time draft: payment is delayed to a later date.
Bills of lading
Issued to the exporter by the carrier. Three roles:
Role | Meaning
Receipt | The carrier has received the goods described.
Contract | The carrier must transport the goods for the agreed charges.
Document of title | Used to obtain payment, or a written promise of payment, before the goods are released to the importer.
A typical trade transaction
Bank X is the exporter's bank; Bank I is the importer's bank.
Importer orders goods.
Exporter agrees to fill the order.
Importer arranges an L/C with Bank I.
Bank I sends the L/C to Bank X.
Bank X advises the exporter of the L/C.
Exporter ships the goods.
Exporter presents the draft and documents to Bank X.
Bank X presents them to Bank I.
Bank I accepts the draft (promising to pay in 60 days) and returns it to Bank X. An accepted time draft is a banker's acceptance.
Bank X sells the acceptance to an investor.
Bank X pays the exporter.
Bank I obtains the importer's note and releases the shipment.
Importer pays Bank I.
The investor presents the acceptance at maturity and is paid by Bank I.
Result: the exporter is paid early without waiting 60 days, the importer gets the goods on credit, and the investor holds a short-term claim on Bank I rather than on the importer.
