h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.1 Why money and banking matter: “that is where the money is”
x:
“Banks can fail” is true but is not a reason for special regulation, because retailers and airlines can fail too without licensing, capital rules and constant supervision. The deeper reason banks are regulated is that banks are where the money is: they are the machinery through which the economy’s money is created, held and moved.
Banks run the economy’s payment clearing system. Almost every payment (salaries, rent, card purchases, EFTs, invoices) is settled by moving a balance from one bank’s ledger to another’s. If a large bank stopped processing these entries, wages, groceries and taxes could not be paid. A bank failure is therefore a failure of the payment system, which is a public good the state must protect.
Banks create most of the broad money supply when they lend. Each new loan creates a new deposit (section 1.4): a R2 million home loan creates R2 million of new money. Whoever controls bank lending influences the amount of money, inflation, asset prices and the business cycle, so this power cannot be left to profit-seeking shareholders alone.
The banking system is inherently fragile, because of (a) liquidity transformation – long-term, illiquid loans are funded with short-term deposits that can be withdrawn on demand; (b) information asymmetry – managers know far more about the loan book than depositors, who cannot tell a sound bank from a shaky one; and (c) agency conflicts – shareholders and managers are rewarded for taking risk with other people’s money (deposits), while depositors bear the loss.
Does money and banking change nothing in the real economy?
The real economy is the production and exchange of actual goods and services (factories, farms, labour); the monetary/financial economy is the money, credit, deposits and debts that sit on top of it.
Classical view – “money as a veil”. Money is a neutral window on real activity. Every debt is someone else’s asset (if Thabo owes Lerato R100, Thabo is R100 poorer and Lerato R100 richer), so financial assets and liabilities net to zero across the economy, and only the real economy needs to be modelled.
Why this is wrong. The models used before the 2008 global financial crisis (GFC) – the worldwide banking crisis that began with US sub-prime mortgage losses and peaked with the collapse of Lehman Brothers in September 2008 – failed to foresee it because they ignored banking, money creation and leverage (debt relative to own capital). Although debts net to zero, who holds them matters: a bank has a few rand of capital supporting dozens of rand of liabilities, so a small fall in asset values wipes out its capital, it stops lending and sells assets, credit collapses, house prices fall and unemployment rises.
Model answer: does money and banking change nothing in the real economy? No. (1) Banks create money and allocate credit, which decides which investments are funded, so they affect output, employment and prices. (2) Debts and credits cancel only in aggregate; their distribution matters, because highly leveraged banks and borrowers are forced to cut back when asset values fall. (3) The GFC caused a deep recession although no factory, worker or farm had changed. (4) Money and banking must therefore be modelled and regulated; the “money as a veil” view is wrong.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.2 What is money?
x:
Definition and functions
Working definition: “Anything widely accepted as payment, particularly by the government as payment of tax, is, to all intents and purposes, money.” Money performs three functions:
Medium of exchange – accepted in payment, which avoids barter.
Unit of account – prices are quoted in it.
Store of value – it keeps purchasing power until spent.
The more widely something is accepted, the better it performs these functions. Money lies on a spectrum: at one end commodity money, whose value comes from the material itself (gold, silver, salt, cattle – things that can be consumed, melted, worn or used in production); at the other end pure abstraction – money as a social scorekeeping system, numbers in a ledger that everyone accepts. Modern money is near the abstract end.
The Rai stones of Yap
The inhabitants of the Yap Islands (Micronesia, western Pacific) used huge carved limestone discs called Rai stones as money; some were several metres across and weighed over 500 kg.
The stones were never moved. When ownership changed (to pay a debt, buy goods or settle a marriage payment) the stone stayed where it was and the community simply acknowledged the new owner. The community’s shared memory of who owned what was the ledger.
One stone sank to the ocean floor (about 40 m deep) while being transported. It kept its full value and continued to be used in transactions, because the shared record of ownership was what mattered, not the physical stone.
Milton Friedman compared this to the gold held in the vault of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York: when foreign governments settle with each other the gold is rarely moved; ledger entries of ownership of particular bars are simply reassigned.
Model answer: are Rai stones commodity money? No. Commodity money is valued for the intrinsic worth or use of the material. Nobody consumed or used the limestone, the stones were never moved, and a stone at the bottom of the sea kept its value. The value lay in the community’s social agreement and collective record of ownership – an abstract ledger. Rai stones are therefore close to the abstract end of the spectrum, like modern bank deposits, which are also ledger entries accepted by social and legal convention. Money is a ledger/trust system, not a physical object.
The forms of money: central bank money and commercial bank money
Things counted as money: banknotes and coin, central bank reserves, commercial bank deposits and (arguably) gold. Only banknotes and coin and commercial bank deposits circulate among the public.
Central bank money = banknotes, coin and central bank reserves. Reserves are the balances commercial banks hold in their accounts at the SARB: a liability of the SARB and an asset of the bank. Reserves circulate only within the interbank settlement network at the SARB – the public cannot hold them. Banks use them to settle with each other and to obtain banknotes for customers. The SARB can create them electronically at will.
Commercial bank money = bank deposits (e.g. current accounts). This is the money the public actually holds and spends. It is a claim (IOU) on a commercial bank, accepted at par (R1 of deposit = R1 of cash) because it can be converted into cash or central bank money on demand.
Hierarchy of money: central bank money is the ultimate settlement asset at the top; commercial bank money is a claim convertible into it. Public trust that this conversion will always be possible is exactly what bank regulation protects.
What gives fiat money its value? Fiat money has no intrinsic value and no commodity backing; it is money by government decree (fiat = “let it be so”). Its value comes from acceptance: the state requires taxes to be paid in rand, under threat of penalties and ultimately imprisonment, so everyone must acquire rand, which puts a permanent floor under its acceptability. The rest is confidence that the SARB will keep inflation low – which is why central bank independence matters.
Why not return to a 100% gold standard?
It wastes real resources. Society would dig a hole about 4 km deep on the Witwatersrand, extract and refine the gold, then bury it again in a central bank vault under armed guard. Those resources could build roads, schools and hospitals; a legal scorekeeping system does the same job almost for free.
Money supply would be tied to gold supply, not to the needs of the economy. If the economy grows faster than the gold stock, the result is deflation (falling prices), which raises the real burden of debt and discourages investment.
No emergency, counter-cyclical response in a crisis. A gold-backed system stops the state injecting emergency liquidity (creating money to lend to banks in a downturn) to stop runs and panics, as in the Great Depression of the 1930s.
Modern money is not gold-backed anyway: gold is only about 5.2% of M3 in South Africa (below).
What counts in the money supply (and what does not)
Item | Money? | Why
Physical notes and coin | Yes | Central bank money held by the public; circulates.
Commercial bank deposits | Yes | The largest part of broad money; created when banks lend; paid with by EFT and card.
Central bank deposits (reserves) | Yes (base money) | Used by banks to settle with each other and to meet reserve requirements.
Gold | Historically yes | Commodity money (coin, bullion, the gold standard).
Cheques / card payments | Not separately | A cheque is an instruction to transfer a deposit; it moves money already counted in deposits.
Loans | Never | A loan is a credit contract (the bank’s asset, the borrower’s debt). Lending creates deposit money, but the loan itself is never handed over as a means of payment.
Bitcoin | No | A private crypto-asset outside central bank control; not legal tender in South Africa; excluded from official money-supply statistics.
Official money supply statistics (SARB Quarterly Bulletin)
The money supply is the total stock of money in the economy. The SARB publishes it in its Quarterly Bulletin as a ladder of aggregates, from the most liquid (spendable immediately) to the least liquid. Liquid means readily convertible into cash or spendable with little delay or loss of value. Each rung adds a less liquid type of bank deposit.
Component | Aggregate
Notes and coin in circulation + banks’ reserve balances at the SARB | M0 (monetary base / central bank money)
Notes and coin held by the public + current and transactional account deposits | M1A
+ Other demand deposits | M1
+ Other short- and medium-term deposits | M2
+ Long-term deposits | M3 (broadest measure)
M0 (the monetary base) is central bank money only – the SARB’s own liabilities. M1A is what the public can spend on the spot (cash plus cheque and transactional accounts). Other demand deposits are payable on demand but not used for day-to-day transactions (M1). Short- and medium-term deposits (notice and fixed deposits of up to a few years) give M2, and long-term deposits give M3. The broader the measure, the less “moneyish” the last item added – but M1A to M3 are all claims on banks, i.e. created by banks.
M0 is not on the slide (which starts at M1A); it is the standard name for the monetary base and is added for completeness.
Two percentages from the bulletin data are exam targets:
Cash share of M3 = (physical notes and coin)/(M3)=(R150 bn)/(R5 800 bn) ≈ 2.6%
Gold share of M3 = (R290 451m held by the SARB+R12 267m held by banks)/(M3)=(R302 718m)/(R5 800 000m) ≈ 5.2%
Cash is only about 2.6% of broad money. The other 97.4% exists only as electronic entries in commercial bank ledgers. If everyone tried to withdraw their deposits as cash at once, only about 2.6% of claims could be met. A run on the whole banking system can therefore never be met from banks’ own resources, which is why confidence, deposit insurance and a lender of last resort are needed.
Gold is only about 5.2% of M3, so the rand is clearly not a gold-standard currency; even all the country’s gold would back only a small fraction of deposits.
Exam focus: 2023 Final A3 (which item has never been money – loans); 2021 Final A6 (which item is not in the money supply – Bitcoin); 2023 Final C3.1 (name of the Yap stone money – Rai stones). Know the 2.6% and 5.2% figures and what they mean.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.3 What is a bank?
x:
Legal definition
Legally, a bank is a public company registered as a bank in terms of the Banks Act 94 of 1990. Registration and supervision are done by the Prudential Authority (PA), the bank supervisor housed inside the SARB (created in 2018 under the Financial Sector Regulation Act; under the “Twin Peaks” model the PA supervises safety and soundness, while the Financial Sector Conduct Authority, FSCA, supervises how firms treat customers). The defining activity is “the acceptance of deposits from the general public”. A deposit is money an institution must repay on the agreed terms (often on demand); “from the general public” means as a regular business from anyone. Because only registered banks may take deposits from the public, the licence is the legal gateway into the banking system.
Model answer: does holding a customer’s credit balance make Vodacom a bank? No. If you overpay your account by R1 000, Vodacom owes you R1 000, but you cannot use that credit to pay a third party: it is trade credit (a prepayment for Vodacom’s own services), not a deposit. A bank deposit can be transferred to someone else’s account (EFT, card, cheque) and thereby legally discharges a debt – a shop accepting your card treats the debt as paid. That “moneyiness” (working as a medium of exchange) is what makes bank liabilities money, and why the state regulates who may issue them.
What banks do for customers
Pooling – collecting funds from many depositors.
Information processing – screening the creditworthiness of borrowers more cheaply than each depositor could.
Financial intermediation – channelling pooled funds to borrowers (indirect finance, as opposed to direct finance where savers lend to borrowers themselves).
Maturity/liquidity transformation – funding long-term loans with short-term deposits.
Banks reduce risk and information asymmetry through diversification and screening; they never eliminate them.
Why banks exist and why they are dangerous: three foundation theories
Three ideas explain why banks exist (asymmetric information and delegated monitoring), why they are dangerous (moral hazard) and why they are regulated differently from ordinary firms (agency theory in banking).
1. Asymmetric information and delegated monitoring
Asymmetric information: one party knows more than the other. A borrower knows far more about their own finances and willingness to repay than a saver does. Two problems follow: adverse selection (before the loan, the riskiest borrowers are keenest to borrow, so good and bad cannot be told apart) and moral hazard (after the loan, the borrower may take more risk than promised).
If savers lent directly, each would have to screen and monitor borrowers (check accounts, enforce covenants, chase non-payment) – costly, duplicated thousands of times, and open to free-riding.
Banks solve this with scale advantages in delegated monitoring: savers deposit with the bank, and the bank’s specialist credit staff and models screen and monitor borrowers once, on everyone’s behalf, at far lower cost per rand.
Diversification makes the delegation credible: lending to thousands of borrowers makes total losses fairly predictable, so the bank can promise savers a fixed return even though each loan is risky. Savers need watch only the bank. “Who monitors the monitor?” – in practice, the regulator.
2. Moral hazard
Moral hazard: taking excessive risk because the cost of that risk falls on someone else (an insured driver driving carelessly).
Banks are highly geared: roughly 90–95% debt/deposits and only 5–10% equity (an ordinary company might be 50/50), so shareholders have little “skin in the game”. With limited liability shareholders keep all the upside of risky bets while their loss is capped at their small stake – “heads shareholders win, tails depositors/taxpayers lose”. A bank near insolvency has the strongest incentive to “gamble for resurrection”.
Illustration: assets R100 funded by R8 equity and R92 deposits. A risky strategy has a 50% chance of a R10 gain (equity becomes R18) and a 50% chance of a R10 loss. The loss exceeds the R8 equity, so the extra R2 falls on depositors (or the deposit insurer). Shareholders’ downside is capped at R8 but their upside is not, so the gamble is attractive to them even if it is bad for the economy.
Banking contains many moral hazards: (a) shareholders versus depositors; (b) deposit insurance removes depositors’ reason to monitor or withdraw; (c) too-big-to-fail expectations let large banks borrow cheaply and take more risk; (d) the lender of last resort may encourage banks to hold less liquidity; (e) managers’ bonuses reward short-term profit without penalising later losses; (f) borrowers may take more risk after receiving a loan. Capital, liquidity, supervision and resolution rules exist to counter these.
3. Agency theory in banking
Agency theory studies conflicts when an agent decides on behalf of a principal and their interests differ. In an ordinary firm the conflict is shareholders (principals) versus managers (agents), handled with audits, share options, bonuses and board oversight.
In a bank the more dangerous conflict is shareholders and management together versus depositors, debt holders and society. Shareholders and managers are aligned in wanting high risk and high ROE (options and bonuses reward risk). Depositors fund about 90% of the bank, are not represented on the board and cannot easily monitor it.
The regulatory response is to water down shareholder rights, transferring some control to the regulator as the representative of depositors and society: the PA must approve directors and the CEO (“fit and proper” tests); dividends need confirmation of capital adequacy; limits are imposed on capital structure, leverage, liquidity and concentration (e.g. single-borrower limits); and the regulator can remove management, block bonuses or place the bank in curatorship/resolution. A bank is therefore closer to a regulated public utility than an ordinary private company.
Three theories of how banks and money work
Three competing theories explain what banks do and how money comes into existence. What makes banks unique is their ability to expand the money supply.
Theory | Claim | Assessment
Financial intermediation | Banks are passive middlemen that gather existing savings and lend those same funds to borrowers. | Incorrect for the banking system as a whole.
Fractional reserve | Each bank is an intermediary, but the system multiplies money through re-depositing: the central bank injects reserves, each bank keeps a fraction R and lends the rest. Money multiplier = 1/R. | Outdated textbook model; misrepresents how reserves and lending work.
Credit creation | Banks do not wait for deposits or “lend out” reserves. Making a loan simultaneously creates a new deposit: loan (asset) and deposit (liability) created “ex nihilo” by double-entry bookkeeping. | Correct – the modern reality, confirmed by the Bank of England (2014).
Financial intermediation. Savers deposit R100, the bank lends that R100 and earns the margin between lending and deposit rates; banks add value by pooling, information processing and maturity transformation. Banks do perform these functions, but as a description of how the system funds loans it is wrong: loans do not need prior savings. The deposit is created at the moment of lending – savings are the result of the loan, not its source.
Fractional reserve. A reserve requirement is the share of liabilities a bank must hold as reserves (2.5% in South Africa). Example with R = 10%: the central bank injects R1 000; Bank A keeps R100 and lends R900; the R900 is deposited at Bank B, which keeps R90 and lends R810; and so on. Total deposits = 1 000 × 1/0.10 = R10 000 (multiplier 10). Why it is outdated: (a) banks make the loan first and find reserves afterwards (the central bank supplies reserves on demand at its policy rate); (b) the central bank does not choose a quantity of reserves to hit a money-supply target; (c) many countries have no reserve requirement and their banks still lend. Reserves matter for settlement, not for limiting lending.
Credit creation. The bank lends by crediting the borrower’s deposit account; it takes money from nobody first. Dr Loan (asset) / Cr Deposit (liability): both sides of the balance sheet grow and new money exists, created from nothing but a promise to repay.
Model answer: which theory of banking is correct, and why? The credit creation theory. The Bank of England stated in 2014 that banks do not lend out deposits – loans create deposits. The intermediation and fractional-reserve models assume deposits and reserves come first and lending second; in reality lending comes first and creates the deposit, and reserves are needed only afterwards to settle payments to other banks. Implications: banks create money (the feature that makes them special and a key reason to regulate them), and lending is limited by profitability, borrower demand, capital and confidence, not by a stock of savings or reserves.
Exam focus: 2026 Mid-term 1.4 (bank functions: pooling, information processing, intermediation). The three theories and money creation are standard MCQ and short-answer material.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.4 Money creation and settlement – worked example

Scenario: Mr X borrows R100 from Absa to buy a car. The car dealer banks at Standard Bank. The SARB is the settlement agent. Settlement is the final transfer of value that completes a payment between two banks. (Dr/Cr: in double-entry bookkeeping a debit increases an asset or reduces a liability; a credit increases a liability or reduces an asset.)
Step 1 – Absa grants the loan: money is created
Absa hands over no cash and moves no reserves. It records: Dr Loans and advances (asset) R100; Cr Mr X deposit (liability) R100. The loan is Absa’s asset because Mr X owes it; the deposit is Absa’s liability because Absa owes Mr X.
Absa
Assets | Liabilities
Loan to Mr X | +100 | Mr X deposit | +100
Both sides of Absa’s balance sheet expand. Mr X has R100 of new broad money; nobody else’s deposit fell. Absa’s reserves at the SARB are unchanged at this point.
Step 2 – Mr X pays the dealer: settlement through the SARB
Absa cannot edit Standard Bank’s ledger, so settlement happens across the banks’ reserve accounts at the SARB, moved in real time by the SARB’s settlement system. Reserves are the ultimate settlement medium because they are a claim on the central bank, which cannot go bankrupt in its own currency.
Absa: Dr Mr X deposit (liability ↓) R100; Cr Reserves at SARB (asset ↓) R100.
SARB: Dr Absa reserve account (liability ↓) R100; Cr Standard Bank reserve account (liability ↑) R100.
Standard Bank: Dr Reserves at SARB (asset ↑) R100; Cr Car dealer deposit (liability ↑) R100.
Absa
Assets | Liabilities
Reserves at SARB | −100 | Mr X deposit | −100
Standard Bank
Assets | Liabilities
Reserves at SARB | +100 | Car dealer deposit | +100
SARB
Assets | Liabilities
Absa reserve account | −100
Standard Bank reserve account | +100
Result. Total deposits in the economy are still R100 higher than before (the deposit moved from Mr X to the dealer). Absa ends with a R100 loan but R100 less reserves: its balance sheet is back to its original size but the composition changed – an illiquid, interest-earning loan replaced liquid reserves. Standard Bank gained R100 of reserves and a R100 deposit.
Key principle: money creation requires only a single bank making a loan; money settlement across the banking system requires central bank reserves as the ultimate settlement medium.
What if Absa has too few reserves? It must obtain reserves before it can settle: borrow from other banks in the interbank market, or from the SARB against collateral (a repo, section 1.10). The central bank supplies reserves at its policy rate, so the quantity of reserves is decided by the banks; the central bank sets the price.
What stops banks lending too much? The cost of reserves and funding (driven by the policy rate), the creditworthiness of borrowers, and capital and liquidity rules. This is why the SARB raises its policy rate to slow credit and inflation.
The same mechanism applies to cross-border payments, except that banks settle across correspondent accounts at foreign banks (see SWIFT, section 1.7) instead of at the SARB.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.5 Implications of commercial bank money creation
x:
Central banks do not directly control the quantity of money or reserves. They set the price of reserves (the policy rate) and supply whatever quantity banks demand at that price; otherwise payments would fail and interbank rates would spike. Monetary policy therefore works through interest rates, not direct quantity control.
Minimum capital requirements are only an indirect constraint. Capital is the bank’s shareholder funding; Basel rules require capital against risk-weighted assets, the best quality being CET1 (Common Equity Tier 1: ordinary shares plus retained earnings). No system checks capital at the moment a loan is approved – the ratio is measured afterwards, and a shortfall brings supervisory action, dividend restrictions and higher funding costs. The main determinant of lending is “confidence that the loan will be repaid and confidence in the liquidity and solvency of other banks and the system as a whole” (Bank of England). Capital is a loss-absorbing buffer and an indirect brake, not a hard cap on each loan. Because money creation is not automatically limited, regulators impose capital and liquidity rules (including the LCR – enough high-quality liquid assets for 30 days of stressed outflows – and the NSFR – stable funding for long-term assets).
Banks prefer lending against collateral (an asset pledged to the lender, e.g. a house under a mortgage) because of credit risk. This creates a feedback loop: rising house prices raise collateral values, banks create more credit, which pushes prices higher. Example: at 80% loan-to-value a R1m house supports an R800 000 loan; if prices rise 20% to R1.2m, the same house supports R960 000, so more new money chases the same houses. In a downturn the loop reverses (falling prices, tighter lending, forced sales). This pro-cyclicality is why regulators use loan-to-value limits and countercyclical capital buffers.
Banks cannot create unlimited money. Each is limited indirectly by finding creditworthy borrowers, the cost of funding and reserves, capital and liquidity requirements, and the central bank’s interest rate. These limits rest on confidence, which can break down in a boom – hence the need for regulation.
Three myths about money creation (Bank of England, 2014)
Myth 1 – banks lend out existing deposits. Fact: loans create deposits; lending expands broad money.
Myth 2 – the money multiplier controls money creation. Fact: central banks set interest rates, not reserve quantities; loan demand drives reserves. Banks lend first and obtain reserves afterwards if needed.
Myth 3 – quantitative easing (QE) gives banks free money. QE is central bank purchase of bonds paid with newly created reserves, to lower long-term rates when the policy rate is near zero. When the central bank buys R100 of bonds from a pension fund, the pension fund’s bank gains R100 of reserves (asset) and owes R100 more to the pension fund (deposit liability). The bank’s capital is unchanged, so it is not free money.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.6 CBDC versus Bitcoin
x:
A central bank digital currency (CBDC) is a digital form of central bank money available to the public. Today the public can hold central bank money only as physical notes and coin; digital central bank money (reserves) is restricted to banks. With a CBDC, individuals hold accounts or tokens directly with the central bank and commercial banks are bypassed. It may use distributed ledger technology (a shared record kept in several places) and tokenisation (representing a claim as a digital token), but it remains under complete central control.
Feature | CBDC | Bitcoin
Issuer / control | The central bank; “the final evolution of fiat money: money totally under the control of the issuing government” | Decentralised; no government or central bank can create more
Supply | Set by the central bank | Capped at 21 million coins
Privacy | Fully traceable – the state can see every transaction (cash is anonymous) | Outside state control
Status | Central bank money (legal tender if issued) | Not legal tender in South Africa, very volatile, not in the money supply
Why people want it | Safe, digital central bank money | Like gold: demand for something outside the control of central banks and governments
Programmability risk: CBDC money could carry conditions – an expiry date, limits on what it may buy, links to a social-credit system. E.g. a government seeking to cut cattle-farming emissions could block a wallet from buying more than two hamburgers a month.
Cost: it may cost more than cash to run (the central bank must maintain the technology and customer accounts).
Threat to banks: if the public could hold safe accounts at the central bank, deposits would leave commercial banks, especially in a crisis (an instant “digital bank run”), reducing banks’ funding and credit-creation capacity. This is why the SARB and many other central banks move cautiously.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.7 The South African Reserve Bank
x:
Functions
The SARB is South Africa’s central bank. It (a) sets monetary policy; (b) issues banknotes and coin; (c) is banker to the government (tax receipts sit in government accounts at the SARB) and to the commercial banks; (d) runs payment-system settlement (interbank payments settle finally on banks’ accounts at the SARB); (e) holds the country’s gold and foreign-exchange reserves; (f) acts as lender of last resort (lending to a solvent but illiquid bank when no one else will, to stop a liquidity problem becoming a collapse); and (g) houses the Prudential Authority, which licenses and supervises banks. National Treasury (the Minister of Finance’s department) is separate: it runs fiscal policy (tax, spending) and borrows by issuing government bonds and Treasury bills.
The SARB balance sheet
The central bank is itself a bank with a balance sheet, and accounting classification determines economic function: moving an amount from one line to another (e.g. from a liability to capital) changes what it can be used for. When the SARB lends to a bank it creates an asset (the loan) and a liability (the new reserves) at the same time – it does not need to have the money first.
Item | Side | What it is
Banks’ reserve accounts (minimum reserves) | Liability | Banks must hold a minimum of 2.5% of liabilities here; earns 0%. The ultimate risk-free electronic cash; effectively a small tax on banks that guarantees a base demand for central bank money. About R181bn.
Banks’ current accounts (surplus reserves) | Liability | Balances above the minimum. Since 2022 they earn the policy rate up to each bank’s quota and the policy rate less 1% above it. About R180bn.
Government accounts | Liability | The government’s deposits (the SARB is its banker).
Notes and coin in circulation | Liability | Physical central bank money.
Accommodation to banks | Asset | Repo loans to banks. About R50bn (the largest asset) under the old shortage system; about nil now.
Gold and foreign-exchange reserves | Asset | The nation’s reserves, priced in foreign currency.
GFECRA and other capital/contingency reserves | Capital / reserves | The Gold and Foreign Exchange Contingency Reserve Account records rand valuation gains and losses on the gold and FX reserves (section 1.13). Reclassifying funds from liabilities into capital makes them a permanent buffer that Treasury cannot spend, strengthening the SARB’s solvency.
Reserves are not capital. Reserves are an asset of the commercial bank (balances at the central bank) and protect against liquidity problems; capital is the regulator-recognised excess of assets over liabilities (a source of funding) and protects against solvency problems (losses). Reserves are part of the asset base that should exceed liabilities.
Mandate
Constitutional mandate (section 224): protect the value of the rand – its internal value (low inflation) and external value (exchange rate) – in the interest of balanced and sustainable economic growth.
Primary objective: price stability, measured by CPI (consumer price index – the price of a typical household basket). Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level; high or volatile inflation erodes savings, makes contracts and wage talks uncertain, and hurts the poor most (they hold cash and cannot protect themselves with assets).
Inflation target: historically a 3%–6% range (operational midpoint 4.5%); a 3% point target with a ±1 percentage-point tolerance band (2%–4%) was announced in November 2025.
Secondary mandate: financial stability.
Contrast: the US Federal Reserve has an explicit dual mandate (price stability and maximum employment). Critics argue the SARB’s inflation focus hurts growth and jobs, but monetary policy cannot by itself solve South Africa’s structural unemployment, which stems from skills mismatches, labour-market rigidity and low investment rather than from interest rates.
Central bank independence and political incentives
Politicians periodically call for the SARB (a statutory body with private shareholders) and the large commercial banks to be nationalised (brought under state ownership or direct control). The reasons, and the case against, explain why central banks are independent and why banks are regulated rather than owned by the state.
Model answer: why are politicians so keen to nationalise banking, why should banks be regulated, and why are central banks independent?
1. The incentive problem – why politicians want control.
Short electoral horizons: politicians face elections every five years, so they favour policies with benefits before the vote and costs later. Banks and the central bank are where spending power can be created without raising taxes or visible borrowing.
Control of the central bank = control of the printing press: a captured SARB could create money to fund grants, wage increases, bailouts of state-owned enterprises or a bigger deficit (monetary financing of the deficit, or fiscal dominance – fiscal needs dictating monetary policy).
Control of commercial banks = control of credit allocation: banks decide who gets new money. Politicians could direct unvetted loans to favoured constituencies, connected firms, municipalities or friends – in effect buying votes. Since lending creates money, this too is spending without a budget.
Seigniorage and cheap funding: the profit from issuing money (seigniorage) and forcing banks to buy government bonds at low yields (financial repression) are tempting sources of cheap finance.
2. The price – inflation. Newly created money is spent → money chasing goods grows faster than the economy’s output → prices rise → the rand loses purchasing power; savings, pensions and wages lose real value, the poor most of all. Investors demand an inflation and risk premium on rand bonds, the currency depreciates and imports become dearer, adding to inflation. This is the time-inconsistency problem: a government may promise low inflation but is tempted each year to break the promise for short-term gain; the public knows this, expects higher inflation, and the promise is not believed.
3. The solution – an independent central bank. Independence means the central bank sets monetary policy free of day-to-day political instruction and cannot be forced to print money for government – tying the government’s hands (Ulysses tied to the mast). In return it has an explicit, accountable mandate (section 224; inflation targeting). Benefits: (a) credibility – wage- and price-setters expect low inflation, which keeps inflation and interest rates low; (b) no political business cycle (loose policy before elections, painful tightening after); (c) foreign investors and rating agencies trust that the currency will not be debased, lowering the country’s borrowing cost; (d) unpopular but necessary decisions (raising rates, refusing a bailout) can be taken.
4. Why banks must be regulated – “partial nationalisation”. Banks take public deposits, create money and run the payment system. They are fragile (liquidity transformation – no bank can repay all depositors at once, so a run can sink even a solvent bank), failures spread (contagion through interbank exposures, panicking depositors and fire-sales) and impose costs on outsiders (an externality owners ignore), depositors cannot assess loan quality (information asymmetry), and shareholders gain from risk while depositors and taxpayers bear the downside (agency conflict / moral hazard, worsened by the safety net). Regulation – capital, liquidity, governance, fit-and-proper tests – is the price of the safety net. It restricts shareholders’ choice of leverage, dividends, directors and business lines: a form of partial nationalisation without state ownership.
5. Why full nationalisation is not the answer. A very large economy such as China can impose state control because the world must accommodate its size. A small open economy like South Africa depends on foreign investors, banks and trade. If politicians fully controlled the banking system, foreign banks would doubt that South African deposits were backed by sound lending and sound central bank policy and would stop accepting deposits from our banks; access to correspondent banking and SWIFT would be at risk, and trade would fall back on physical cash or dollar prepayment – costly, risky and slow.
Conclusion: control of banking offers politicians short-term money without visible cost; the cost is inflation, lost credibility and lost international acceptance. The balance is an independent central bank with an inflation mandate, regulated (not nationalised) commercial banks, and a regulator acting in the public interest.
SWIFT and correspondent banking
What SWIFT is: the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication – a secure messaging network, not a bank or payment system. It holds no accounts and moves no money; it carries standardised payment instructions between institutions. It is a cooperative owned by its member banks (a Belgian-law society), links banks in more than 200 countries and identifies each institution by a BIC (“SWIFT code”).
Correspondent banking: a bank cannot edit a foreign bank’s ledger or hold an account at a foreign central bank, so banks hold accounts with each other. A bank’s account at a foreign bank is its nostro (“ours, with you”); the same account in the foreign bank’s books is a vostro (“yours, with us”).
Example – a South African importer pays a German supplier €10 000: (1) Absa debits the importer’s rand account at the exchange rate; (2) Absa sends a SWIFT message to its euro correspondent in Frankfurt, where it holds a euro nostro account, naming the beneficiary and the beneficiary’s bank (BIC); (3) the correspondent debits Absa’s nostro by €10 000 and credits the supplier’s bank directly or through the euro payment system, which credits the supplier; (4) if there is no direct relationship, intermediary banks are chained together, each charging a fee – which is why cross-border payments are slower and dearer. Money moves on the correspondent banks’ books; SWIFT carries only the message. Domestically, the equivalent settlement is across banks’ accounts at the SARB.
Why being connected matters: correspondents keep accounts only for banks they trust – properly regulated and supervised, compliant with anti-money-laundering rules and backed by a credible central bank. Losing that trust means losing the ability to pay for imports, receive export proceeds, repatriate dividends or receive remittances. The price of staying connected is credible, independent, internationally accepted regulation.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.8 Monetary policy: inflation targeting and transmission
x:
Inflation targeting
Monetary policy is the central bank’s management of the cost and quantity of money and credit to meet a macroeconomic objective – here, stable prices.
Inflation targeting: the central bank announces a numerical inflation goal, forecasts inflation and moves its interest rate so the forecast returns to the goal. A clear public target anchors expectations: if workers, firms and lenders believe inflation will stay near target, they set wages and prices accordingly, making the target self-fulfilling.
Goal dependence, instrument independence: the target is set by National Treasury in consultation with the SARB; the SARB decides independently how to achieve it.
The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) – the Governor, Deputy Governors and senior officials – sets the SARB policy rate (SPR), formerly called the repo rate, a short-term rate that influences all other rates. It is announced every two months (six scheduled meetings a year).
The SARB does not target the money supply directly. It targets it indirectly through interest rates: banks create new money when they lend, and the central bank can control one price precisely (the overnight rate) but not directly how much money banks create.
The transmission mechanism, step by step
The monetary policy transmission mechanism is the chain through which a change in the policy rate reaches inflation. The main channel is the credit / bank-lending channel:
Inflation above target → SARB raises the policy rate
↓
Banks raise prime and other lending rates → borrowing becomes dearer → fewer loans demanded and granted
↓
Less bank lending → less new money created → less money in circulation
↓
Aggregate demand cools → less pressure on prices → inflation falls towards target
Step 1 – bank rates follow the policy rate. Banks’ cost of funds is anchored to the policy rate, so when it rises they raise their prime lending rate (the benchmark for most variable-rate loans; historically policy rate + 3.5 percentage points) and deposit rates.
Step 2 – borrowers pay more and fewer borrow. Instalments on variable-rate debt rise, leaving households with less disposable income; fewer new borrowers qualify; car finance, credit cards and business loans react the same way.
Step 3 – money creation slows. Every loan not granted is a deposit not created, so money-supply growth slows.
Step 4 – demand falls and price pressure eases. Less spending chases the same goods, so firms raise prices by less. Saving also becomes more attractive than spending.
When inflation is below target and growth is weak, the process runs in reverse: the SARB cuts the rate to encourage borrowing and spending.
What makes the transmission mechanism effective?
The SARB controls only one rate directly: the overnight policy rate. The framework is effective if that rate is the benchmark that all other interest rates reference, so that when it moves, interbank rates, the government yield curve, prime and deposit rates all move in the same direction by about the same amount – ideally a parallel shift of the whole yield curve. (The yield curve plots government bond yields against time to maturity, 2 to 30 years.)
Why transmission should happen: (1) the floor – no bank lends for less than the policy rate it can earn risk-free at the SARB, so overnight rates cannot drift away from it; (2) arbitrage – an investor can hold a 2-year bond or roll overnight deposits; if the bond yielded much less than the expected path of the policy rate, investors would sell it until yields were consistent, so long yields are averages of expected future policy rates plus a premium; (3) banks price loans off the policy rate.
Evidence: after a 50 basis-point cut (1 bp = 0.01 percentage point), the South African government yield curve from 2 to 30 years shifted down roughly in parallel (August 2025 compared with 1, 6 and 12 months earlier). The short end moves because it is closest to the overnight rate; the long end moving too shows markets expect the lower rate to persist, i.e. the SARB is credible.
Qualification: long-term yields also contain a term premium for inflation, fiscal and political risk, which the SARB does not control, so a parallel shift is a sign of success, not a guarantee.
Model answer: what does the SARB see as a well-functioning transmission mechanism? The SARB wants its policy rate to be the benchmark interest rate in the money market: when it adjusts the policy rate, all other interest rates (interbank, deposit and lending rates, and the yield curve) should adjust in lock step, so the change passes through to the cost of credit, spending and inflation.
Model answer: what is the SARB trying to achieve by raising interest rates? Its mandate is price stability. If inflation is too high and rates rise, borrowers have less to spend (repayments on variable-rate debt rise and new credit is dearer), saving becomes more attractive, less credit and money are created, and demand falls. All else equal, there is less pressure on prices, and inflation returns towards target.
Exam focus: 2023 Final C3.4 (well-functioning transmission mechanism) and C3.8 (economic logic of raising rates).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.9 Implementing monetary policy: the shortage system versus the surplus system
x:
The core problem: making the policy rate bite
The SARB controls only the price of its own money (reserves). For its rate to become the price all other short-term rates follow, it must arrange the supply of reserves so that banks either must borrow from it (shortage system) or can always place their surplus with it (surplus system). Both make the policy rate the reference for the money market, but the mechanics run in opposite directions. South Africa switched from the first to the second in June 2022.
The old shortage (repo) system – until 2022
The SARB deliberately kept the banking system short of cash and lent the shortfall to banks through repurchase (repo) agreements. Hence the name “repo rate” for the policy rate.
How the shortage was engineered: the SARB drained liquidity through (a) the reserve requirement; (b) issuing SARB debentures (short-term SARB paper that banks pay for, locking away their cash); (c) reverse repos (the SARB takes cash from banks against its own collateral) and foreign-exchange swaps (rand swapped for dollars for a period, absorbing liquidity); and (d) holding government’s cash in SARB accounts. It estimated the daily shortage and lent exactly that amount at its daily repo auction against collateral.
Why the repo rate bit: because banks as a group were short, they had to borrow at the repo rate every day. The repo rate was therefore their marginal cost of funds; overnight interbank rates sat close to it, and loan and deposit rates were priced off it. The repo rate was a lending rate.
The new surplus (tiered-floor) system – from June 2022
Banks are given more reserves than they need for reserve requirements and interbank payments. The SARB offers a deposit facility where banks place surplus balances overnight and earn the policy rate.
Ample reserves push market rates down; the deposit facility forms a floor. No bank lends to anyone at less than the policy rate, because it can earn that rate risk-free at the SARB. Example: with the policy rate at 7%, Bank A with surplus reserves declines a request to lend at 6.5%; the borrower must offer at least 7% plus a premium for its credit risk. 7% is the minimum price of overnight money.
Change in meaning: the policy rate is now mainly a deposit rate (what a bank earns on surplus reserves), not a lending rate. Its name changed from the repo rate to the SARB policy rate (SPR).
Banks rarely borrow from the SARB through repos any more – they can, but with ample liquidity they do not need to. Weekly repo auctions are kept (fixed rate at the policy rate, fixed allotment, capped to avoid overfunding) as a backstop for emergency liquidity.
The tiers: the interest the SARB pays on (and charges for) reserves
Tier (from the bank’s point of view) | Rate
Overdraft at the SARB (standing lending facility) | SPR + 100 bps
Surplus reserves up to the bank’s quota (banks’ current accounts) | SPR – the floor
Surplus reserves above the quota | SPR − 100 bps
Minimum required reserves – 2.5% of liabilities (banks’ reserve accounts) | 0% (non-interest-bearing)
The bottom layer, the required minimum, must be held and earns nothing – a cost (tax) on banks. Surplus up to the quota earns the full SPR. Surplus above the quota earns only SPR − 1%, so the bank loses 1% on it and has a reason to lend it to other banks. A bank that runs short pays SPR + 1% on an overdraft at the SARB, so it borrows from other banks first. SPR − 1% and SPR + 1% form the edges of a corridor for interbank rates, with the SPR as the floor of the normal range.
Quotas: the SARB sets a total market liquidity target (e.g. R50bn–R100bn) and allocates quotas to banks by their share of banking liabilities. Quotas (1) stop the SARB’s balance sheet, and the interest it pays, ratcheting upwards (without them every extra rand of reserves would sit at the SARB at the full rate) and (2) push surplus banks to lend in the interbank market, keeping it alive. Quotas include a R10bn shock buffer for daily swings in notes and coin and government cash flows (tax receipts drain reserves from banks into the government’s SARB account; government spending returns them).
Illustration – what a bank earns under the tiered floor
SPR 7%; required reserves R5bn; quota R10bn; the bank holds R14bn of surplus reserves.
Layer | Amount | Rate | Interest a year
Required reserves | R5bn | 0% | nil
Surplus up to quota | R10bn | 7% | R700m
Surplus above quota | R4bn | 6% | R240m
If the bank lends the R4bn to another bank at, say, 6.8%, it earns more than the 6% from the SARB, and the borrower pays less than the 8% overdraft rate. Both gain – which is exactly what the quota is designed to encourage.
Comparing the two systems
Dimension | Old shortage (repo) system – to 2022 | New surplus (tiered-floor) system – from June 2022
Liquidity position | Structural cash shortage, engineered by the SARB | Structural surplus / ample reserves
Policy rate | Repo rate – rate on collateralised loans from the SARB | SARB policy rate – rate on deposits at the SARB (up to quota)
Role of the SARB | Source (lender) of reserves | Sink (recipient) of surplus reserves
Transmission | Cost-of-funding channel: the lending rate sets banks’ marginal cost of funds | Floor / opportunity-cost channel: the deposit rate is the minimum a bank can earn
SARB balance sheet | Asset “Accommodation to banks” ≈ R50bn (largest asset) | Accommodation ≈ nil; liabilities: banks’ reserve accounts ≈ R181bn and current accounts ≈ R180bn
Interbank market | Banks borrowed daily from the SARB against government securities | Surplus banks lend to short banks; banks still use secured repos among themselves
Standing facilities | Standing repo at repo + 100 bps; standing deposit at repo − 100 bps | Overdraft at SPR + 100 bps; deposits above quota at SPR − 100 bps
Interbank market: banks lend reserves to each other, mostly overnight. Secured lending (a repo) is backed by collateral; unsecured lending is not and carries credit risk.
SHORTAGE: SARB drains cash → banks are short → a bank sells securities to the SARB under a repo → SARB credits its reserve account → bank buys the securities back later at the repo price (“accommodation to banks”)
⇩ June 2022 ⇩
SURPLUS: SARB supplies ample reserves → banks hold surplus → banks deposit overnight at the SARB → earn SPR up to quota (SPR − 100 bps above quota)
2023 exam memo: the benchmark rate is named “the repo rate”, and asked whether it is a rate on deposits at the SARB or on loans from the SARB, the memo answer is both – it is paid on surplus deposits up to the quota and is also the rate at which banks borrow from the SARB against collateral (the weekly repo auctions are at the policy rate). In explaining the current system, stress that it now works mainly as a deposit rate.
Evidence from the SARB’s financial statements
The SARB’s deposits note shows what it owes to banks, the government and others – all liabilities – split into non-interest-bearing and interest-bearing balances, so the tiers can be seen in actual numbers.
Item (R million) | Amount | Meaning
Banks’ reserve accounts (non-interest-bearing) | 180 664 (prior year 165 113) | Required minimum reserves – earn 0%
Other current accounts | 4 692
SA government accounts | 118 535 | The government’s deposits
Non-interest-bearing total | 303 891 (Group) / 303 818 (SARB)
Banks’ current accounts (interest-bearing) | 179 766 (prior year 168 799) | Surplus balances earning the SPR up to quota
Call deposits | 206 552 | Withdrawable at short notice / margin placements
Interest-bearing total | 386 318 (Group) / 179 766 (SARB)
Reserve accounts (≈ R181bn, earn nothing) and current accounts (≈ R180bn, earn the SPR) are almost the same size: the banking system holds about as much surplus as required reserves, which is what an ample-reserves regime looks like. Roughly half of banks’ reserves earn interest.
“Group” includes SARB subsidiaries (e.g. the South African Mint and the banknote printer), so Group and SARB totals differ.
Model answer: what does it tell us that “Accommodation to banks” fell from about R50bn to about nil? Under the shortage system banks borrowed from the SARB every day (repos) to cover the shortage the SARB engineered, so loans to banks were its largest asset (≈ R49–50bn). A near-nil balance (a residual of about R353m) means no bank needs to borrow from the SARB: reserves are so plentiful that banks have more than they need, fund each other, and use the SARB only to park surplus – visible on the liability side as ≈ R180bn of interest-bearing current accounts. It confirms the shift from a shortage to a surplus system and that the repo is no longer the working policy tool. It is a sign of ample liquidity, not of weakness.
Why did the SARB change the system?
The system had been in structural surplus for two decades (since the early 2000s). When the SARB buys dollars to build FX reserves it pays with newly created rand reserves; unless it drains them again (sterilisation), the system moves into surplus.
The draining tools stopped working: there was minimal demand for SARB debentures and none for reverse repos. COVID-19 operations added more liquidity: SARB purchases of government bonds (paid with reserves) to calm yields, the government loan guarantee scheme, and National Treasury drawing down its sterilisation deposits at the SARB.
Flexibility: in a floor system the rate is set by the deposit facility, not the quantity of reserves, so the SARB can expand or shrink its balance sheet (e.g. buy bonds in a crisis, unwind later) without losing control of the policy rate.
Efficiency and simplicity: interbank lending had shrunk and become inefficient; the new system needs no daily forecasting of the shortage and no daily auctions.
International practice: the Fed, ECB, Bank of England, RBNZ and Norges Bank run surplus/floor frameworks – after the GFC and QE flooded their systems with reserves, they had to pay interest on reserves to hold rates up. Aligning with the norm makes the framework easier for investors to understand.
Structural surplus since the early 2000s (FX-reserve purchases) + COVID-19 liquidity
↓
Draining tools (debentures, reverse repos, FX swaps) fail → shortage can no longer be enforced
↓
June 2022: move to the surplus / tiered-floor system
Model answer: why did the SARB move from the shortage to the surplus system? (1) The premise of the old system no longer held: a shortage system works only if banks must borrow from the central bank, but FX-reserve purchases since the 2000s and COVID-19 support left the system in permanent surplus. (2) The SARB lost its draining tools: minimal demand for debentures and none for reverse repos meant it could no longer force a shortage. (3) Flexibility: a floor system lets the balance sheet expand or shrink without losing control of rates. (4) Efficiency: the interbank market had become inactive, and the new system is simpler to run. (5) International practice: the Fed, ECB, BoE and others use ample-reserve floor systems. Result: the policy rate now works through a deposit facility (opportunity cost) rather than a lending facility, and “Accommodation to banks” disappeared from the SARB balance sheet.
Reading: SARB, A new framework for implementing monetary policy in South Africa (May 2022) – needed for background knowledge
The points below add the paper’s detail to the summary above. The reform is technical: it does not change the inflation target or the MPC’s policy stance.
System | How the policy rate is enforced | Weakness
Scarce reserves (mid-corridor) – SA’s old system, 1998–2022 | The central bank supplies just enough reserves for the overnight rate to equal the policy rate. End-of-day lending and deposit facilities priced above and below the policy rate form a corridor that caps volatility. | Needs precise daily forecasting and an efficient interbank market. An over- or under-supply sends rates to zero or very high.
Pure floor (ample reserves) | The central bank saturates demand and pays the policy rate on all excess reserves, so no bank lends below it. | Surplus banks park everything at the central bank, so other banks run short and push rates up. The central bank must keep adding reserves (the “ratchet” effect), and its balance sheet keeps growing.
Tiered floor – SA from June 2022 (also Norway, New Zealand) | Ample reserves earn the policy rate, but only up to a quota. Balances above it earn repo − 100 bps. | A compromise: it works with a smaller, more stable supply of reserves than a pure floor while keeping an incentive to lend in the interbank market. The cost is extra complexity.
Why the shortage system no longer suited SA (paper’s reasons):
A structural surplus since the 2000s came from FX-reserve accumulation. COVID-19 made it much larger through the Bond Purchase Programme, NT drawing down its sterilisation deposits, the Loan Guarantee Scheme and foreign-currency inflows.
The draining toolkit was failing. Demand for debentures was minimal and for reverse repos nil, the market was oversaturated with FX swaps, and the SARB held most of the CPD (Corporation for Public Deposits) call funds. Large draining operations distorted markets and cost money.
The interbank market had weakened because of:
the large-exposures framework, which discourages interbank exposures;
tighter risk limits after the sovereign downgrade below investment grade;
different square-off times for small and large banks;
a shift to secured lending.
Banks over-borrowed at repo auctions, so the “zero-surplus” system usually closed the day more than R5bn long. Small banks held most of that surplus and earned only the penal standing-deposit rate.
A floor system is simpler and copes better with shocks and with balance-sheet policies in a crisis.
Transition without expanding the balance sheet: the SARB let its draining liabilities (FX swaps, CPD call deposits, the remaining debentures) mature. They were converted into excess reserves, so the balance sheet did not grow materially.
How quotas are set (four rules)
The SARB sets a liquidity target, the surplus it wants banks to hold. It mirrors the old “shortage target”: a positive amount deposited with the SARB rather than a negative amount borrowed from it.
A shock buffer of R10bn is added. It absorbs over 99% of daily swings in notes and coin, cash reserve requirements and CPD funds, so the SARB need not fine-tune every day.
The total (e.g. R50bn + R10bn = R60bn) is split by each bank’s share of total liabilities. The share uses the average of the last three months’ BA 900 returns and is updated about every six months.
Each quota is rounded up:
Large banks (≥ 10% of liabilities): to the nearest R1bn.
Medium banks (0.2%–10%): to the nearest R500m.
Small banks (< 0.2%): to the nearest R200m.
Inactive banks get no quota.
Rounding up gives small banks relatively generous quotas, which eases their liquidity management. It also makes total quotas larger than the actual supply of reserves, so there is always quota space somewhere for a long bank’s surplus. A new bank gets the minimum quota for its group at once (R200m small, R500m medium, R1bn large).
Example from the paper’s appendix (April 2022 data, R50bn target + R10bn buffer): Standard Bank (24.4% of liabilities) R15bn; FirstRand (21.6%) R13bn; Absa (20.7%) R13bn; Nedbank (16.6%) R10bn; Investec (7.7%) R5bn; Capitec (2.3%) R1.5bn. With a R100bn target, Standard Bank’s quota is R27bn. Quotas are published on the SARB website.
Repo auctions: fixed rate and fixed allotment, not full allotment. The consultation paper proposed unlimited (full-allotment) repos at the policy rate, but this was rejected:
The SARB would become a lender of first rather than last resort.
Banks could overfund and push others (especially small banks) into the penal standing deposit facility.
Short banks would borrow from the SARB instead of from surplus banks, which undermines the quotas.
The SARB therefore announces a capped weekly amount, which leaves the shock buffer intact. Bidding is optional, and oversubscribed auctions are pro-rated. Fixing both price and quantity is unusual internationally; the SARB kept the old format to limit the number of changes at once.
Standing facilities kept at ±100 bps: 100 bps is a meaningful penalty, and a smaller spread could make the quotas ineffective. Keeping the familiar width was also the simplest option.
Supplementary auctions are only for tail shocks. They are used when system liquidity is more than R10bn away from the target, never to fix banks’ own over- or under-bidding. Example: target R50bn, actual R61bn → a R1bn supplementary reverse repo drains the excess. Actual R39bn → a R1bn supplementary repo. They expire the next business day.
Transmission:
The policy rate is the return on the safest, most liquid rand asset (an overnight deposit at the SARB), and it pins down the short end of the yield curve.
Arbitrage links other rates to it. Banks holding excess reserves sell reserves to buy assets that are cheap relative to the policy rate, or sell assets that are dear, until prices line up.
The SARB monitors a range of rates (a “pluralist” approach, including the new reference rates such as ZARONIA) rather than only the unsecured ZARIBOR, because interbank lending may become mostly secured.
Managing demand for reserves over time:
At the start, about R100bn of extra liquidity (against required reserves of about R125bn) was expected to saturate demand.
Quotas dampen demand passively. In Norway (quotas from 2011), demand fell from about NOK60bn to NOK33bn. In New Zealand (tiers from 2007), demand settled at about NZD7.5bn, until COVID-era QE brought back a pure floor.
Where more liquidity is needed, it comes through repo auctions, not bond purchases. Repos are roughly cost-neutral (lent at repo, deposits paid at or below repo) and easy to withdraw, because they mature weekly.
Routine bond buying could look like monetising government debt and damage credibility. The SARB buys bonds only for financial-stability reasons when markets are dysfunctional.
The old draining tools (long-term reverse repos, debentures, bilateral buy/sell-backs, outright bond sales) were discontinued, though they can be reintroduced.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.10 SARB repo mechanics
x:
What is a repo?
A repurchase agreement (repo) is short-term borrowing secured by government securities. The bank sells the security to the SARB for reserves and agrees to buy it back at a slightly higher price after a few days. Legally a sale and repurchase; economically a collateralised loan. The price difference is the repo interest – the SARB’s income.
Why structure it as a sale? Ownership passes to the lender, so if the bank cannot repay, the SARB already owns the security and can sell it immediately without a legal process to seize collateral. That makes repos cheap, quick and low-risk.
Collateral: typically Treasury bills (government paper of up to 12 months, issued at a discount and repaid at face value) and government bonds – liquid, with a market price and very low credit risk.
Repo or reverse repo? It depends on perspective. For the party selling the security and agreeing to repurchase it (the bank needing liquidity) it is a repo; for the party buying it and agreeing to sell it back (the SARB, providing cash) it is a reverse repo. Same transaction, named from each side – a classic MCQ trap.
Banks still use repos for secured lending among themselves: a bank with spare reserves earns a secured return; a short bank borrows cheaply because the lender’s risk is covered.
The haircut (market value adjustment)
Credit risk is the risk that the bank does not repay; market risk is the risk that the collateral’s price falls before it can be sold (e.g. bond yields spike). If the SARB lent 100% of the collateral’s value, a price fall would leave the loan under-secured.
The haircut is a safety margin: the SARB lends less than the market value of the collateral. It divides market value by a haircut (adjustment) factor; a factor of 1.01 means the collateral must be worth 1% more than the amount owed.
Why longer-maturity instruments have larger factors: longer-maturity bonds have a longer duration, so their prices are more sensitive to interest-rate movements and can fall further during the few days the loan is outstanding. A larger haircut is needed to keep the loan covered. (Example factor table: bonds > 10 years 1.035; bonds 1–10 years 1.025; Treasury bills and short instruments 1.010.)
Adjusted (haircut) value = (Market value of security)/(Haircut factor) ≥ Repo price = X × (1 + interest factor)
Maximum liquidity X=(Adjusted value)/(1+interest factor) where interest factor = ( (annual rate)/(12) ) × ( (days)/(30) )
Interest earned by the SARB = Adjusted value − X Daily accrual = (Interest)/(days)
Method: (1) pick the haircut factor from the residual maturity of the security (years left until it matures, e.g. a bond maturing in 2030 used in 2023 has 7 years left); (2) divide market value by the factor; (3) compute the interest factor for the holding period; (4) divide to find X, the maximum cash the bank can raise; (5) interest = adjusted value − X. The logic: the most the SARB will pay today is the amount which, grown at the repo rate over the period, exactly equals the haircut value of the collateral.
Worked example – maximum repo liquidity and SARB interest
Repo rate 8.25% NACM (nominal annual, compounded monthly); collateral = Treasury bill of R10 000 000; haircut factor 1.01; holding period 5 days. How much liquidity (X) can the bank raise, and how much does the SARB earn?
NACM: the monthly rate is (8.25%)/(12) = 0.6875%. A month is taken as 30 days, so 5 days is 5/30 of a month and the interest factor for 5 days is 1 + 0.006875 × 5/30.
Step | Amount (R)
1. Value after haircut: (10 000 000)/(1.01) | 9 900 990.10
2. Interest factor: 1 + ( (0.0825)/(12) ) × ( (5)/(30) ) = 1 + 0.006875 × 0.166667 | 1.001145833
3. X = (9 900 990.10)/(1.001145833) (maximum cash raised) | 9 889 658.20
4. Total interest earned by the SARB: 9 900 990.10 − 9 889 658.20 | 11 331.90
5. Daily accrual: (11 331.90)/(5) | 2 266.38
Answer. The bank can raise at most R9 889 658.20 for 5 days against the R10m Treasury bill. The R110 341.80 gap between face value and cash raised is the haircut cushion (R99 009.90, ≈ 1%) plus the interest (R11 331.90). The SARB earns R11 331.90, i.e. R2 266.38 a day – small relative to the amount lent (about 0.11% for 5 days). In 5 days the bank repays R9 900 990.10 and gets its Treasury bill back.
Correct figures: R9 900 990.10 and R9 889 658.20; the slide shows R9 900 990.01 and R9 889 658.11 (digits transposed). The interest (R11 331.90) and daily accrual (R2 266.38) are the same either way.
Journals and T-accounts in the books of the SARB
For the SARB, assets (e.g. repo loans) increase with a debit; liabilities (e.g. banks’ deposits) increase with a credit. The entries show that the SARB creates money: the bank’s account is credited with new reserves at the start, and those reserves are destroyed at maturity.
Day 0: Dr Accommodation to banks (asset ↑) R9 889 658.20; Cr Deposits – bank current account (liability ↑) R9 889 658.20. The SARB creates reserves electronically: a new claim on the bank and a new debt to the bank.
Days 1–5 (daily): Dr Accommodation to banks R2 266.38; Cr Interest received (income statement) R2 266.38. Interest accrues daily: the loan balance grows and income is recognised over time.
Day 5 (maturity): Dr Deposits – bank current account R9 900 990.10; Cr Accommodation to banks R9 900 990.10. The bank repays principal plus interest (R9 889 658.20 + R11 331.90) from its reserves; the loan is cleared and the reserves created on Day 0 disappear.
