h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.11 Implications for banks’ cash holdings
x:
Before 2022: reserves above the minimum earned nothing, so banks held only the minimum and lent or invested any excess. Physical cash (also earning nothing) and reserves were almost interchangeable.
Now: surplus reserves earn the SPR while vault cash still earns 0%, so banks prefer reserves over physical cash. Holding notes and coin has an opportunity cost, so banks minimise cash in ATMs and branches. (The Fed likewise pays interest on reserves.)
Example: at a 7% policy rate, R1bn of banknotes in ATMs and vaults costs R70m a year in forgone interest (R1bn × 7%) compared with leaving the same value in the reserve account. Before 2022 the alternative earned 0%, so the cost was nil. Banks therefore economise on cash: fewer, fuller-service ATMs, optimised cash-in-transit and more encouragement of digital payments (cash is also costly to store, insure and transport).
Even without regulation, bank management wants a liquidity buffer at the SARB to meet withdrawals and settle payments, avoiding the cost of emergency funding or a run. But required reserves earn nothing, so holding more of them lowers profitability.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.12 Policy developments
x:
Phasing out the prime rate. The SARB plans to phase out prime (historically policy rate + 3.5%) so loans and mortgages price directly off the SPR (e.g. SPR + 2%). Prime is a historical convention layered on top of the policy rate; removing it makes pricing more transparent and the link from policy to loan rates more direct.
JIBAR to ZARONIA. JIBAR (Johannesburg Interbank Average Rate) is to be discontinued on 31 December 2026 and replaced by ZARONIA (South African Rand Overnight Index Average). JIBAR is quote-based – banks submit estimates of what they could borrow at, with few actual trades – so it can be manipulated (as in the LIBOR scandal, where banks rigged submissions, prompting the global move away from such rates). ZARONIA is built from actual overnight wholesale transactions, so it is harder to manipulate and more robust. All floating-rate loans, bonds and derivatives priced off JIBAR must move to the new rate.
New inflation target. A move from the 3%–6% range to a 3% point target ± 1 percentage point was announced in November 2025. If the public believes inflation will be around 3% rather than 4.5%, wage and price setting adjusts, inflation expectations fall, and interest rates (which include an inflation premium) can be structurally lower, supporting borrowing and growth.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 1 – Money, banks and the central bank > 1.13 The Gold and Foreign Exchange Contingency Reserve Account (GFECRA)
x:
The SARB holds the country’s foreign-exchange reserves (dollars, euros etc., mainly in foreign bonds and deposits) and gold. They are priced in foreign currency, but the SARB reports in rand. When the rand depreciates, each dollar is worth more rand, so the rand value of the reserves rises; when the rand strengthens, it falls. These are unrealised valuation gains or losses – nothing has been sold and no cash received.
The gains belong to National Treasury (the reserves are the nation’s, and exchange-rate profits and losses are for the government’s account) but are held on the SARB’s balance sheet in the GFECRA. The balance reached about 3% of GDP in 2024. Losses (when the rand appreciates) are charged against it.
The question: why should Treasury borrow at high interest rates if it could simply use this balance?
Settlement: R100 billion was paid to National Treasury to reduce expensive government borrowing; R25 billion went to the SARB’s contingency reserves, and the remaining balance stays in the GFECRA as a buffer.
The R100bn payment to Treasury is the firm figure; a “R150 billion distributed” total also circulates but does not reconcile with R100bn + R25bn plus a retained balance.
Model answer: why borrow if the GFECRA balance could simply be spent?
The case for using it. Government borrows by issuing bonds at high rates, and debt costs are among the largest items in the budget. A large balance owed to Treasury by the SARB earns Treasury little. Using R100bn to repay or avoid debt saves interest every year – borrowing while holding the balance is like paying credit-card interest while leaving a deposit untouched.
Why it is not that simple. (1) The gains are unrealised and not cash: they exist because the rand fell. To pay Treasury, the SARB must create money or sell assets, which adds liquidity to the banking system that may need to be sterilised. (2) Reversibility: if the rand strengthens, the gains shrink or become losses charged against the account. (3) The SARB’s own capital: the buffer protects the SARB against future losses; paying everything out would leave it exposed – hence the contingency reserve and retained balance.
Conclusion. A moderate, agreed settlement (R100bn to Treasury) captures most of the benefit – lower debt and interest – while keeping a buffer and respecting the SARB’s independence.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 2 – Why banks are special and must be regulated
x: All bank regulation questions are answered from the regulator’s perspective: the point of view of the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) and its Prudential Authority (PA), the unit inside the SARB that licenses and supervises banks. The regulator asks “what could go wrong for the public and the financial system, and what would a rule to prevent it cost society?”, not “how does this bank maximise profit?”.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 2 – Why banks are special and must be regulated > 2.1 Why banks are different from other firms
x:
“Because they can fail” is not a sufficient reason to regulate banks: retailers and airlines also fail, yet nobody imposes licensing, capital rules and daily supervision on them. Banks are different because that is where the money is: banks are the machinery through which the economy’s money is created, stored and moved, and they finance most of their assets with other people’s money.
What banks do that no other firm does
Function | What it means | Why a failure hurts everyone
Money creation | When a bank grants a loan it credits the borrower’s account with a new deposit, and that deposit is money. Most of broad money (M3 = notes and coin + all bank deposits) is created this way, not printed by the central bank. Example: a R2 million home loan creates R2 million of new money. | A failure destroys money (deposits) and cuts the flow of new credit.
Safe storage of wealth | Households and firms keep their savings and working cash in banks. | A failure wipes out or freezes public savings.
Payment system (transfer of wealth) | Almost every payment (salaries, rent, card purchases, EFTs, supplier invoices) is settled by debiting one bank account and crediting another. | If a large bank cannot process entries, wages, groceries and taxes cannot be paid. The payment system is a public good.
Credit allocation | Banks decide who gets a loan and so which projects are funded. | Whoever controls lending influences the money supply, inflation, asset prices and the business cycle.
Economies of scale in information (delegated monitoring) | Banks screen and monitor borrowers on behalf of many small savers, who could never do it themselves (see 2.4). | The information and relationships are lost when a bank fails, and borrowers lose their source of credit.
Economies of scale in transaction costs | Banks process deposits, loans and payments at a far lower cost per unit than individuals could. | –
Maturity transformation | Short-term deposits fund long-term loans (borrow short, lend long). | Makes banks vulnerable to runs (see 2.8).
Liquidity transformation | Depositors have instant access to their money while the loans that use it are illiquid (cannot be sold quickly). | No bank can repay all depositors at once.
Credit (risk) transformation | A large, diversified loan book is safer than any single loan, so the depositor holds a claim on a safer pool than the risky loans behind it. | –
In short, a bank pools funds from many depositors, does the information processing (assessing creditworthiness more cheaply than each depositor could) and performs financial intermediation (channelling the pooled funds to borrowers). This is indirect finance: the saver lends to the bank, not directly to the borrower. Banks reduce risk and information asymmetry; they never eliminate them.
About 90% or more of a bank’s funding is other people’s money (deposits and debt), against roughly 20%–50% for a typical industrial firm.
Because of these functions banks behave like public utilities: essential services that the whole economy depends on, provided by privately owned firms under heavy state control.
Bank failure also matters to non-bank firms
A company’s treasury manager (the person who looks after its cash, funding and bank relationships) must understand bank failure, because a bank deposit is in effect an unsecured loan to the bank.
Case – MultiChoice/Naspers in Nigeria. MultiChoice (the DStv pay-TV group, then controlled by Naspers) held about US$21 million at a Nigerian bank that failed and was liquidated by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC), Nigeria’s deposit insurer and liquidator of failed banks. MultiChoice wrote the amount off as a “$21m receivable”.
Why deposit insurance did not help: (1) the insured cap per depositor is tiny relative to US$21 million; (2) deposit-insurance schemes are designed for small retail depositors, not for large corporates, financial institutions and treasury deposits, which are expected to assess counterparty risk themselves; (3) covering big depositors would need taxpayer money and would remove market discipline (moral hazard).
Lessons for a treasurer: set limits per bank by credit rating and capital strength, spread cash across sound banks, keep deposits short-term, and never assume that the state or deposit insurance will cover large balances. In liquidation unsecured depositors above the insured limit rank as ordinary creditors and often recover only a fraction, years later. Losing such a deposit is a governance and treasury-policy failure, not just bad luck.
Knowledge of banking also helps a non-bank employer negotiate finance: knowing how banks price loans (cost of funds, risk premium, expected credit loss, collateral; see 2.9) lets the firm present a stronger credit case and obtain lower rates.
Exam focus: 2019 Q4.1 (what makes banks different and important enough to need special regulation – one mark per function); 2026 mid-term MCQ 1.4 (pooling, information processing, intermediation); 2023 Q5.4 (using banking knowledge for a non-bank employer).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 2 – Why banks are special and must be regulated > 2.2 Why banks must be regulated
x:
There are three reasons. They are often grouped as two categories – (1) systemic importance and externalities, which covers both the function and the vulnerability, and (2) conflicts of interest – but the full answer names all three.
Banks fulfil an important function (payments, money creation, credit allocation, safe storage; see 2.1). A failure imposes externalities: costs on third parties who had no part in the bank’s decisions (other banks, firms that cannot pay wages, households locked out of their savings, taxpayers). Because the bank’s owners do not bear these costs, they ignore them when choosing how much risk to run, so the state must take them into account for them.
Banks are inherently vulnerable. Maturity and liquidity transformation mean that a loss of confidence, even a baseless rumour, can cause a bank run that brings down a sound bank. Banks are interconnected (interbank loans, shared payment systems, similar assets), so one failure spreads to others as contagion. They are also highly leveraged (equity only about 4%–10% of assets), so a small fall in asset values wipes out the equity.
Banking is rife with conflicts of interest. Depositors, shareholders and managers want opposite things from the same balance sheet (see 2.3). Depositors cannot monitor the bank (information asymmetry), shareholders gain from gambles whose losses fall on depositors and taxpayers, and the normal corporate-governance tools do not work in banks (see 2.4–2.5).
Model answer: why must banks be regulated?
Function. Banks run the payment system, allocate savings to borrowers and create most of the money supply. These functions are public-utility-like, so a failure damages third parties (businesses that cannot pay wages, households that cannot reach their savings, other banks exposed to the failed one). That damage is an externality the owners do not bear, so left alone banks take more risk than is good for society.
Vulnerability. Banks borrow short (demand deposits) and lend long (20-year mortgages), so they can never repay all depositors at once; a loss of confidence causes a run. Interconnection spreads one failure to others (contagion). Equity of only 4%–10% of assets means a small fall in asset values makes the bank insolvent.
Conflicts of interest. Depositors want safety and liquidity; shareholders and managers want a high ROE, achieved through high leverage and risky lending. Depositors cannot monitor the bank, deposits are designed to be insensitive to the bank’s credit quality (so there is no market discipline), and shareholders put up only a sliver of the funding, so they gain from gambles whose losses fall on depositors and taxpayers. Disclosure, audit and bonuses do not fix this.
Conclusion: because neither depositors nor shareholders can discipline the bank, and failure imposes large costs on society, the state regulates: it sets minimum capital and liquidity, supervises lending, approves directors and, through deposit insurance and the central bank as lender of last resort, backstops the system. Regulation is a balance between safety and credit affordability.
The central trade-off: safety versus affordable credit
A regulator can make bank failure virtually impossible: force banks to hold, say, 30% capital and 20% cash, and almost no realistic loss or run could sink them.
But capital is the most expensive funding a bank has (shareholders demand a high return because they take the first loss and are paid last), while deposits are cheap. Cash earns nothing. So more capital and more cash raise the bank’s cost of funds and cut its earning assets. To still earn its target ROE the bank must charge higher loan rates or lend less (see 2.9).
Loans then become so expensive that households and firms cannot borrow to buy homes, start businesses or study; investment and growth fall, and borrowing moves to less-regulated lenders (loan sharks, shadow banks).
Therefore regulators aim for a failure probability that is low enough, not zero, and adjust the rules after each crisis as society learns what failures cost versus what credit costs. Too little capital: frequent, costly crises. Too much capital: credit that nobody can afford.
Model answer: can banks be regulated so that they never fail? Yes in principle – very high capital removes insolvency risk and very high liquid assets remove illiquidity risk – but not for free. Capital is the dearest source of funding and liquid assets earn little, so the bank’s cost of funds rises and it must charge higher loan rates or lend less. Credit becomes unaffordable, growth falls and borrowing moves to unregulated lenders. Safety and cheap credit pull in opposite directions, so regulation is a trade-off chosen by society, aimed at a low, not a zero, probability of failure.
Exam focus: essay-type questions on why banks are regulated are answered from the regulator’s perspective using function, vulnerability and conflicts of interest.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 2 – Why banks are special and must be regulated > 2.3 What each stakeholder wants
x:
What depositors want
The depositor is anyone whose salary is paid into a bank or whose savings are held there. The whole system is funded with deposits, so the depositor is the most important person in banking: ultimately it is their money at risk. Depositors want three things:
Liquidity – the bank has enough cash and easily sold assets (such as government bonds) to repay a deposit the moment it is demanded (“I’m at the ATM, I want my money”). A bank that is solvent on paper but cannot pay today has still failed the depositor.
Prudent lending – the bank lends only to borrowers who will repay (prudent credit underwriting), so it stays solvent. A bank is solvent when its assets are worth more than its liabilities (positive equity); bad loans reduce asset values and enough of them make the bank insolvent.
Capital resilience – an adequate equity buffer so that an unforeseen shock (recession, pandemic, commodity-price collapse) does not make the bank fail. Equity is the owners’ own money in the bank; losses are deducted from it first, so the thicker it is, the more losses can be absorbed before depositors are touched.
Depositors want to avoid both loss and inconvenience. When Saambou failed in 2002 depositors did not lose their principal, but the bank was placed under curatorship (an independent curator appointed to run the bank and protect depositors) and their money was trapped for about six months. For a household that needs rent or school fees, being locked out is serious harm even if the money returns later.
In sum depositors want safety, liquid availability and stability. They are paid a fixed interest rate whatever the bank earns, so they get nothing extra when the bank takes more risk.
What management and shareholders want
Management (and the shareholders who appoint and reward them) want to maximise return on equity (ROE), because bonuses, share options and dividends all rise with ROE.
Because ROE = ROA × leverage (see 2.7), the cheapest way to raise ROE is to hold as little equity as possible (fund assets with deposits and debt), to hold as little cash as possible (cash earns nothing) and to make higher-yielding, riskier loans.
Shareholders are paid for risk-taking; depositors are not. The two groups therefore want opposite things from the same balance sheet.
Model answer: what does bank management want, and how does it differ from what the depositor wants? Management and shareholders want to maximise ROE, because their bonuses, options and dividends rise with it. Since ROE = ROA × leverage, the cheapest route is minimum equity, maximum leverage and higher-yielding (riskier) loans. The depositor wants the opposite: more equity, less leverage, less risky loans and more liquid assets. The depositor cannot control management because of information asymmetry, so the regulator acts on the depositor’s behalf.
Society wants two conflicting things
Party | What they want
Bank shareholders and managers | Minimum capital and liquidity, to maximise leverage, ROE and bonuses.
Society as depositors | High capital and liquidity, so that the probability of failure is as low as possible.
Society as borrowers | Low interest rates and accessible credit.
The same person is both a depositor (wanting a safe bank) and a borrower (wanting cheap loans). That is why the optimum is a compromise, and why there is no single “correct” capital ratio – only one that society judges acceptable. Managers push for minimum capital because they are paid on ROE while the cost of failure falls largely on others (limited liability, deposit insurance, bail-outs); regulation exists to push the cost of risk back onto the bank.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 2 – Why banks are special and must be regulated > 2.4 Information asymmetry and the agency problem
x:
Information asymmetry: why banks exist
Information asymmetry means one party to a transaction knows more than the other. It is the economic reason banks exist.
Depositor (principal)
↕
Bank (managers = agents; delegated monitoring)
↕
Borrower (knows own creditworthiness)
A saver lending directly could never judge a borrower’s true creditworthiness, income and intentions, and would spend a fortune checking and chasing them. The borrower knows far more and has an incentive to look better than he is, so savers would not lend directly to strangers.
The bank solves this with delegated monitoring: thousands of depositors delegate the job of screening and policing borrowers to the bank, which uses scale (specialist credit analysts whose cost is spread over millions of loans), credit-scoring models and experience. Example: instead of every Capitec saver judging each borrower, Capitec’s models score each applicant and the bank bears the credit risk.
A large loan book also gives diversification: the defaults of a few borrowers are offset by the repayments of the rest, so losses from idiosyncratic risk (risk specific to one borrower, such as a retrenchment) become predictable. Diversification cannot remove systemic risk (a recession that hits all borrowers at once).
The second agency problem: who monitors the monitor?
Putting the bank in the middle creates a new problem: depositors now cannot see the borrowers and cannot see how safe the bank’s loan book is. The managers know the true state of the book; the depositors do not.
An agency problem is a conflict that arises when people entrusted to look after others’ interests (the agents) use the authority given to them for their own benefit instead of for the principals. In banking the principals are depositors (and shareholders) and the agents are the managers. Managers’ pay is tied to ROE, so they have an incentive to take risks that boost short-term profit and bonuses while the downside falls on others.
Depositors must therefore trust the bank, or the regulator must check on their behalf. This is a core reason for regulation.
Agency theory with three stakeholders: competition and cooperation
Traditional agency theory (any firm). Shareholders are treated as the owners and the firm should be run for them. Managers (agents) look after themselves first, so shareholders and managers compete over perks, effort and risk. Bonuses and share options tied to profit or share price align management with shareholders, and the two then cooperate to maximise equity returns.
Banking changes the picture. Shareholders fund only about 4%–10% of a bank; depositors fund most of it. Limited liability (shareholders can lose at most what they invested) caps the shareholders’ loss. Once managers are aligned with shareholders, the two have an incentive to cooperate against depositors: they gamble with depositors’ money.
Asymmetric pay-off (risk-shifting). If the gamble pays off, shareholders and managers keep the gain (dividends, bonuses, a higher share price). If it fails, the loss beyond the thin equity layer falls on depositors and, through deposit insurance and bail-outs, on society. This is moral hazard (taking more risk because someone else bears the cost) and risk-shifting (moving risk from shareholders to creditors).
Result. Depositors are the group that competes with the other two and are the least able to protect themselves. That is the reason for regulation: capital requirements, supervision and deposit insurance.
Example: the asymmetric pay-off
A bank has R100 of assets funded by R5 of equity and R95 of deposits. It makes a risky bet:
The assets gain 10% (R10): equity rises from R5 to R15 – the shareholders treble their money.
The assets lose 10% (R10): equity of R5 is wiped out and the next R5 of loss lands on depositors (or the deposit insurer or taxpayer). Shareholders never have to repay it.
Shareholders keep all the upside but bear only R5 of the downside, so they favour the bet even when it is bad for depositors and society.
Three layers of agency conflict in a bank
Shareholders versus management – the traditional conflict found in every firm.
Shareholders versus depositors/debtholders – amplified by 90%+ debt funding and by deposit insurance: limited liability shifts the downside to creditors, and insured depositors do not even bother to monitor the bank.
Bank shareholders versus society/taxpayers – failure costs fall on deposit-insurance funds, taxpayers and the real economy.
The standard corporate-governance model (“maximise shareholder value”) addresses only layer 1, which is why it is the wrong model for banks.
Exam focus: 2019 Q4.3 (use agency theory to explain how management, shareholders and depositors compete and cooperate – 5 marks).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 2 – Why banks are special and must be regulated > 2.5 Why the normal corporate-governance fixes fail in banks
x:
In a non-financial firm the manager–shareholder conflict is eased by (1) financial disclosure, (2) independent audits and (3) performance-based pay (bonuses and options tied to profit or share price). In a bank each of these breaks down or backfires.
Optimal opaqueness – full disclosure is not desirable. A bank deposit is money, and money must be insensitive to credit events by legal fiat: R100 in your account must always be worth R100, whatever happens to the bank’s loans. That fixed value is what lets deposits be used for payments. If a bank disclosed the quality of its loan book in full and in real time, depositors would keep revaluing their deposits and a minor impairment could trigger a run. Contrast a large, diversified, trusted bank (Standard Bank) with one that collapsed after heavy unsecured lending (African Bank, 2014). Some opaqueness is therefore deliberate, which also means depositors cannot discipline the bank.
Shareholders have little skin in the game. “Skin in the game” means having your own money at risk. Shareholders fund roughly 50%–80% of an industrial firm but only about 4%–10% of a large bank; depositors and debtholders fund 90%–96%. With limited liability shareholders keep the upside and bear little of the downside, so they encourage speculative, high-yield bets. Aligning managers with shareholders (through bonuses) therefore does not protect depositors – it aligns both against them.
No market discipline from depositors. Depositors have no information (opaqueness) and little reason to care (deposits are fixed in value and often insured), so they do not punish risky banks by moving their money. Shareholder discipline, in turn, promotes risk-shifting.
Conclusion: neither depositors nor shareholders can discipline the bank, so the state must step in.
Case: Credit Suisse – shareholder primacy fails in banking
After shareholder activism, Credit Suisse removed capital-adequacy targets (CET1, Common Equity Tier 1: the highest-quality capital, essentially ordinary shares and retained earnings) from management bonuses, to make management more responsive to shareholders. This led to risk-shifting and serial scandals – Archegos (a family-office fund whose collapse cost the bank about US$5 billion) and Greensill (a supply-chain financier whose collapse froze billions of client funds) – and to the bank’s collapse in 2023, when the Swiss authorities forced its takeover by UBS. Lesson: making bank management answer more strongly to shareholders is dangerous, because shareholder interests are not aligned with those of depositors and society.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 2 – Why banks are special and must be regulated > 2.6 Do shareholders own the bank?
x:
Company law calls shareholders the owners of a company, and corporate finance tells managers to maximise shareholder wealth. For banks this shortcut fails.
Shareholders own shares, not the company. A share is a bundle of specific statutory rights: to vote at the annual general meeting (AGM), to receive a dividend once it has been declared, and to share in what is left on liquidation. It does not give ownership of the bank’s assets. Agency theory treats these rights as ownership, but that is only a thinking shortcut, especially for minority shareholders.
Bank shareholders’ rights are even weaker, because the regulator:
signs off appointments of executive directors and board chairs (the fit and proper test: honesty and integrity, competence and experience, financial soundness) and can veto a CEO or chair;
can restrict or prohibit dividends when capital buffers are inadequate (in 2020, during COVID-19, the SARB asked banks to hold back dividends to preserve capital for losses and lending);
sets binding constraints on capital structure, leverage, reserve and liquidity holdings and loan-underwriting standards, and inspects the credit quality of loans;
receives daily and monthly regulatory returns (the monthly BA900 balance-sheet return), so the state sees the bank’s position in more detail than most owners.
Why: about 90% of the bank is funded by the public, and its payment and credit services are essential to the economy. Failure imposes losses on third parties, so society takes a share of control in return for the protection it provides (deposit insurance, lender of last resort). The rights of other stakeholders (depositors, society) therefore weigh more in banking than in other firms.
Conclusion: a bank is best seen as a public utility with private equity participation: owners supply capital and receive returns, but the regulator controls the essential decisions. Regulation “waters down” shareholder autonomy – a form of partial nationalisation: the state does not own the bank but limits what the owners may do, because the bank’s decisions have public consequences.
Case: the Absa chair dispute (2021)
Absa’s lead independent director, Sipho Pityana, took the Prudential Authority to court, claiming that his nomination as board chair had been unfairly blocked. Points the case illustrates:
Bank management (and the board) is not fully in control of the bank: the regulator must approve directors.
A lead independent director does not automatically become chair; the board nominates and, in a bank, the regulator must approve.
Banks are extremely sensitive to rumours and must guard their reputation.
The regulator’s veto is a statutory power that must be exercised under the rule of law: predictably, on criteria known in advance, and open to challenge in court. The “common good” does not automatically override individual rights; otherwise a regulator could block appointments for political reasons.
How a bank shareholder protects himself
Bank shareholders have little “voice”: a vote at the AGM cannot change the bank’s risks, the regulator protects depositors and the system (not shareholders), and no court can force a dividend (a dividend is owed only once declared, and the regulator can block it). The primary protection is therefore exit: sell the shares and invest elsewhere (or diversify).
Model answer: why do the shareholders of a bank not own the bank?
Shareholders do not own the firm; they own shares, which give specific rights such as a dividend once declared and a vote at the AGM.
Agency theory treats these rights as ownership, but they are not equivalent to ownership rights, especially for minority shareholders.
Bank shareholders’ rights are weaker still because banks are tightly regulated: the regulator approves directors and the CEO, can restrict dividends and sets binding capital, leverage and liquidity limits.
Consequently the rights of other stakeholders (depositors, society) matter more in banking, leaving shareholders with less than ownership. A bank is better seen as a public utility, funded about 90% by the public.
Exam focus: 2020 Q4(b) (why shareholders do not own the bank – 4 marks); 2021 MCQs on the Absa chair dispute and on how bank investors protect themselves (exit).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 2 – Why banks are special and must be regulated > 2.7 Return on equity, leverage and the conflict over ROE
x:
Simplified DuPont decomposition
Three measures are needed:
ROA (return on assets) = (net profit after tax)/(total assets) : how profitable the assets are.
Leverage (equity multiplier) = (total assets)/(equity) : how many rands of assets the bank controls per rand of its own equity.
ROE (return on equity) = (net profit after tax)/(equity) : what shareholders earn on their own money.
ROE = Leverage × ROA = ( (Assets)/(Equity) ) × ( (Net profit after tax)/(Assets) )Capital ratio = (Equity)/(Assets ) ;⇒ Leverage = (1)/(Capital ratio ) ;⇒ ROE = (ROA)/(Capital ratio)
The assets cancel, leaving ROE = (profit)/(equity) ; the split shows where ROE comes from: how profitable the assets are, and how thinly equity is spread over them. (This two-factor version isolates the link between capital adequacy and ROE; the multi-factor DuPont, which also splits margin, asset turnover, cost efficiency and tax, belongs to bank financial analysis.)
Note that exam questions sometimes call (equity)/(assets) the “leverage ratio” (e.g. “a leverage ratio of 10%”): this means a capital ratio of 10%, i.e. an equity multiplier of 10.
Key principle: holding ROA constant, management can raise ROE simply by reducing equity. Example: ROA 1%. With 10% equity (leverage 10×) ROE = 10%; with 5% equity (leverage 20×) ROE = 20%. The bank is no more profitable – it is just twice as fragile. If bonuses are tied to ROE, managers are rewarded for making the bank more fragile.
Worked example: Standard Bank 2021 (R million)
Given | R million
Total assets (loans and advances ≈ R1.2 trillion) | 1 725 074
Total liabilities ≈ R1.6 trillion (deposits ≈ R1.4 trillion)
Total equity | 118 968
Net profit after tax (NPAT) | 14 547
Step | Calculation | Answer
1. Capital ratio | (118 968)/(1 725 074) | 6.9%
2. Leverage | (1)/(0.069) | 14.5×
3. ROA | (14 547)/(1 725 074) | 0.84%
4. ROE | 0.84% × 14.5 | 12.2%
Correct figure: about 12.2% ( (14 547)/(118 968) = 12.23%; 0.84% × 14.5 = 12.18%); the source report shows 12.3%.
Only R6.90 of every R100 of assets belongs to the owners; the other 93.1% is funded by depositors and debtholders. A 6.9% fall in asset values (e.g. from loan defaults) would wipe out all equity.
An ROA of 0.84% is tiny compared with industrial firms (often 20%+). Banking is a low-margin, high-volume business: the bank earns a thin spread on each rand and needs a balance sheet many times its equity to produce an ROE shareholders accept.
Comparison: Kenya’s KCB earns a much higher ROA (about 3%) at much lower leverage, for a similar ROE (about 15%–20%), because Kenyan interest rates are high and competition is weaker. South African banks are more leveraged than Kenyan banks but less than European and US banks, which ran leverage of 20×–30× before 2008.
Where a high ROE comes from
A high ROE alone does not prove that customers are being abused. It can come from three sources, and the regulator’s response differs for each:
Source | Mechanism | Regulator’s view
Pricing power | Little competition lets the bank charge high loan rates and fees and pay low deposit rates. | Customers are exploited: competition policy, fee caps, entry of new banks.
High leverage | Thin capital multiplies profit per rand of equity. | Not exploitation, but fragile; risk shifted to depositors and taxpayers: minimum capital rules.
Operational efficiency | The same business done at lower cost (e.g. Capitec’s cheaper IT and branch model; the older big banks still run 1970s mainframe systems under modern front ends, while a new bank can run on the cloud). | The healthy source: more profit without higher prices or more risk.
To judge a bank reporting an ROE of 30%–35% (as some Tanzanian banks have), decompose ROE into its margin, cost and leverage components (net interest margin, cost-to-income ratio, (equity)/(assets) ) and compare with peers.
The conflict over ROE
Management and shareholders want a high ROE (about 20%–25% in South Africa, e.g. FNB), because it brings bonuses and dividends. The quickest route is minimum equity and maximum leverage.
Depositors and the regulator want high capital and low leverage, even though ROE then falls to about 10%–12%, because a bigger equity buffer absorbs losses before depositors are hit.
Why ROE targets push banks to low equity: equity is the bank’s most expensive funding (shareholders demand a high return because they bear the first loss and are paid last; deposits are cheap because they are safe and often insured). For a given ROA, every rand of equity replaced by deposits raises ROE. Rand profit actually falls slightly (deposits carry interest, equity does not), but ROE rises because the smaller profit is spread over much less equity.
Systemic risk from ROE targeting: every bank chases the same ROE benchmark, so they all thin their capital and hold similar assets at the same time. One shock then hits many banks at once. Systemic risk is the risk that one failure, or a weakness shared by many institutions, spreads through the financial system and damages the whole economy.
Trade-off: larger capital buffers make banks safer but raise their cost of funds, so they charge higher loan rates and credit becomes dearer and scarcer (see 2.2 and 2.9).
Capitec case – choice of pay metric: Capitec benchmarked executive bonuses mainly on earnings per share (EPS) growth rather than ROE. Advantage: managers cannot inflate EPS by shrinking capital. Disadvantage: EPS is an unadjusted accounting measure that rewards rapid credit growth through high-yield, high-risk unsecured loans (no collateral, higher defaults, higher rates). Lesson: any single pay metric will be gamed, so the metric chosen shapes the risk the bank takes.
2019 MCQ (Section A Q6), “likely false” statement: the memo answer is (c) “shareholders prefer a bank with less equity capital”, on the reasoning that shareholders also want a safe, well-capitalised bank. On the ROE logic above, (b) “holding higher reserves implies higher profitability” also reads as false (reserves earn little or nothing); the memo nevertheless gives (c).
Moussu (2018): bank capital and ROE – erroneous beliefs
Bank executives remain fixated on maximising ROE and minimising equity despite post-2008 research showing that the beliefs behind this are wrong.
Industry belief | Evidence
Higher capital requirements lower profitability and constrain credit. | Better-capitalised banks lend more, gain market share, survive crises better and have higher valuations (Berger and Bouwman 2013; Thakor 2014). Any reduction in credit is absent or short-lived: safe banks fund themselves more cheaply and can keep lending when weak banks must cut back.
A high ROE shows long-term shareholder value creation. | Pre-crisis ROE is a risk measure, not a performance measure (Moussu and Petit-Romec). High-ROE banks suffered the greatest value destruction in the crisis and show no risk-adjusted outperformance otherwise: high ROE is mostly leverage and risk-taking.
Allocating capital by ROE aligns divisions with value creation. | Goodhart’s Law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. ROE-based allocation pushes divisions into high-yield, high-risk assets and leverage; the division taking most risk looks best until the risk materialises.
Regulatory arbitrage: exploiting loopholes in the rules to cut capital charges. Example: sovereign bonds carried a zero risk weight (no capital needed), so European banks hoarded Greek government debt before 2011 and suffered huge losses when it was restructured. What looks risk-free to the rulebook is not necessarily safe.
Originate-to-distribute: ROE targets drove securitisation (pooling loans and selling their cash flows to investors as bonds). Banks originated weak (subprime) loans and sold them on to keep capital constant while booking upfront fees. A bank that keeps a loan has an incentive to check the borrower; one that sells it does not (Purnanandam 2011). This was a core cause of the 2008 crisis.
Moussu (2018) – further detail (reading needed for background knowledge)
Why it matters: the 2007–09 crisis cost an estimated $6–14 trillion. Bank failures impose huge negative externalities on society, and the crisis was driven by excessive risk-taking. Risk-taking follows executives’ incentives and beliefs, which have barely changed since 2008.
Banks’ two arguments against higher capital: (1) it lowers profitability and so weakens banks; (2) it cuts lending and slows recovery. The evidence (Berger and Bouwman 2013, covering all US banks 1984–2010) shows the opposite. Higher capital raised market share and survival for small banks at all times, and for medium and large banks during banking crises. Moussu calls the arguments a rhetorical device rather than scientific evidence.
The transition: the best way to raise capital is to cut dividends (retain earnings). That is not a problem if the retained profit funds value-creating projects. Few banks did this voluntarily during the crisis.
Four reasons banks resist higher capital | Explanation
1. Political bargaining | Opposing regulation is part of bargaining between bankers, regulators and politicians (Thakor 2014). Lobbyists repeat the same messages whatever the evidence, even when the regulation is in banks’ own interest.
2. Subsidised debt | Debt is cheaper than equity because interest is tax-deductible and creditors enjoy an implicit or explicit government guarantee (they expect a bail-out). Evening out the tax treatment of debt and equity raises capital levels. Removing the guarantee would require a credible promise never to rescue a bank, which is impossible.
3. Wealth transfer | Extra equity makes the bank safer, so part of the gain goes to creditors (their debt becomes safer) or to taxpayers (lower bail-out risk), not to existing shareholders.
4. The focus on RoE | RoE automatically falls when capital rises (RoE = (ROA)/(capital ratio) ), so RoE-driven managers resist capital.
Origins of RoE as the key metric:
It grew out of risk-based capital allocation, where each asset carries a capital charge (set by the regulator or internally) and every division maximises profit per unit of economic capital. Bankers Trust wrote to the New York Fed in 1979 that equity, not assets, is the scarce resource, so businesses should be compared on RoE.
Banks are decentralised, with specialist knowledge in each business line. RoE lets capital allocation be compared across and up the organisation, which reinforces its use.
Regulators liked the approach as “scientific”. Two criticisms: models estimate future (extreme, systemic) risk from past data, and once RoE becomes a target it stops being a good measure (Goodhart).
RoE is a “false prophet” – the evidence:
In crises (1998, 2008): banks’ pre-crisis RoE closely predicts their loss of shareholder value and their systemic-risk measures. This link does not appear in other industries, so banks are “special”: their headline metric can be inflated by risk-taking.
Pay: absolute or relative RoE targets appear in executive bonus criteria in the US, France and elsewhere in Europe, and bankers’ pay is highly sensitive to RoE.
In normal times: high RoE brings only very short-term share outperformance, followed by underperformance over one to three years, and higher shareholder risk. Ranking banks by RoE, high RoE adds no value. Adjusted for risk, only low-RoE banks outperform.
Business-model shift: RoE targets moved banks from a relationship model (screening and monitoring borrowers, the source of banks’ information advantage) to a transaction model (“originate to distribute”). The new model has not been shown to create more value, and the crisis exposed its weakness. A 2005 head of securitisation at a French bank described it: securitise every €30m pool, so profits rise, capital stays the same and RoE goes up.
Conclusions and policy recommendations:
There is no conflict between shareholder value and financial stability. Better-capitalised banks are more resilient and valued more highly in crises and in normal times.
Capital requirements should not be relaxed.
RoE-based pay incentives should be abolished.
Regulators should anticipate how rules shape bankers’ beliefs, because beliefs determine how resilient the business model is.
Exam focus: 2019 Q4.2 and 2023 Q4.1 use ROE = ROA × leverage as the first step of loan pricing (see 2.9).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 2 – Why banks are special and must be regulated > 2.8 The yield curve and the bank business model
x:
What the yield curve is
The yield curve plots market interest rates against time to maturity for credit-risk-free government securities (government bonds in the state’s own currency, where default is assumed away). Because every point on it has the same (zero) credit risk, it holds credit risk constant and shows only the price of time. A statement that “the yield curve includes credit risk, with riskier instruments paying higher rates” is false.
Normal (upward-sloping) curve | Inverted curve
Shape | Long-term rates above short-term rates. | Short-term rates above long-term rates.
When | Normal times. | Crises (e.g. the 2008 global financial crisis).
Why | The distant future is more uncertain than the near future (duration risk: the longer money is locked up, the more can go wrong with inflation, interest rates and one’s own cash needs). Investors demand a higher return – a premium for waiting and for uncertainty – to tie money up for longer. | Flight to safety: cash is the safest asset in a crisis and has no maturity, so demand for cash and short-maturity assets rises, pushing up the rate required on them. Investors also dump risky long-maturity assets, increasing their supply and driving long rates down. Short rates end up above long rates.
Effect on banks | Borrowing short and lending long earns a positive margin. | The maturity-transformation margin shrinks or turns negative.
The South African curve does not always match the textbook “normal” shape, so check the actual curve before assuming the margin described below exists.
How banks profit from the curve: maturity transformation
The bank funds itself at the short end (call and short-notice deposits at a low rate) and lends at the long end (e.g. 20-year mortgages at a higher rate). Maturity transformation is borrowing short and lending long; liquidity transformation is turning illiquid assets (loans) into liabilities that can be withdrawn at once (deposits).
Balance sheet item | Position on the curve | Result
Liabilities (deposits) | Short end – lower rate y | Interest paid = y
Assets (loans) | Long end – higher rate x | Interest earned = x
Bad debt | Nil on a risk-free (government) curve | “Guaranteed” profit = x – y
Net interest margin (NIM) = interest earned on (long-term) assets – interest paid on (short-term) liabilities – bad debt
Example: the bank lends at 11% for 20 years and pays 4% on call deposits: it keeps a 7% spread for as long as the curve stays upward-sloping and depositors stay.
Once the bank lends to private borrowers, bad debt is no longer nil. Example: the bank pays 5% on deposits and lends at 9% (long end plus a credit premium): margin before bad debt is 4% of the loan book; if bad debts cost 1.5% a year, NIM is 2.5%. If bad debts exceed the spread, the bank makes losses that eat into capital.
Two separate sources of margin: an interest (maturity) margin earned from maturity transformation, and a credit margin earned from taking credit risk. Both are compensation for risk, not free money. The risks banks run are exactly how they make money, so the most profitable activities are the risky ones.
Model answer: how can a bank profit from an upward-sloping yield curve? It raises deposits at the short end of the curve at a low interest rate and makes loans at the long end at a higher rate. Interest earned on the loans less interest paid on the deposits is the bank’s interest margin. This is maturity transformation.
The risks the business model creates
Liquidity risk (maturity mismatch; refinancing risk – the risk that short-term funding cannot be renewed when it matures). Depositors can withdraw at any time while loans repay over 10–20 years. If many withdraw together, the bank cannot call in its loans; it must sell assets at fire-sale prices (creating losses that can make it insolvent) or borrow from the central bank. This is the root of bank runs, and it is the risk named when asked what the yield-curve margin exposes a bank to.
The central bank is the lender of last resort (LLR): it lends freely, against good collateral, to banks that are solvent but illiquid. The SARB provides intraday and overnight liquidity against collateral at the repo rate and has an emergency LLR role. It should not lend to an insolvent bank, because that would be a bail-out with taxpayers’ money.
Interest-rate risk. The margin holds only while short rates stay below long rates. If short rates rise above the fixed long rates (or the curve inverts), the margin shrinks or turns negative.
Credit risk. To earn more than government yields, banks lend to private borrowers and add a credit spread (extra interest as compensation for the chance of default). Banks must charge for expected losses in the loan rate (see 2.9) and hold capital for unexpected losses. Example: if the government curve gives 9% and 3% of a pool of unsecured loans is expected to default with nothing recovered, the bank must charge about 12% just to cover credit losses. If defaults exceed the capital buffer, assets fall below liabilities and the bank is insolvent.
Hence the division of labour in regulation: the central bank handles liquidity problems (LLR, liquidity ratios) and capital handles credit losses.
The incentive to hold as little cash as possible
Vault cash and non-interest-bearing reserves at the central bank earn nothing, so every rand not lent out costs profit. Banks therefore run liquidity as low as they dare. (Even without a rule, management keeps some reserves at the SARB to meet withdrawals and settle payments, because emergency funding or a run is far more costly.)
Society, through the regulator, iterates to the right level: South Africa’s mandatory cash reserve is 2.5% of total liabilities. If a bank failed for lack of cash, society might raise it to 3%, but cash has an opportunity cost (the interest forgone by not lending it), which is passed on to borrowers as higher loan rates.
The same incentive applies to capital: capital is thin (5%–10%) and shareholders have limited liability, so banks are tempted to gamble with depositors’ funds (see the asymmetric pay-off in 2.4).
Endowment and anti-endowment effects
It is often wrongly assumed that rising interest rates hurt banks (as they hurt bond prices). In fact rising rates raise bank profits (endowment effect) and falling rates compress them (anti-endowment effect). Two drivers:
Asymmetric repricing: South African retail loans are floating (tied to prime and therefore to repo) and reprice immediately when the SARB hikes, while rates on transaction and demand deposits are sticky and rise slowly (customers rarely shop around for a cheque-account rate). The spread widens.
Free equity funding: equity (about 5%–10% of assets) pays no interest, so the assets it funds earn the higher rate with no extra interest cost. Example: on R100 of assets with R8 of equity, net interest income rises by 8% of any rate increase even if deposit rates rise in step.
Investec case (anti-endowment): when the SARB cut the repo rate by 25 basis points (7.25% to 7.00%; a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point), Investec cut its loan rates by 25 bps but could not cut its demand-deposit rates, which were already about 0.5%, close to the floor of zero. Loan income fell, funding costs stayed flat and the margin was compressed.
Exam focus: 2021 Q1 (10 marks): is the yield curve credit-risk-free (true/false); why it normally slopes upward; why it inverts in a crisis; how a bank profits from it; what risk this creates (liquidity risk).

How loan rates are set
The repo rate is the SARB’s policy rate, the anchor for all other rates. In South Africa loans are quoted relative to the prime rate, traditionally repo + 3.5 percentage points, as prime plus or minus a spread that depends on the client’s risk.
Behind the quoted rate, a bank sets the average loan rate it needs to earn its target ROE, after covering its cost of funds, expected credit losses, operating costs and tax, and allowing for assets (such as cash) that earn nothing.
Loan pricing from a target ROE – method
Work everything per R1 of total assets. Let X be the average interest rate on loans and L the share of total assets that is loans (the rest, e.g. cash, earns nothing).
Step 1 – required ROA after tax: ROE = ROA × leverage ⇒ ROA = target ROE × capital ratio ( (equity)/(assets) ) = (target ROE)/(leverage) Step 2 – gross up for tax: pre-tax ROA = (ROA)/(1-tax rate) Step 3 – pre-tax profit per R1 of assets: pre-tax ROA = L·X – cost of funds – L·(expected bad debt % of loans) + other income – operating costsStep 4 – solve: X = [pre-tax ROA + cost of funds + L·bad debt % – other income + operating costs] ÷ L
Read each percentage carefully: bad debt is usually given as a % of loans (so multiply by L); operating costs, other income and cost of funds are usually given as a % of total assets.
In the past-paper memos the cost of funds (“cost of all funds”, “overall average cost of capital”) is applied to total assets, not only to the liability-funded part. Follow that convention unless the question clearly says otherwise.
Always check the answer by working forwards: revenue – costs = pre-tax profit; × (1 – t) = ROA; ÷ capital ratio = ROE.
Marks are given for formulas and for clearly setting out each step.
Worked example: required average loan rate
Target ROE 18%; capital ratio 8% of total assets; tax rate 27%; loans are 96% of assets and cash (4%) earns nothing; cost of all funds 6% of total assets; expected bad debt 1.2% of loans; other income (fees) 1.5% of total assets; operating costs 3% of total assets.
Step 1 – required ROA after tax.
18%=ROA×(1)/(8%)⇒ROA=18%×8%=1.44%
Step 2 – gross up for tax.
ROA_pre-tax=(1.44%)/(1-0.27)=1.972603%
Step 3 – set up pre-tax profit per R1 of assets. Bad debt = 0.96 × 1.2% = 1.152% of total assets.
1.972603%=0.96X-6%-1.152%+1.5%-3%
Step 4 – solve for X.
0.96X=1.972603%+6%+1.152%-1.5%+3%=10.624603%⇒X=(10.624603%)/(0.96)=11.07%
The bank must charge an average loan rate of about 11.07%.
Check: 0.96 × 11.0673% = 10.6246%; less 6%, 1.152% and 3%, plus 1.5% = 1.9726% pre-tax; × 0.73 = 1.44% ROA; ÷ 8% = 18% ROE.
Variant: if tax is applied in one step, write ROA = [L·X – L·bad debt – cost of funds – operating costs (+ other income)] × (1 – t), multiply by leverage, set equal to the target ROE and solve. Both layouts give the same answer.
What moves the required loan rate
Each input in the pricing equation moves the rate in a predictable direction. Consider each change on its own, all else equal.
Change | Loan rate | Reason (link to the equation)
Central bank raises the policy (repo) rate | Increase | Cost of funds and the base rate rise for all banks.
Credit risk of the average loan higher than thought | Increase | Higher expected bad debt must be recovered.
Stronger property rights; deeds office works efficiently; title more certain | Decrease | Collateral can be registered and realised, so loss given default and expected bad debt fall.
Political uncertainty falls | Decrease | Lower country risk premium in funding costs and required returns; lower expected defaults.
Tax rate cut | Decrease | A lower pre-tax return is needed for the same after-tax ROE.
Same tax rate but fewer deductions allowed | Increase | Higher effective tax rate, so a higher pre-tax return is needed.
Regulator requires more cash to be held | Increase | Cash earns nothing, so the loans must earn more (L falls).
Operating costs rise beyond what volumes justify | Increase | Higher costs must be covered.
Loan volumes fall sharply | Increase | Fixed costs are spread over fewer loans, so cost per loan rises.
Better risk systems reduce risk-weighted assets | Decrease | Less capital needed, leverage rises, so a lower ROA (and rate) gives the same ROE.
Regulator prohibits dividends for some years | Increase | Retained profit builds up capital, leverage falls, so a higher ROA is needed for the target ROE.
Average loan maturity lengthens | Same | Maturity does not appear in the pricing equation (use only the information given).
Lower loan rates increase the supply of houses: more people can afford to repay a home loan, so more loans are taken up and more houses are built.
Should a bank charge more than the risk/return calculation requires if the client is willing to pay? Either answer earns the mark with a reason. Yes: the bank seeks profit, and the client may pay for reasons other than risk/return (convenience, relationship, speed). No: it is abuse of the client, who will leave once he realises it (reputation and competition).
How politics raises loan interest rates
Politicians are tempted to control banks because banks decide who gets credit and create money when they lend; directing lending is a way to spend without a visible budget. The cost appears in loan rates:
Irrecoverable, politically connected loans and bribes. Loans made under political pressure or bribes (“unvetted” loans to connected companies, municipalities, favoured groups) are often never repaid. The bank must recover these losses by charging higher rates on its productive loans, so honest borrowers pay for the bad ones.
Economic and policy uncertainty. Political instability, policy uncertainty and poor governance depress growth and raise future unemployment and defaults. Higher expected bad debt must be recouped through a higher credit-risk premium.
Uncertain property rights. Land and houses are the main security for loans; uncertain ownership (e.g. expropriation without compensation) makes the security uncertain, raising expected losses and rates.
Inflation risk. Politicians who control money creation, or advocate monetary financing of deficits (e.g. modern monetary theory), raise the prospect of higher inflation, and expected inflation is a key component of nominal interest rates. Country risk also raises the rate foreign investors demand on rand funding.
Exam focus: 2020 Q4(a) (two arguments, a paragraph each, on how politics leads to higher loan rates – 4 marks).
Systemically important banks and the cost of capital
A systemically important bank is one so large and interconnected that its failure would damage the whole financial system (“too big to fail”). In South Africa the domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs) are Standard Bank, FirstRand, Absa, Nedbank and Capitec; they must hold an extra capital buffer.
If such a bank is expected always to be bailed out by the central bank, its cost of capital is closer to the risk-free rate than that of a comparable non-bank listed firm: investors and creditors see less risk and demand a smaller premium.
This implicit guarantee is a “too big to fail” subsidy: it lowers the bank’s funding cost without any matching improvement in safety, and it creates moral hazard because owners and creditors expect someone else to absorb the losses. This is one reason systemically important banks face extra capital requirements.
Exam focus: 2019 Q4.2 (10 marks) and 2023 Q4.1 (loan rate from target ROE, tax, expected bad debt, costs, non-earning cash); 2023 Q4.2 and 2021 Q2 (direction of the loan rate after a change – one mark each); 2023 Q4.3; 2020 Q4(c) (cost of capital of a systemically important bank – closer to the risk-free rate).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 2 – Why banks are special and must be regulated > 2.10 Bank governance: lessons still not learned (focus reading)
x:
Source: Marco Becht, Patrick Bolton and Ailsa Röell, Bank Governance: Lessons Still Not Learned, ECGI Working Paper in Law No. 893/2026, January 2026. Cite it as Becht, Bolton & Röell (2026). It updates the same authors’ Why Bank Governance Is Different (2011).
Thesis
Wrong problem. The core governance problem in banks is the agency cost of debt (shareholders against creditors), not the agency cost of equity (shareholders against managers).
Wrong cure. Post-2008 reforms (say-on-pay, deferred equity pay, more shareholder engagement) tie managers more closely to shareholders, so they amplify risk-taking rather than reduce it.
The real culprit is risk-shifting: shareholders, boards and managers together move risk onto debtholders, deposit insurers and taxpayers.
Supervision is reactive. It intervenes only after problems materialise.
Credit Suisse followed every post-crisis prescription and kept capital above the minimum, yet failed in 2023. The cause was too much shareholder influence, not too little.
Remedy – “prophylactic governance”: change incentives in advance so that risk-shifting cannot operate. Pay executives in creditor-type instruments, and give creditors and deposit insurers governance powers (board seats) that match their exposure to risk.
Against “maximise shareholder value, subject to regulation”: that view needs optimal regulation, which is unattainable. Regulation lags innovation (Clark’s 1916 “twilight zone”) and can be captured, so bank executives should answer to a broader common good.
Against relying on capital alone (Admati, Hellwig and Portes, 2023): it depends on regulators setting the right level, resisting lobbying and acting promptly, which crises show they cannot do, and its cost to the economy is disputed.
Theory: why bank governance is different
There are three layers of agency conflict (see 2.4). The reading adds the following:
Layer 2 (debt against equity) is amplified by leverage of about 10:1 and by deposit insurance and implicit guarantees, which remove creditors’ incentive to monitor. It arises whatever the ownership structure. Jensen & Meckling (1976): large firms financed almost entirely by debt are rare in other industries; banks are the exception.
Layer 3 (bank against society) cannot be solved by private contracting. Even when the combined value of debt and equity is maximised, shareholders and creditors may jointly choose risks whose social costs exceed their social benefits.
Call-option view (quoted from the Liikanen Report): with limited liability, shareholders and the managers acting for them hold a call option on the bank’s assets, so they gain when asset volatility rises.
Example: gambling for resurrection
A bank has assets of $30 and owes creditors $30. A $10 project pays $80 with probability 10% and $0 otherwise (NPV = 0.1 × 80 − 10 = −$2).
Outcome | Assets | Creditors | Shareholders
Success (10%) | 20 + 80 = 100 | 30 | 70
Failure (90%) | 20 | 20 | 0
Expected | 21 (−9) | 7 (+7)
Shareholders gain $7 and creditors lose $9 (the reading’s figures; the table shows how they arise), so a manager acting for shareholders takes a value-destroying project. The pull grows as the bank nears insolvency.
Debt overhang (Myers 1977): shareholders refuse to inject equity that would raise the bank’s total value, because much of the gain makes creditors safer. The state may then have to force recapitalisation or supply the capital itself. Example: Lehman’s CEO Dick Fuld delayed raising equity until June 2008 and raised too little, too late. The flip side is excessive payouts (dividends and buybacks) near insolvency.
No run discipline: short-term funding would normally dry up as a firm nears insolvency, but insured deposits stay, so supervision must take over. In the savings-and-loan crisis of the late 1980s, troubled thrifts gambled on junk bonds, which raised the final cost to taxpayers.
Cheap debt: insured depositors do not monitor, and uninsured creditors of systemically important banks expect bail-outs. Debt is therefore cheap and banks are biased towards leverage (the too-big-to-fail subsidy; see 2.9).
Speed and opacity: risk can be built up fast through trading and off-balance-sheet positions that are hard to value, so governance must be forward-looking. Universal owners (pension funds) could internalise the costs but have no governance role and face a double agency problem.
Social cost: 325 US bank failures in 2007–10 cost the deposit insurance fund $79.3bn; TARP put $245bn into banks as capital.
Evidence of risk-shifting
Study / case | Finding
Landier, Sraer & Thesmar – New Century (subprime lender), 2004–06 | After the Fed’s 2004 tightening hit its loan book, it doubled down on interest-only loans, concentrated lending geographically and raised its payout ratio from 5% to 90%. (Likewise, many banks kept paying dividends until late 2008.)
UniCredit rights issue, January 2012 (debt overhang) | A €7.5bn rights issue at €1.943 against €4.14. The share price fell 45% and shareholders lost about 28% in five days even after counting the rights. Of the 31 EU banks short of €115bn of capital, most shrank, cut dividends or sold assets rather than issue equity.
Fringuellotti & Kroen (2024) – COVID payout limits on US banks, 2020 | When the limits were imposed, equity values fell and debt values rose. When they were lifted, equity rose and CDS spreads widened. Restricted banks lent less to risky borrowers, so payouts and risk-taking go together.
Hermalin & Wallace (1994) and others – savings-and-loan crisis | Mutual thrifts (no shareholders) took less risk than stock thrifts, so limited-liability shareholders drive the risk.
Peydró et al. – Italy (counter-evidence) | Fragile banks cut risk. But measured risk is not the same as risk-shifting: a bank can cut overall risk while tilting towards payoffs that favour equity.
Boards and risk management: the problem is the objective, not competence
Study | Finding
Minton, Taillard & Williamson (2014), US | More financial expertise among independent directors went with more risk before the crisis. Either experts pursued risk under a shareholder mandate, or risk-seeking banks hired them.
Hau & Thum (2009), Germany | State Landesbanken, whose boards included political appointees with limited financial expertise, lost three times as much as private banks: incompetent boards approve risks they do not understand.
Erkens, Hung & Matos (2012) | More independent boards suffered larger crisis losses. Independence from management made boards more responsive to shareholders.
Ellul & Yerramilli (2013): Risk Management Index, 72 large US bank holding companies | The index covers six features: a CRO with enterprise-wide remit, the CRO’s executive rank, the CRO among the top five earners, CRO centrality ( (CRO pay)/(CEO pay) ), risk-committee experience, and risk-committee meeting frequency. 80% had a CRO, 40% gave the CRO executive rank, 20% placed the CRO in the top five earners, and the CRO earned on average 31% of CEO pay. Centrality mattered most. Banks with a higher index had lower tail risk, fewer NPLs and better crisis performance; the effect showed under stress and was small in normal times.
A powerless risk function: at Lehman, managers overrode risk limits, and the CRO and head of fixed income were removed in 2007 after opposing risky positions; at HBOS, a risk officer was allegedly made redundant for raising concerns; SVB had no CRO for eight months, and none of the seven members of its risk committee had held a senior risk role.
Key line: banks do not lack competent directors; competent directors are given the wrong objectives.
Why the lessons are still not learned
The misdiagnosis: the crisis was framed as temporal (short-termism) and as an agency cost of equity, when the problem is structural. Shareholders of a leveraged bank gain from volatility whatever their horizon: a manager with five-year deferred equity pay still benefits from more volatile assets. Deferral, malus and clawback change only when pay is received, not the shape of the payoff.
Report / rule | Diagnosis and prescription | Critique
de Larosière (EU, 2009); Walker Review (UK, 2009); EC Green Paper (2010) | Short-termism (de Larosière), boardroom “groupthink” and weak shareholder engagement (Walker). The cure: pay aligned with long-term shareholder value, more investor engagement and stewardship. The Green Paper admitted shareholders may have encouraged risk, but proposed no powers for creditors. | Set the temporal framing; assumed shareholders wanted prudence, without evidence.
Liikanen (EU, 2012) | Closest to correct: the call-option diagnosis. It still prescribed equity-based long-term pay; its proposal that part of bonuses be paid in bail-in bonds was never legislated. | Right diagnosis, wrong cure.
CRD III–V (EU, 2010–19) | Deferral (up to 5 years), at least 50% of variable pay in shares or instruments, malus and clawback, bonus cap (100% of fixed pay, 200% with shareholder approval), risk committees, CROs, fit-and-proper tests. | Fit-and-proper rules check that directors can serve shareholders, not whom they serve. Independence from management is not independence from shareholders.
EBA (2021); ECB Guide on Governance and Risk Culture (2024) | The EBA admits “heads I win, tails I still win” pay. The ECB asks for a strong, challenging board. | Still temporal and shareholder-aligned, even after Credit Suisse.
Dodd-Frank (US, 2010) | Empowers shareholders through proxy access (s971), say-on-pay (s951) and the end of broker voting (s957). Section 956, which would ban incentive pay that encourages inappropriate risk, is the only provision aimed at the agency cost of debt and is still unimplemented (proposals 2011, 2016, 2024). Powell (March 2024) said he “would like to understand the problem”. | Coffee: the governance provisions work against the Act’s systemic-risk aim, because shareholders favoured pay that induced risk and leverage; reforms weaken after enactment (the “regulatory sine curve”).
Why still not learned: (1) the misdiagnosis (equity against debt; temporal against structural); (2) shareholder primacy is still assumed; (3) correct diagnoses are not acted on (Liikanen, s956); (4) political economy: lobbying, disagreement between agencies, US deregulation, a muted response to SVB; (5) supervision stays reactive; (6) responses after 2023 (FINMA’s Senior Managers Regime, the FDIC’s 2023 governance guidelines with three lines of defence, the Basel Committee, FSB, EU CMDI reform, the ECB 2024 Guide) refine existing frameworks and never ask whose interests the board serves.
Credit Suisse: four governance failures
For the timeline, the AT1 write-down and the UBS deal, see Part 4; for the CET1 point, see 2.5.
Failure | Evidence
1. The shareholder-alignment paradox | Binding say-on-pay (the Minder initiative, 2013). After opposition reached 40% in 2017, the board removed CET1 from pay in favour of return on tangible equity and tangible book value per share, and raised the CEO’s shareholding requirement from 350 000 to 500 000 shares. Opposition then fell below 20%. After Archegos ($5bn loss) and Greensill ($10bn of client funds frozen) in 2021, approval fell to 53%, risk-committee chair Gottschling resigned before the AGM and the chair was replaced. Shareholders wanted risk better executed, not less risk.
2. Compensation | CHF 33bn of variable pay over ten years against a cumulative net loss of CHF 2.1bn, so variable pay had become effectively fixed. Shareholders approved every pay report. Swiss rules were “comply or explain”, and FINMA felt it lacked the legal basis to object.
3. The board served shareholders | Repeated weaknesses went unremedied, and the chair and CEO each changed twice in 2020–22. FINMA disclaims any role in strategy or in selecting directors; its proposed Senior Managers Regime is still reactive. People were accountable, but to shareholders.
4. Reactive supervision | FINMA had no power to limit strategy before non-viability, and about 40 staff for both Swiss G-SIBs against hundreds of bank staff. Information asymmetry, clawbacks that are hard to enforce, and litigation (a PostFinance capital ruling took about six years).
Not a capital failure: Credit Suisse was adequately capitalised to the end and failed in a “competence run”, a loss of confidence in management rather than balance-sheet insolvency. By every regulatory standard it was a well-governed bank. AT1 holders lost $17bn (100%) while shareholders kept some value and executives kept most of their past pay.
Same pattern at SVB and Signature (2023): growth without investment in risk management, and pay not linked to risk. Shareholders approved executive pay with 89% (SVB) and 94% (Signature) in 2022.
Objection acknowledged: supervisors have had successes (risk-based scorecards, cuts to bonus pools, blocked candidates), but these depend on particular individuals, not on the design of the rules.
Recommendations: prophylactic governance
Principle: give governance power to those who bear the cost of failure (creditors, deposit insurers, taxpayers) by putting creditor-aligned decision-makers inside the bank, instead of relying on outside supervisors to restrain boards aligned with shareholders.
For a systemically important bank the optimal probability of failure is zero, and reactive supervision can only reduce it marginally. (Contrast 2.2: regulators aim for a failure probability that is low, not zero.) Hellwig (1995) had already argued that supervisors should take an active part in banks’ strategy.
Mechanism (most to least practical) | How it works and its strengths | Limits
1. Credit-risk-adjusted pay | Pay executives partly in CoCos/AT1/bail-in debt. Credit Suisse executives paid in AT1 would have lost their deferred pay. This uses existing instruments, counts as regulatory capital, can start now, and has a legal basis already (s956; Liikanen). | Leaves the shareholder-centric board, which sets strategy, unchanged.
2. Board nomination or appointment by deposit insurers, supervisors or creditor representatives | Appointment (strong form): the director serves at the appointing body’s will. Nomination (weak form): shareholders still elect the candidate. Loyalty follows whoever nominates, appoints and can remove a director, which a fit-and-proper test cannot override (Credit Suisse’s directors passed theirs). Precedent: at Safran (French defence) the state holds about 11% of the equity but appoints directors and holds vetoes, because its risk exceeds its stake. | Risk of political capture (Italian banks in the 1980s), so the power should go to financially exposed parties, not politicians.
3. Two-tier equity (Goodhart & Lastra 2020) | “Insiders” (executives, directors, activist shareholders on the board) face enhanced personal liability if the bank fails, which matches liability to power. It reaches further than clawbacks, which cover few people and are hard to enforce. | Complex; needs changes to corporate law.
4. State equity with enhanced rights | The deposit insurer or an agency holds stakes with extra votes, nomination rights and vetoes. | The Landesbanken precedent; no obvious competent agency (state holding companies lack expertise; state pension funds report ROE); politicisation. Last resort only.
Verdict: board nomination and appointment is the most direct and cost-effective option, because it puts creditor-aligned people where risk is approved, without equity investment or new corporate law. CoCo pay can start immediately. The options complement one another.
Who should hold the powers? The agency must (1) have incentives aligned with preventing failure, (2) have the competence and staff, and (3) be independent of politics. The answer is the deposit insurer with a supervisory role (e.g. the FDIC): it bears the losses, gains nothing from upside, does not report ROE and understands banks. Where insurers are weak (the EU patchwork), the answer is to build capacity: an insurer that pays out but cannot prevent failure is incomplete.
Capital gives supervisors “breathing space” before insolvency (Hellwig 2010), but it cannot fix governance failures that are visible for years. It complements prophylactic governance; it does not replace it.
Area | Current (shareholder-centric) approach | Becht, Bolton & Röell
Board | Fit and proper, independence, risk committees | Directors nominated or appointed by deposit insurers or creditor representatives; competent directors given the right objective
Risk management | A CRO, three lines of defence | A risk function with real power (rank, pay relative to the CEO), backed by creditor-aligned directors
Pay | Deferred equity, malus and clawback, bonus cap, ROE and TSR metrics | CoCo/AT1/bail-in debt pay; capital metrics kept in pay; implement s956; personal liability for insiders
Shareholders | More engagement, say-on-pay, proxy access | Part of the problem: limit their exclusive control over pay, strategy and board selection
Supervisors | Reactive, ex post, comply-or-explain, no role in strategy | Prophylactic: governance rights inside the bank; a stronger, better-resourced deposit insurer
Culture | Risk-culture guides, tone at the top, Senior Managers Regime | Culture work inside a shareholder-value mandate does not change behaviour; change whose interests the board serves
Links and South African application
Moussu (2.7) agrees that ROE-based pay drives risk but argues that shareholder value and stability do not conflict (high-ROE banks underperform once risk is accounted for). Becht et al. argue the conflict is structural: ex ante shareholders gain from volatility, even if ex post they lost at Credit Suisse.
Annotations on the course copy (not part of the paper): South Africa’s deposit cover is low, but concentration makes most banks too big to fail, so the problem returns; reforms aimed at the agency cost of equity leave South African bank debt too cheap, to shareholders’ benefit; shareholders should not be able to vote out the director in charge of risk oversight (next to the Gottschling episode); the King Code’s stakeholder focus clashes with shareholder-protecting Companies Act measures, which are inappropriate for banks in a bank-heavy economy.
Essay structure (“Post-2008 reforms were misdirected – discuss”): thesis; why banks differ; evidence; reforms and their temporal framing; Credit Suisse; remedies and their limits; conclusion that banks are not ordinary corporations.
Exam focus: agency cost of equity against agency cost of debt; why say-on-pay and deferred equity pay can raise bank risk (“structural, not temporal”); risk-shifting, gambling for resurrection and debt overhang, with an example (the $30 bank, Lehman, UniCredit); board evidence (expertise and independence went with more risk; CRO centrality); Credit Suisse as a case of too much shareholder influence and of the limits of reactive supervision; reactive versus prophylactic governance; ranking the four reforms and why the deposit insurer should hold the powers; why fit-and-proper tests and capital are insufficient; s956 and Liikanen’s bail-in bonds; MCQ facts (January 2026, 10:1 leverage, $17bn AT1 loss, CHF 33bn against CHF 2.1bn, 89% and 94% say-on-pay approval at SVB and Signature, about 40 FINMA staff, Safran’s ~11% state stake); South African application (concentration and too big to fail, King against shareholder primacy).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance
x: A bank fails in one of two ways. It becomes insolvent (losses on its assets exceed its capital, so its assets are worth less than what it owes) or it becomes illiquid (it is unable to find cash to pay depositors and creditors when they ask for it). Regulation attacks both: capital rules guard against insolvency, liquidity rules (cash reserves, LCR, NSFR) guard against illiquidity, and deposit insurance removes small depositors’ reason to start a run. This Part builds the rules up in that order and gives a step-by-step method for every ratio that is examined.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance > 3.1 The regulator’s problem: safety versus affordable credit
x:
