Regulation exists because the groups affected by a bank want different things.
Party | What they want | Why
Bank shareholders and managers | Minimum capital and liquidity | Less capital means more leverage and a higher return on equity (ROE = (profit)/(shareholders’ equity) ), and managers’ bonuses are tied to ROE. Liquid assets earn little or nothing, so holding them costs profit.
Society as depositors | High capital and liquidity | The probability that the bank fails, and that their savings are lost, should be as low as possible.
Society as borrowers | Low interest rates and accessible credit | Households and firms need affordable loans to buy homes, study and invest.
“Society” appears twice: the same person is a depositor (wanting a safe bank) and a borrower (wanting cheap loans). The optimum is therefore a compromise, not a corner solution, and there is no single “correct” capital ratio, only one society judges acceptable.
Managers push for minimum capital because the cost of failure falls largely on others (limited liability, deposit insurance, bail-outs). Regulation exists to impose the cost of risk back on the bank.
Example of the trade-off: forcing 30% capital and 20% cash would make a bank extremely safe, but equity is the dearest funding and 20% of the balance sheet would earn nothing. To still earn its target ROE the bank would have to charge very high loan rates, stifling growth.
Model answer: can banks be regulated so that they never fail? Yes in principle, but not for free.
How: remove both causes of failure. Force the bank to hold a very large capital cushion (shareholders’ money that absorbs losses before depositors are touched) and a very large stock of liquid assets (cash and government bonds that can be sold immediately). With, say, 30% capital and 20% cash, almost no realistic loss or run could sink the bank.
Cost: capital is the most expensive funding a bank has (shareholders demand a high return for taking first loss; deposits are cheap), and cash earns little or nothing. More capital and cash raise the average cost of funds and cut earning assets, so the bank must charge higher loan rates or lend less.
Consequence for society: loans become unaffordable, investment and growth fall, and borrowing moves to less-regulated lenders (loan sharks, shadow banks), which is itself dangerous.
Conclusion: safety and cheap credit pull in opposite directions. Regulators aim for a failure probability that is low enough, not zero, and adjust the rules iteratively (typically after each crisis) as society learns what failures cost versus what credit costs.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance > 3.2 Who regulates banks
x:
National regulation: the SARB and the Prudential Authority
South Africa uses the Twin Peaks model, legislated in the Financial Sector Regulation Act of 2017 (introduced after the 2008 crisis). Twin Peaks means two separate regulators, each with its own objective.
Peak | Regulator | Objective
Prudential | Prudential Authority (PA), inside the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) | Safety and soundness of regulated financial institutions (banks, insurers and similar): “will this bank stay solvent and liquid?” It licenses banks and enforces the Banks Act and the Basel rules.
Conduct | Financial Sector Conduct Authority (FSCA) | How institutions treat customers: fair pricing, disclosure, mis-selling, market abuse.
The national rules work at four points:
Entry requirements. The right people with a history of ethical behaviour, and minimum capital of R250 million to register a new bank. Owners must have real money at stake (so they bear losses before depositors do), and keeping reckless or dishonest people out from the start is cheaper than supervising them afterwards.
Fit and proper requirements for directors and executives: honesty and integrity, competence and experience, financial soundness. Appointments of executive directors must be approved by the regulator. Example: the regulator objected to the proposed chair of Absa’s board because of his history, which led to legal disputes. The power must respect the rule of law (everyone, including the state, acts under clear, public, consistently applied rules): criteria must be known in advance and decisions open to legal challenge, otherwise appointments could be blocked for political reasons.
Credit inspections. The regulator inspects how banks grant credit, checking that loans are for productive purposes (uses that let the borrower generate the income to repay, such as a student loan for a degree that improves employability) rather than speculation or consumption the borrower cannot afford. It examines underwriting standards (affordability checks, collateral, concentration limits), not only loans already in default.
Ongoing reporting and control. Banks file daily and monthly regulatory returns (the BA900 is the standard monthly balance-sheet return), and the regulator can restrict dividends when capital is inadequate (as the SARB did during COVID-19 in 2020).
International standards: the BIS and the Basel Committee
Banks lend across borders, and a failure in one country spreads to others, so supervisors co-ordinate internationally.
The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), in Basel, Switzerland, is owned by central banks and is known as the “central banks’ central bank”: it is a forum for central-bank co-operation and a banker to central banks.
The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), formed by the governors of the major central banks, meets at the BIS and writes the global standards: the Basel Accords (Basel I, II, III).
Basel rules are international best practice, not international law. The BCBS cannot force anyone; each country must pass its own laws to apply the rules. Compliance is enforced by markets: foreign banks and investors lend to banks from non-compliant countries only at higher rates, or not at all, because they cannot trust that those banks are safe. The penalty for non-compliance is a higher funding cost.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance > 3.3 Why capital is the main tool of regulation
x:
Capital is the part of the balance sheet funded by the owners (equity and similar instruments) rather than by depositors and creditors. In accounting terms it is the excess of assets over liabilities; regulatory capital is the part of that excess the regulator accepts as able to absorb losses.
Model answer: why do regulators put so much emphasis on minimum capital?
Insolvency is the ultimate form of bank failure, and capital is the buffer between the bank and insolvency: losses are absorbed by capital before depositors lose anything.
Regulators do not want banks to fail because of the extreme public cost (lost savings, a frozen payment system, a shrinking money supply, bail-outs).
More capital means a larger buffer and a lower chance of insolvency.
Capital protects the bank against unforeseen events. It also aligns incentives: the more of the owners’ own money is at risk, the less attractive it is to gamble with depositors’ money.
Model answer: how should a bank protect itself against known (expected) risks? By charging for them: expected losses are priced into interest rates and fees and covered by provisions. Capital is held for the unexpected losses.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance > 3.4 Basel I, II and III
x:
The Basel Accords set a minimum ratio of capital to the bank’s risk, called the capital adequacy ratio (CAR) (also “capital ratio” or “Cooke ratio”). The denominator is not total assets but risk-weighted assets (Section 3.5), so a bank with riskier assets needs more capital.
Basel I (1988, with the 1996 amendment): CAR = (Capital (Tier1+Tier2))/(Credit risk+Market risk) ≥ 8%Basel II (2004/2008): CAR = (Capital (Tier1+Tier2))/(Improved credit risk+Market risk+Operational risk) ≥ 8%Basel III: CAR = (Capital (CET1Tier1andTier2))/(Improved credit risk+Market risk+Operational risk) ≥ 8% + buffers and surcharges
Basel I (1988) and the 1996 Market Risk Amendment
Followed the growth of cross-border banking and the fear that competition between countries was driving capital down. Set a universal minimum CAR of 8% of risk-weighted assets, against credit risk (the risk that borrowers do not repay), using simple regulator-set risk-weight buckets.
1996 amendment: large international banks were universal banks (commercial lending plus investment banking) holding trading books (shares, bonds, currencies and derivatives held to trade). Market risk (loss from changes in market prices, interest rates or exchange rates) was added to the denominator.
Basel II (2004/2008)
Added operational risk: the risk of loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems, or from external events (fraud, corruption, fire, earthquake, an employee unplugging the mainframe). It includes legal risk but excludes strategic and reputational risk, so someone deliberately damaging a company’s reputation is not, in Basel terms, an operational-risk event.
Improved the credit-risk measure: large banks may use their own Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) models. The bank estimates each borrower’s probability of default and the likely loss, and (after regulatory approval) these are converted into risk weights. This made capital more risk-sensitive but also gave banks room to game the numbers (Section 3.9).
Recognised that a number alone is not enough, and rested the framework on three pillars:
Pillar | Name | Content
1 | Minimum capital requirements | The formula-driven minimum: CAR ≥ 8% of risk-weighted assets for credit, market and operational risk.
2 | Supervisory review | The bank assesses how much capital it needs for all its risks, including those Pillar 1 ignores (concentration risk, interest-rate risk in the banking book). This self-assessment is the ICAAP (internal capital adequacy assessment process). The supervisor reviews it and can demand extra capital or better risk management before the bank is in trouble (early intervention).
3 | Market discipline | Mandatory public disclosure (Pillar 3 reports) on capital, risk exposures and risk management, so shareholders, depositors, rating agencies and wholesale lenders can compare banks and punish risky ones with higher funding costs or withdrawals. The market helps the regulator.
Basel III (after the 2008 crisis)
Tighter definition of capital (stricter criteria and more deductions) and more, better-quality capital, with the focus on Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) (Section 3.6).
Capital conservation buffer of 2.5% CET1 on top of the 4.5% CET1 minimum (total 7.0%). Banks build it in good times; if it is used up in a downturn, the bank is automatically restricted from paying dividends and bonuses until it is rebuilt.
Surcharges for systemically important banks: global (G-SIBs) and domestic (D-SIBs; in South Africa Standard Bank, FirstRand, Absa, Nedbank and Capitec) must hold an extra 1.0%–2.5%. A systemically important bank is so large and interconnected that its failure would damage the whole financial system (“too big to fail”), so it must be safer than others.
A leverage ratio (minimum 3%) as a backstop against gaming of risk weights (Section 3.9).
Liquidity regulated explicitly for the first time: the LCR (30-day stress survival) and the NSFR (one-year structural funding) (Section 3.11).
Total statutory capital requirements in South Africa typically range from 12% to 14%+ of RWA once minimums, buffers, surcharges and supervisory (Pillar 2) add-ons are stacked.
Basel I vs II vs III
Basel I (1988; 1996 amendment) | Basel II (2004/2008) | Basel III
Denominator | Credit risk (+ market risk from 1996) | Improved credit risk + market risk + operational risk | Same risks as Basel II, measured more strictly
Numerator | Tier 1 + Tier 2 | Tier 1 + Tier 2 | CET1, Tier 1 and Tier 2; tighter definition, more deductions, more and better capital
Minimum | 8% | 8% | 8% + buffers and surcharges (CET1 4.5% + 2.5% buffer = 7.0%; D-SIB add-on 1%–2.5%)
Risk weights | Simple regulator buckets | Risk-sensitive; large banks may use internal (IRB) models | 0%–1 250%; leverage ratio backstops model gaming
Liquidity | None | None | LCR and NSFR
Other | – | Three pillars | Leverage ratio ≥ 3%; conservation buffer
Exam focus: 2023 MCQ 8 (operational risk excludes reputational risk; the LCR horizon is 30 days, not 25).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance > 3.5 Risk-weighted assets (RWA)
x:
Capital is not set as a flat percentage of total assets, because R1 000m of government bonds and R1 000m of unsecured personal loans do not carry the same risk of loss. A flat ratio would punish safe lending and push banks towards riskier assets. Basel therefore multiplies each asset by a risk weight (a percentage reflecting how likely and how severe losses are) and sums the results.
RWA = Σ (exposure × risk weight) + RWA from off-balance-sheet items | Capital required = RWA × minimum CAR
Typical risk weights and why
Asset type | Risk weight | Reason
Sovereign (own-currency government) debt, central bank reserves, cash | 0% | The government or central bank can create rand to repay its own-currency debt, so default risk is treated as nil.
Interbank claims / OECD banks | 20% | Short-term claims on regulated banks in rich countries. The OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) is a club of mostly high-income countries, used under Basel I as a proxy for low risk.
Residential mortgages | 50% | Secured by a house the bank can sell.
Commercial loans, unsecured retail, credit cards | 100% | No or weak collateral; the standard weight.
High-risk / non-performing, venture exposures | 150% | Loans already overdue or highly speculative need extra capital.
Very risky items (some securitisation and equity exposures) | up to 1 250% | At 1 250% × 8% = 100%, the item is in effect fully deducted from capital.
Worked example: RWA and capital required (CAR assumed 10%)
Asset portfolio | Risk profile | Risk weight | RWA | Capital required (10%)
R2 000m | Sovereign debt / central bank reserves | 0% | R0m | R0m
R1 000m | Interbank claims / OECD banks | 20% | R200m | R20m
R5 000m | Residential mortgages | 50% | R2 500m | R250m
R3 000m | Commercial loans, unsecured retail, credit cards | 100% | R3 000m | R300m
R1 000m | High-risk / non-performing, venture | 150% | R1 500m | R150m
R12 000m | R7 200m | R720m
For each row RWA = exposure × weight (R5 000m × 50% = R2 500m) and capital = RWA × 10% (R250m). Shortcut: total capital = total RWA × CAR = R7 200m × 10% = R720m.
RWA is 60% of total assets; the capital needed (R720m) is only 6% of total assets. Capital is measured against risk, not size.
South African benchmark: in 2019 total banking-system assets were R5.7 trillion but RWA only R3.0 trillion (SARB Annual Report), so RWA is typically about half of total unweighted assets. Use this as a sense check on any RWA you calculate.
Incentive effect: because weights differ, banks are drawn towards low-weight assets (government bonds, mortgages), which frees capital and raises ROE. This can steer credit towards safer, secured lending, but it also concentrates banks in assets labelled “safe” whose weights may be wrong (the Greek bond example, Section 3.9).
How to calculate total RWA (method)
List every asset on the balance sheet with the risk weight given in the question.
Give 0% to all government-related items: cash and cash equivalents, balances and mandatory reserve deposits at the central bank, government securities, and amounts owed by the Receiver of Revenue (SARS).
Leave out items that are deducted from capital (goodwill, intangible assets, capitalised software, the deferred tax asset that depends on future profits). They are removed from capital instead, so they carry no capital charge in the denominator.
Multiply each remaining exposure by its weight and add up: this is on-balance-sheet RWA.
Add the RWA contribution of off-balance-sheet items if given (guarantees, letters of credit, undrawn facilities).
If the question already gives total RWA “inclusive of credit, market and operational risk”, use that figure directly and do not recalculate.
Exam focus: 2020 Section B Q3(a) (calculate total RWA from given weights plus an off-balance-sheet amount).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance > 3.6 Capital tiers
x:
Capital is divided into tiers by how well it absorbs losses. The key distinction:
Going-concern capital absorbs losses while the bank is still operating and solvent, so it prevents failure.
Gone-concern capital absorbs losses only after failure (in resolution, curatorship or liquidation), so it protects senior depositors and creditors but does not stop the bank failing.
Tier | Nature | Components
Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) | Core capital; going concern; highest quality | Ordinary share capital, share premium, retained earnings (appropriated and unappropriated), other/statutory reserves, less the regulatory deductions (Section 3.7).
Additional Tier 1 (AT1) | Going concern | Perpetual non-cumulative preference shares; undated hybrid instruments with contingent write-down / bail-in features.
Tier 2 | Gone concern | Term subordinated debt that is Basel III compliant; general debt impairment allowances (up to 1.25% of credit RWA); long-term revaluation reserves.
Tier 1 = CET1 + AT1 | Total capital = Tier 1 + Tier 2
CET1 terms: ordinary share capital is money paid in for the par value of shares; share premium is the amount paid above par; retained earnings are past profits not paid out as dividends; statutory reserves are reserves set aside under law. All absorb losses with no legal default and no fixed claim on the bank: the bank can simply stop paying dividends.
AT1 terms: perpetual means no maturity date; non-cumulative means a skipped dividend is not owed later; contingent write-down / bail-in means that if capital falls below a trigger, the instrument is written off or converted into ordinary shares automatically, so the investor takes the loss. Bail-in (investors absorb losses) contrasts with bail-out (the state injects money).
Tier 2 terms: term subordinated debt has a fixed maturity and ranks below depositors and ordinary creditors (but above shareholders) in a failure; general debt impairment allowances are provisions for losses expected but not yet linked to specific loans; revaluation reserves are unrealised gains from revaluing assets such as property.
Not capital at all: deposits, ordinary long-term debt instruments, derivative liabilities and provisions. Only subordinated debt that is stated to be Basel III compliant counts (as Tier 2).
The problem with tiers: why Basel III focuses on CET1
Under Basel I and II, capital was defined broadly as Tier 1 + Tier 2. Hyun Song Shin (2009) showed that before the 2008 crisis the total capital ratio looked flat and healthy (above 10%), and the Tier 1 ratio (which included preference shares) even rose slightly, but the common equity (CET1) ratio was falling sharply (for example at Northern Rock, the British bank that suffered a run in 2007). Regulators watching the headline ratios saw nothing wrong while the real loss-absorbing core shrank.
Banks were replacing ordinary shares and retained earnings with preference shares (fixed dividend, rank ahead of ordinary shares, no ownership upside) and subordinated debt.
Why subordinated debt cannot prevent failure: interest on it is a contractual obligation, and skipping it is a default that itself causes failure. It absorbs losses only once the bank is already in liquidation or curatorship (gone concern). Ordinary equity, in contrast, can stop paying dividends and absorb losses with no legal default.
Why banks preferred these hybrids: they are cheaper than ordinary equity (investors have more protection, so demand a lower return), and interest on debt is tax-deductible. Counting them as capital let banks meet the ratio at a lower funding cost, which raised ROE, the managers’ target.
Basel III therefore sets a separate minimum for CET1, tightens what counts as AT1 and Tier 2, and requires the deductions in Section 3.7.
Basel III minimum capital ratios
Ratio | Formula | Minimum
CET1 ratio | (CET1)/(RWA) | 4.5% (7.0% with the 2.5% conservation buffer)
Tier 1 ratio | (Tier1)/(RWA) | 6.0% (8.5% with buffer)
Total capital ratio (CAR) | (Tier1+Tier2)/(RWA) | 8.0% (10.5% with buffer), plus D-SIB surcharge of 1%–2.5% and Pillar 2 add-ons
Leverage ratio | (Tier1)/(exposure measure) | 3%
The Tier 1 minimum of 6% and the “with buffer” totals for Tier 1 and total capital are the standard Basel III figures; the course material states the 8% total, the 4.5% + 2.5% CET1 and the 3% leverage minimums. In an exam, use whatever minimum the question gives.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance > 3.7 From accounting equity to regulatory capital: the deductions
x:
Accounting equity includes items that look like capital but would not absorb losses in a crisis. Basel requires them to be removed. The test for every item is: would it still be worth something to pay depositors if the bank were failing and being wound up?
Mandatory deductions (taken out of CET1, and therefore also out of Tier 1 and total capital)
Item | What it is | Why it is deducted | How much
Goodwill | The premium paid when buying another company for more than the fair value of its net assets. | Has no market value on its own and vanishes if the business fails. | 100%
Intangible assets, including capitalised software | Assets with no physical form; “capitalised” means the cost was recorded as an asset rather than expensed. | Nobody will pay for a failed bank’s legacy IT code or other intangibles; no liquidation value. | 100%
Deferred tax asset (DTA) dependent on future taxable income | Tax relief the bank can use only against future tax bills (for example after tax losses). | Only valuable if the bank makes future taxable profits, which is precisely what a failing bank does not do. | Only the portion stated as dependent on future profits (or not allowed as capital). A DTA from temporary differences may be allowed (subject to caps of 10%/20% of CET1).
Cash-flow hedging reserve | An equity reserve holding unrealised gains or losses on derivatives used to hedge future cash flows. | Volatile and reverses as the hedged cash flows occur; not a permanent loss absorber (a “prudential filter”). | 100% (whatever its sign: a positive reserve is deducted)
Reciprocal cross-holdings / significant investments in other financial institutions’ capital | Bank A holds capital of bank B and B holds capital of A. | The same rand is counted as capital twice, and losses at one bank travel to the other (contagion). | As prescribed
What is not deducted: money owed to the bank by the Receiver of Revenue (a tax refund receivable from SARS) is a real claim on the government and stays in capital. Read “Taxation assets” carefully: deduct only the deferred-tax part that depends on future income, or the part stated as not allowed.
Wording traps: “90% of the DTA is dependent on future taxable income” → deduct 90%. “80% of the DTA is due to temporary differences and is allowed as capital” → deduct the other 20%.
Items that are not deductions but move between tiers
Preference shares and AT1 instruments are in accounting equity and in Tier 1, but are not common equity. Remove them to get from Tier 1 to CET1; keep them for Tier 1, total capital and the leverage ratio.
Basel III compliant subordinated debt sits in liabilities. It is Tier 2: add it for total capital only. It never enters CET1, Tier 1 or the leverage ratio.
Regulatory adjustment for provisions
A provision for bad debt (impairment) is an expense that reduces profit, retained earnings and therefore equity. If the regulator judges the provision to have been overly aggressive (too large) by an amount X, equity is understated by X; the excess is in effect a hidden reserve that can absorb losses, so add X back to capital. (If a provision is judged too small, the reverse applies: deduct the shortfall.) Tax effects are ignored unless the question gives them.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance > 3.8 How to calculate the capital ratios step by step
x:
All capital questions follow the same ladder. Start from total equity on the balance sheet, then walk down or up.
Total equity (from the balance sheet)
↓ less mandatory deductions: goodwill, intangibles/capitalised software, DTA dependent on future profits, cash-flow hedging reserve (± provision adjustment)
Tier 1 capital (still includes preference shares and AT1)
↓ less preference shares and AT1 instruments
CET1 capital
Tier 1 capital
↓ plus Basel III compliant subordinated debt (and other Tier 2 items)
Total capital
CET1 ratio = (CET1)/(RWA ) ;| Tier 1 ratio = (Tier1)/(RWA ) ;| Total capital ratio = (Total capital)/(RWA)
Method
Write down total equity exactly as given. Ignore deposits and other ordinary liabilities: they are not capital.
Deduct goodwill, intangible assets and capitalised software in full.
Deduct only the stated portion of the deferred tax asset (dependent on future income / not allowed). Leave tax receivable from SARS in.
Deduct the cash-flow hedging reserve if it appears in equity.
Adjust for provisions if the regulator says they were too aggressive (add back) or too low (deduct). The result is Tier 1.
For CET1: from Tier 1, subtract preference shares and AT1 instruments.
For total capital: to Tier 1, add Basel III compliant subordinated debt (Tier 2).
Divide by RWA (never by total assets or total liabilities) and compare with the minimum. State clearly whether the bank complies.
Common errors (the wrong options in multiple-choice questions)
Dividing by total assets instead of RWA (that is an unweighted equity-to-assets measure).
Forgetting to remove preference shares and AT1 from CET1 (this gives a Tier 1 ratio, which is higher).
Adding subordinated debt into CET1 (it is Tier 2 only).
Adding cash and SARB balances to capital (they are assets: liquidity, not capital).
Deducting the whole taxation asset instead of only the dependent DTA portion.
Dividing liquid assets by liabilities (that is the cash reserve ratio, Section 3.10).
Worked example: Bank Y – Tier 1, CET1 and total capital ratios
Balance sheet of Bank Y (R million):
Assets | Liabilities and equity
Cash and cash equivalents | 6 000 | Deposits | 320 000
Mandatory reserve deposits at the SARB | 9 000 | Derivative liabilities | 14 000
Government securities | 40 000 | Long-term debt instruments | 10 000
Loans and advances to clients | 300 000 | Subordinated debt (Basel III compliant) | 3 000
Derivative assets | 15 000 | Total liabilities | 347 000
Taxation assets* | 1 000 | Ordinary share capital and premium | 8 000
Capitalised software | 3 000 | Retained earnings | 19 000
Goodwill | 2 000 | Cash-flow hedging reserve | 1 000
Property | 4 000 | Perpetual preference shares | 2 000
AT1 instruments | 3 000
Total equity | 33 000
Total | 380 000 | Total | 380 000
* 40% of taxation assets is a refund owed by SARS; 60% is a DTA dependent on future taxable income. Risk weights: government-related items 0%; loans 60%; derivatives 100%; property 100%. Off-balance-sheet items add 20 000 to RWA.
Step 1 – RWA. Loans 60% × 300 000 = 180 000; derivatives 100% × 15 000 = 15 000; property 100% × 4 000 = 4 000. On-balance-sheet RWA = 199 000; plus off-balance-sheet 20 000; total RWA = 219 000. (Cash, SARB deposits, government securities and the SARS refund are 0%; software, goodwill and the dependent DTA are left out because they are deducted from capital.) Sense check: (219 000)/(380 000) = 58% of assets, close to the “about half” benchmark.
Total equity | 33 000
Less cash-flow hedging reserve | (1 000)
Less DTA dependent on future income (60% × 1 000) | (600)
Less capitalised software | (3 000)
Less goodwill | (2 000)
Tier 1 capital | 26 400
Less perpetual preference shares | (2 000)
Less AT1 instruments | (3 000)
CET1 capital | 21 400
Total capital = Tier 1 26 400 + subordinated debt 3 000 = 29 400.
Ratios: CET1 ratio = (21 400)/(219 000) = 9.77% (above 7.0%); Tier 1 ratio = (26 400)/(219 000) = 12.05%; total capital ratio = (29 400)/(219 000) = 13.42% (above 8%).
Can the bank afford a dividend? (dividend capacity given a minimum ratio)
A cash dividend reduces retained earnings (so CET1, Tier 1 and total capital all fall by the full amount) and reduces cash (so liquid assets fall by the same amount). RWA does not change, because cash carries a 0% risk weight, and liabilities do not change. A dividend is affordable only if the bank still meets every minimum afterwards.
Capital test: required capital = minimum ratio × RWA. Headroom = capital held − required capital. If the ratio is already below the minimum, no dividend can be paid (any payment makes it worse).
Liquidity test: required cash = minimum reserve ratio × total liabilities (Section 3.10). Headroom = cash resources held − required cash.
Repeat the capital test for each ratio given (CET1, Tier 1, total capital).
Maximum dividend = the smallest headroom. The bank can pay the proposed dividend only if it is no larger than this. State which test binds.
Worked example: Bank Y dividend capacity
Bank Y must keep a total capital ratio of at least 12%, a CET1 ratio of at least 7% and a cash reserve ratio of at least 3%. What is the largest dividend it can pay?
Total capital: required 12% × 219 000 = 26 280; held 29 400; headroom 3 120.
CET1: required 7% × 219 000 = 15 330; held 21 400; headroom 6 070.
Cash: required 3% × 347 000 = 10 410; held 6 000 + 9 000 = 15 000; headroom 4 590.
Maximum dividend = 3 120: the total capital requirement binds. After paying 3 120, total capital is 26 280 (exactly 12.0%), CET1 is 18 280 (8.35%) and cash is 11 880 (3.42%).
Interpretation: a bank can pass the liquidity test and still be unable to pay a dividend because it fails the capital test (or the reverse). Both must be checked.
Exam focus: 2019 MCQ 3 (CET1 ratio with preference shares, goodwill and a partly-dependent DTA); 2020 Section B Q3(b)–(d) (Tier 1 from total equity, then CET1, then CET1 ratio); 2021 Section C Q3(a)–(c), (e) (why capital matters, pricing known risks, total capital ratio with sub-debt and provision add-back, dividend affordability against an 8% capital and 3% cash minimum); 2023 MCQ 5 (CET1 ratio with cash-flow hedging reserve and a 20% disallowed DTA).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance > 3.9 The leverage ratio
x:
Leverage ratio = (Tier 1 capital)/(Exposure measure) ≥ 3%Exposure measure = on-balance-sheet assets (less the assets already deducted from capital) + off-balance-sheet exposures (after credit conversion factors)
Why it exists: banks were gaming the risk-weighting process, choosing (especially with internal models) risk weights that were too low so that they needed less capital. Example: in 2013 European banks held Greek government bonds (Greece had a sovereign debt crisis and its bonds lost value in 2010–12). Some assigned a 0% risk weight (OECD status) while others used 50% or 60%: the same asset carried very different weights because models were being used to minimise capital.
The leverage ratio uses no risk weights, so it cannot be gamed in this way. It is a backstop: a simple, hard-to-manipulate second line of defence behind the risk-based ratios. However low the risk weights are pushed, the balance sheet cannot grow beyond about 33 times Tier 1 capital ( (1)/(3%) ).
Off-balance-sheet exposures are commitments that are not assets today but can become real exposures, converted with credit conversion factors (CCFs) (percentages estimating how much of the commitment will actually be drawn). Examples: an undrawn overdraft or credit facility (a R1m limit with a nil balance becomes an on-balance-sheet loan if the client draws it, and clients draw exactly when the economy is bad); letters of credit (a bank’s promise to pay a seller on behalf of a buyer, used in trade finance) and guarantees (a promise to pay if a third party defaults), which become real claims if the counterparty defaults.
Levels: Basel III minimum 3%; South African banks hold about 5%–8%.
How to calculate the leverage ratio (method)
Numerator = Tier 1 capital: total equity less goodwill, intangibles/software, the dependent DTA and the cash-flow hedging reserve. Keep preference shares and AT1 (they are Tier 1). Do not add subordinated debt (Tier 2).
Denominator = exposure measure: start with total assets (not RWA); subtract the assets that were deducted from capital (goodwill, software/intangibles, dependent DTA), so that they are counted neither as capital nor as exposure. The hedging reserve is not an asset, so it is not subtracted from the denominator.
Add off-balance-sheet exposures if given (after CCFs if these are given).
Divide and compare with 3%.
Worked example: Bank Y leverage ratio
Using Bank Y above, with off-balance-sheet exposures (after CCFs) of 25 000.
Tier 1 = 26 400 (from Section 3.8; preference shares and AT1 kept, sub-debt excluded).
Exposure measure = 380 000 − 600 (DTA) − 3 000 (software) − 2 000 (goodwill) + 25 000 = 399 400.
Leverage ratio = (26 400)/(399 400) = 6.61%, above the 3% minimum. (Without off-balance-sheet items: (26 400)/(374 400) = 7.05%.)
Common errors: dividing by RWA (the leverage ratio deliberately ignores risk weights); adding Tier 2 sub-debt; computing (total assets)/(total equity) (that is the equity multiplier from the ROE decomposition, not the Basel leverage ratio).
Exam focus: 2023 MCQ 6 (Basel III leverage ratio with deductions taken from both numerator and denominator).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance > 3.10 Liquidity (1): the SARB cash reserve requirement
x:
A bank can be solvent on paper and still fail because it is illiquid: it cannot meet withdrawals as they fall due because its assets are long-term loans that cannot be sold quickly. Banks “borrow short and lend long” (maturity transformation), so they can never repay all depositors at once.
Bank reserves (settlement balances) are the balances commercial banks hold in their accounts at the SARB. They are an asset of the commercial bank and a liability of the SARB. Banks use them to settle payments with one another.
The cash reserve requirement: banks must hold a minimum of 2.5% of their liabilities as reserves at the SARB. These minimum reserves earn 0% interest, so they are effectively a small tax on banks; their purpose is mainly to guarantee a base level of demand for central bank money.
Under the SARB’s surplus (tiered-floor) system since 2022, reserves above the minimum earn the policy rate up to a quota per bank and the policy rate less 1% above the quota; vault cash (notes and coin) still earns nothing. Banks therefore prefer surplus reserves to physical cash and economise on notes in ATMs and vaults (at a 7% policy rate, R1bn of notes costs R70m a year in forgone interest).
Why the level is a social choice: every rand held as non-interest-bearing reserves is not lent out, so banks push liquidity as low as they dare. If a bank failed for lack of cash, society might raise the requirement to 3%, but the opportunity cost is passed on to borrowers through higher loan rates.
How to calculate the cash reserve ratio by the SARB method
Cash reserve ratio = (Cash resources)/(Total liabilities) Cash resources = cash in vaults / cash and cash equivalents + balance at the SARB / mandatory reserve deposits with the central bank
Numerator: add only the bank’s cash resources: vault cash (or “cash and cash equivalents”) plus the balance or mandatory reserve deposits at the SARB. Do not include government securities, loans or a committed SARB overdraft facility (an unused facility is not cash held).
Denominator: total liabilities, the claims that could be withdrawn. Exclude equity: dividing by total liabilities and equity (i.e. total assets) is the classic wrong answer. Do not use deposits alone, total assets or RWA.
If the question says to treat off-balance-sheet liabilities as on-balance-sheet, add them to total liabilities.
Divide and compare with the required minimum (2.5%, or the rate the question gives).
How to calculate excess liquidity
Required reserves = minimum ratio × total liabilities.
Held = cash resources (as above).
Excess liquidity = held − required. A positive result is excess; a negative result is a shortfall.
Worked example: Bank Y cash reserve ratio and excess liquidity
Cash resources = 6 000 + 9 000 = 15 000. Total liabilities = 347 000 (equity excluded).
Cash reserve ratio = (15 000)/(347 000) = 4.32%.
Required at 2.5% = 2.5% × 347 000 = 8 675. Excess liquidity = 15 000 − 8 675 = 6 325.
Wrong denominator check: (15 000)/(380 000) (total liabilities and equity) = 3.95% – incorrect, because equity cannot be withdrawn.
If the bank also had off-balance-sheet liabilities of 50 000 to be treated as on-balance-sheet: (15 000)/(397 000) = 3.78%.
Why banks hold excess liquidity even though it drags on profit
Precaution: the bank expects difficult economic times or abnormal withdrawals and holds a buffer. Even without any regulation, management wants reserves at the SARB to meet withdrawals and settle payments, and so avoid the cost of emergency funding or a run.
Other liquidity rules bind: the reserve requirement is not the only liquidity rule. The LCR and NSFR (Section 3.11) may require high-quality liquid assets well above the simple reserve ratio.
Lack of profitable lending: weak loan demand or too few creditworthy borrowers.
Surplus reserves now earn interest: since 2022, reserves above the minimum (up to the quota) earn the policy rate, so holding them is less costly than before.
The cost side: reserves and cash earn little or nothing, so holding more of them lowers profitability, all else equal.
Relationship between bank reserves and bank capital
Model answer.
Bank reserves are balances held by banks on account at the central bank.
Bank capital is the regulator-allowed excess of a bank’s assets over its liabilities.
Reserves are therefore part of the asset base that must exceed liabilities, but they are not capital: reserves sit on the asset side, while capital is a source of funding on the liability-and-equity side.
Reserves are liquid assets that protect against liquidity problems; capital protects against solvency problems (losses). Cash can be funded by deposits or by capital; holding more cash does not by itself create capital.
Exam focus: 2019 MCQ 4 (reserve ratio by the SARB method: denominator is total liabilities, not total liabilities and equity); 2020 Section B Q3(e)–(f) (excess liquidity at a 2.5% minimum; reasons for holding excess liquidity); 2021 Section C Q3(d) (cash reserve ratio with off-balance-sheet liabilities added to the denominator); 2023 Section C Q5.2 (reserves vs capital); 2019 MCQ 6 (reserves, capital and profitability).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance > 3.11 Liquidity (2): the Basel III LCR and NSFR
x:
The 2007–08 crisis showed that many banks failed because short-term funding dried up, not because capital ran out first. Basel III added two quantitative liquidity ratios. Capital protects against insolvency; these protect against illiquidity.
Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR): surviving 30 days of stress
LCR = (Stock of high-quality liquid assets (HQLA))/(Total net cash outflows over the next 30 days of stress)≥100% Net cash outflows = stressed outflows − stressed inflows
The LCR asks: could the bank meet 30 days of stressed outflows from its liquid assets alone, without selling anything illiquid or relying on markets?
HQLA are assets that can be turned into cash quickly, at little loss, even in a crisis, and that are unencumbered (not already pledged as collateral). In course calculations HQLA = cash in vaults + balance at the SARB + a committed overdraft facility at the SARB (a pre-arranged line the bank is entitled to draw in stress, so it counts as available liquidity), plus government bonds where given.
Stressed outflows are the cash expected to leave in a hypothetical crisis: deposit withdrawals (more for wholesale and uninsured deposits than for stable retail deposits), loss of wholesale funding, drawdowns of committed credit lines. Inflows are cash expected in (for example loan repayments) and are netted off.
HQLA level | Examples | Haircut and limit
Level 1 | Cash, central bank reserves, 0%-risk-weight sovereign bonds | No haircut; no limit
Level 2A | 20%-risk-weight sovereign and public-sector bonds; high-rated corporate and covered bonds | 15% haircut
Level 2B | Lower-rated corporate bonds, certain listed equities, some residential mortgage-backed securities | 25%–50% haircut
Level 2 assets in total may be at most 40% of HQLA (Level 2B at most 15%). Inflows may offset at most 75% of outflows.
The HQLA levels, haircuts, caps and the 75% inflow cap are the standard Basel III rules; the course material defines HQLA in words and, in calculations, counts cash, the SARB balance and a committed SARB facility. Use what the question gives.
How to calculate the LCR (method)
Numerator (HQLA): add cash in vaults, balances at the SARB, any committed SARB facility, and qualifying government bonds (after haircuts if levels are given).
Denominator: the estimated net cash outflow over 30 days of stress (outflows less inflows, if given separately).
Divide; the bank complies if the LCR is at least 100%.
Traps: the ratio is HQLA over outflows, not inverted (outflows over cash); the denominator is never RWA or total assets; the horizon is 30 days, not 25.
Worked example: LCR
A bank holds vault cash of 4 000, a balance at the SARB of 7 000 and government bonds (Level 1) of 9 000, and has a committed overdraft facility at the SARB of 2 000. In a 30-day stress scenario it expects outflows of 24 000 and inflows of 6 000.
HQLA = 4 000 + 7 000 + 9 000 + 2 000 = 22 000. Net cash outflows = 24 000 − 6 000 = 18 000.
LCR = (22 000)/(18 000) = 122%, above 100%: the bank meets the requirement. (Inverted, (18 000)/(22 000) = 82% would wrongly suggest a shortfall.)
Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR): structural funding over one year
NSFR = (Available stable funding (ASF))/(Required stable funding (RSF)) ≥ 100% (one-year horizon)
Long-term, illiquid assets should be funded with stable funding (equity, long-term debt, sticky retail deposits), not volatile short-term wholesale money. It attacks the maturity-transformation problem directly: the more a bank lends long, the more stable funding it needs.
ASF = each funding source weighted by how likely it is to stay for a year (for example equity and liabilities over one year 100%, stable retail deposits about 90%–95%, short-term wholesale funding 0%–50%).
RSF = each asset weighted by how illiquid it is (for example cash and reserves 0%, government bonds about 5%, mortgages about 65%, other loans about 85%, fixed assets 100%).
Lesson behind it: Northern Rock funded long-term mortgages with short-term wholesale money, which disappeared in 2007; the NSFR limits exactly that reliance.
The ASF and RSF factors above are typical standard Basel III values, given for understanding; the course defines the NSFR in words (one-year structural funding, ASF ≥ RSF).
Why both ratios? The LCR covers a sudden crisis in the next month (a run); the NSFR covers the slow build-up of maturity mismatch over a year. The simple cash reserve requirement (2.5% of liabilities) is a separate SARB rule on top of both.
Where a bank sources liquidity
Model answer: where should a treasury manager source liquidity if the shortage is…
Small and completely predictable: from the cheapest source, usually retail deposits, by offering depositors a slightly higher rate. There is time to attract a little extra funding, so no emergency premium has to be paid.
Large and unexpected: this is a potential crisis. Try other banks (the interbank market), which may be cheaper, but news of the shortage can cause contagion; approach the SARB as lender of last resort for emergency, expensive funding against collateral. In practice do both.
Structural (caused by how the bank does business, e.g. funding long loans with short deposits): borrowing each time does not fix it. Change the business plan: lengthen funding (long-term debt, term deposits), hold more liquid assets, shorten asset maturities or reprice products.
Exam focus: 2019 MCQ 5 (LCR including a committed SARB facility); 2020 Section B Q3(f) (LCR and NSFR as reasons for excess liquidity); 2023 MCQ 8 (30-day horizon); 2023 Section C Q5.1 (sourcing liquidity).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 3 – How banks are regulated: capital, liquidity and deposit insurance > 3.12 Deposit insurance and moral hazard
x:
What deposit insurance is and why it exists
Deposit insurance is a scheme in which an agency guarantees that depositors get their money back, up to a limit, if their bank fails, paid from a fund built from premiums (levies) charged to the banks. It has two purposes:
Prevent bank runs. A run is a coordination failure: if depositors fear others will withdraw first, withdrawing is individually rational even at a solvent bank, and the run becomes self-fulfilling. Insured depositors are repaid whatever others do, so they have no reason to run. Deposit insurance is credible only if it pays out fast.
Protect small depositors, who cannot judge a bank’s soundness.
The Corporation for Deposit Insurance (CODI) in South Africa
Feature | Detail
Legal basis and status | Set up under the Financial Sector Laws Amendment Act of 2021; a subsidiary of the SARB. Established 24 March 2023; active from April 2024. South Africa was one of the few G20 countries without explicit deposit insurance before this.
Coverage | R100 000 per qualifying depositor per bank, covering principal and accrued interest on qualifying products (savings accounts, including stokvels).
Aggregation | All accounts at the same bank are added together: R100 000 in each of two accounts at one bank is covered up to R100 000 in total. Each separate bank gives a fresh limit: R100 000 at one bank and R100 000 at another are covered up to R200 000.
Who qualifies | Individuals and small non-financial businesses. Excluded: institutional investors (pension funds, asset managers), financial corporates and large wholesale or treasury deposits, which must monitor bank risk themselves.
Funding | Levies on banks, so the industry pays for the safety net it benefits from; payouts come from the fund, not from taxpayers.
How it works | When a bank fails, CODI pays covered depositors up to the limit from its fund. The failed bank’s loans remain assets of its estate (borrowers must keep repaying), and collecting them is how depositors and CODI are repaid.
Before CODI | No explicit promise: depositors relied on an implicit expectation that the authorities would step in (curatorship, lender of last resort, ad hoc guarantees such as the SARB’s R100 000 guarantee at VBS), which created uncertainty and moral hazard.
Why a limit of R100 000 “per depositor per bank”? It covers the large majority of retail depositors, who are least able to monitor a bank and most likely to panic, while institutions and large depositors stay uncovered and keep the incentive to watch the bank’s health. Full cover would make every depositor indifferent to bank risk.
Example in practice: when Ditsobotla Primary Co-operative Bank failed, CODI paid its depositors up to R100 000 each without a taxpayer bail-out, while borrowers were told their loans remained legally binding.
Why a large corporate depositor is barely protected (MultiChoice’s roughly US$21m in a failed Nigerian bank, where the liquidator was Nigeria’s deposit insurer, NDIC): the cap is tiny relative to the balance; schemes deliberately exclude sophisticated corporates and wholesale deposits, which can assess counterparty risk and diversify; and covering them would require taxpayer money and destroy market discipline. Lesson for a corporate treasurer: treat a bank deposit as an unsecured loan to the bank, set counterparty limits by rating and capital strength, diversify and keep money short-term.
When most deposits are uninsured, runs are fast: over 90% of Silicon Valley Bank’s deposits were above the US$250 000 insurance limit, so depositors had every incentive to run.
Deposit insurance creates moral hazard
Moral hazard is taking more risk because someone else bears the cost of the downside (like an insured driver who drives less carefully).
Insured depositors no longer monitor bank risk or punish a risky bank by withdrawing or demanding a higher rate. The bank pays no price in its deposit rates for taking more risk.
Combined with limited liability and thin capital, this gives shareholders an asymmetric pay-off: “heads shareholders win, tails depositors / the insurer / the state lose”. Example: a bank with R100 of assets and R5 of equity makes a risky bet. A R10 gain triples its equity to R15; a R10 loss wipes out the R5 of equity and loses R5 of depositors’ money, which the shareholders never repay.
Too big to fail (TBTF) is the same problem for a whole bank: if creditors believe the government will rescue a large bank, they lend to it cheaply regardless of its risk, which encourages more risk. The best evidence of a TBTF subsidy is that large, risky banks borrow at unusually favourable rates compared with smaller peers.
Banking contains several moral hazards at once: shareholders versus depositors; deposit insurance; TBTF expectations; the lender of last resort (may encourage banks to hold less liquidity); managers’ bonuses (reward short-term profit, do not penalise later losses); and borrowers who take more risk after receiving a loan.
How regulation contains the moral hazard
Limit the cover (R100 000; exclude institutions) so that large, sophisticated depositors keep market discipline: the pressure on banks from creditors who charge more or withdraw from risky banks.
Charge the banks for the cover through levies, so the industry rather than the taxpayer funds the scheme.
Require more and better capital (CET1), so shareholders have more to lose and failure is less likely; add the unweighted leverage ratio so risk weights cannot be gamed; set minimum liquidity (LCR, NSFR) so that a sudden run can be survived.
Keep intervention triggers vague (constructive ambiguity), so banks cannot count on an automatic rescue.
Model answer: does deposit insurance make the banking system safer? It removes the main trigger of runs (small depositors racing to withdraw) and protects those least able to monitor banks, so it makes runs and contagion less likely. But it creates moral hazard: insured depositors stop monitoring, and shareholders, protected by limited liability, can take more risk at no extra funding cost. The scheme is therefore designed to limit this: capped cover per depositor per bank, exclusion of institutional and wholesale depositors (who keep monitoring), funding by bank levies, and the combination with capital, leverage and liquidity rules that force shareholders to keep enough of their own money at risk.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 4 – Bank failure
x:
Regulation (Parts 1–3) aims to keep banks safe, yet banks still fail. The regulator faces a balance: regulating banks until failure is impossible makes credit so expensive that lending dries up and growth suffers, while letting a systemic bank fail (in South Africa, a bank such as Standard Bank) would bring the economy to a standstill. Bank failure is always analysed from the regulator’s perspective (the SARB and its Prudential Authority, PA), not from that of an equity analyst or investor. An investor asks “can I make or recover money?”; the regulator asks “will the failure spread to other banks and the payment system, and will ordinary depositors be harmed?”. Four concerns drive the regulator:
Financial stability – the financial system keeps working (payments, saving, lending) when shocks hit.
Systemic risk – the risk that one institution’s failure spreads to others and endangers the whole system. A bank is systemic if it is so large or interconnected that its failure would do this.
Moral hazard – people take more risk when someone else bears the downside (for example when shareholders or creditors expect a bail-out).
Depositor protection – ordinary savers cannot assess a bank’s health, so the state protects them.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 4 – Bank failure > What bank failure is
x:
The two buffers: capital and liquidity
A safe bank has plenty of capital and liquidity.
Capital (equity) is assets minus liabilities: the owners’ funds, the cushion that absorbs losses before creditors lose anything. It protects against insolvency.
Liquidity is having cash, or assets that can be turned into cash immediately at close to full value, to meet withdrawals. The best such assets are HQLA (high-quality liquid assets): cash, balances at the central bank and government bonds that can be sold or pledged to the central bank at once. Liquidity protects against illiquidity.
The spectrum of definitions
There is no single line which, once crossed, means a bank has failed. Failure is a grey, multi-dimensional concept involving the balance sheet, cash flow, regulatory action and market confidence. The main definitions (and indicators) are:
Definition | Meaning | SA example
Insolvency (balance-sheet or textbook definition) | The fairly valued liabilities exceed the assets, so equity is negative. Example: assets R95, liabilities R100, equity –R5; even selling everything would not repay all creditors. Fair value = what the assets could realistically be sold for, not their book value. Usually caused by credit losses (borrowers default), market losses on securities, or fraud. | VBS (2018); also Barings (UK)
Illiquidity (operational or cash-flow failure) | The bank cannot pay withdrawals or maturing creditors as they fall due (a run or funding freeze), even though its assets may exceed its liabilities. Not universally accepted as a stand-alone definition: no bank can pay all depositors at once, so every solvent bank is assumed to be able to rely on the central bank as lender of last resort. | Saambou (2002)
Regulatory or administrative intervention | The regulator takes control: curatorship (old regime: a curator takes over running the bank and protects creditors, with a moratorium holding off creditors while a rescue is found) or resolution (new regime: the authority restructures, splits or sells the bank so its critical functions continue, using powers such as bail-in), or the banking licence is withdrawn (deregistration, after which the entity may no longer take deposits and is wound up). Usually the outward sign of one of the other definitions, or of fraud. | African Bank (2014); Ditsobotla (2025, resolution)
Breach of regulatory minimums | The bank fails a statutory capital ratio (e.g. CET1 below 4.5% of risk-weighted assets) or liquidity ratio (LCR below 100%). A breach does not mean the bank is insolvent, but it triggers supervisory action. | –
Rescue (bail-out, state guarantee or forced takeover) | The bank survives only because the state guarantees its liabilities, injects funds or forces a merger. Whether this counts as failure is debatable: the institution disappears or loses independence, but creditors are protected. | BOE (2002); abroad Northern Rock, Credit Suisse
Broad market definition | Sustained loss of confidence by depositors, shareholders or wholesale creditors: share-price collapse and exclusion from funding markets. | African Bank’s two-year slide
Failure (textbook) = insolvency: Liabilities > Assets (equity < 0)
How the definitions relate
Illiquidity can cause insolvency: a run forces fire sales below fair value, and the losses destroy capital.
Insolvency causes illiquidity: once creditors learn (or suspect) that the bank cannot repay everyone, they withdraw or stop lending.
Loss of confidence is the transmission mechanism between the two.
Regulatory intervention is usually the response to one or more of the others (or to fraud), not a separate cause. A regulator may also act before insolvency is proven, so a bank can “fail” on the intervention definition while still solvent (Saambou).
Combinations are possible: solvent but illiquid (Saambou, Northern Rock), insolvent but liquid for a while (VBS, which kept paying out from fresh municipal deposits while its equity was gone).
Failure as a process, not an event
An accountant sees insolvency as a snapshot: solvent on Tuesday, insolvent on Wednesday. To a bank regulator (as explained by Fundi Tshazibana, SARB Deputy Governor and CEO of the Prudential Authority), failure is an ongoing process of deteriorating soundness (rising bad loans, falling profits, thinning capital), an unsustainable business model (e.g. funding long-term loans with volatile short-term money) and loss of confidence. Loss of confidence shows up in three groups:
Depositor run – panicked withdrawal of deposits (queues at branches, mass online transfers).
Shareholder flight – the share price collapses as owners sell, which alarms depositors and makes new equity expensive.
Wholesale creditor freeze – institutions (asset managers, pension funds, corporates, other banks) refuse to roll over (re-lend at maturity) commercial paper, bonds or interbank lines, so the bank cannot refinance and its cash runs out.
Why the regulator cannot wait for insolvency: by the time assets are officially worth less than liabilities, liquid reserves are gone, fire sales (forced sales at distressed prices) have destroyed value and the damage has spread to other institutions (contagion). Failure is self-reinforcing – lost confidence → withdrawals → asset sales at a discount → eroded capital → deeper loss of confidence (a death spiral). The PA therefore intervenes when a bank is judged to be on an irreversible path to failure (bad loans, aggressive accounting, governance scandals), even if management claims the bank is still technically solvent. Early action limits systemic losses.
Why regulators keep the definition grey
Even Havemann’s PhD on South African bank failures (Lessons from South African Bank Failures) contains no formal definition; the supervisor’s explanation was “We all know what bank failure is when we see it.”
Constructive ambiguity: central banks deliberately keep the triggers for intervention or emergency liquidity vague. A published rule (“we always rescue below liquidity level X”) would create moral hazard: executives would run the bank at exactly X+1, and creditors would stop monitoring because they know where the safety net starts.
Flexibility: every crisis differs; ambiguity lets the regulator act before systemic damage occurs without committing to automatic bail-outs.
The trade-off: intervening too late lets asset values deteriorate and raises losses for depositors and taxpayers; intervening too early invites political backlash, shareholder lawsuits and the accusation that the regulator caused the failure. African Bank’s CEO Leon Kirkinis argued the bank would have traded out of its bad loans without curatorship; critics argued the SARB acted prematurely against Saambou (an Afrikaner-oriented bank) while helping larger English-oriented banks.
What is NOT bank failure
Being unable to pay all depositors at the same time. Banks perform maturity transformation: they take deposits withdrawable on demand and lend them out for years (a 20-year home loan funded by cheque-account balances). A bank with R100 of deposits may hold only R10–R15 in cash and HQLA. No bank holds 100% cash; this is what lets banks lend, and is an inherent feature of banking, not a failure.
Temporary system breakdowns (online banking down for a few hours), unless they reflect chronic management incompetence. Solvency and liquidity are unaffected.
A run on a solvent bank that the central bank stabilises without a takeover (Bank of East Asia, 2008, below).
Model answer: What is bank failure? Give and explain three definitions, their relationships and an example of each.
Failure is not a single line. There is no universally accepted point at which a bank fails; solvency, liquidity, regulatory action and market confidence interact. A one-sentence answer is not enough.
Insolvency (classic definition): fairly valued liabilities exceed assets, so there is no equity left. It can result from credit losses, fraud or fire-sale losses in a panic. Relationship: insolvency can result from a liquidity problem when assets must be sold at fire-sale values. Example: VBS Mutual Bank, whose fraudulent loans and looting destroyed its equity.
Illiquidity: the bank cannot pay creditors in the ordinary course of business, even if it is solvent. Not broadly accepted on its own, because no bank can pay all depositors at once and it is normally assumed the central bank will lend to every solvent bank. Example: Saambou (2002).
Curatorship / regulatory intervention: the regulator places the bank under curatorship (now resolution) or withdraws its licence, usually because of liquidity problems, insolvency or fraud. Example: African Bank (2014).
Relationships: illiquidity turns into insolvency through fire sales; insolvency triggers illiquidity once creditors discover the losses; curatorship is typically the regulator’s response to either (or to fraud), so the three are often found together. Conclusion: insolvency is the textbook definition and the ultimate cause of most failures, but in practice failure is judged by combining the liquidity, regulatory and market-confidence views.
Exam focus: 2020 Q5 (three definitions, relationships, examples – 10 marks); 2019 Q4.4 (was African Bank a failure? – answer it through the definitions). MCQs test why regulators prefer ambiguity (prevents moral hazard; flexibility to act early without automatic bail-outs).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 4 – Bank failure > Solvency versus liquidity
x:
Dimension | Solvency | Liquidity
Definition | Fair value of assets exceeds liabilities (positive equity). A stock concept: is there enough value? | Ability to meet short-term outflows and on-demand withdrawals as they fall due. A timing concept: is there enough cash today?
Where on the balance sheet | Net equity / capital buffer (Assets – Liabilities = Equity). | Asset side: cash, SARB deposits and unencumbered government bonds (not already pledged, so free to sell or pledge).
Cause of failure | Credit losses, market write-downs or fraud eroding capital below zero. | Sudden deposit withdrawals or inability to roll over wholesale funding.
Remedy | Capital injection, bail-in (creditors’ claims written down or converted to equity), curatorship or resolution. | Lender of last resort (LLR): the central bank lends against good collateral to a solvent bank facing a temporary squeeze.
Interaction | Insolvency causes liquidity flight when creditors discover losses. | Illiquidity forces fire sales whose losses destroy solvency.
Solvent but illiquid: assets R1 000 (mostly long-term loans), liabilities R900, equity R100, but only R50 of cash. A withdrawal of R200 cannot be met without fire sales – solvent on paper, failing in practice. Examples: Saambou, Northern Rock, Bank of East Asia (rescued).
Insolvent but liquid: a bank with large hidden losses can keep paying depositors for a long time because new deposits cover old withdrawals, until the truth emerges. Example: VBS.
Worked example: how a liquidity problem becomes a solvency problem
A bank holds R100 of long-term loans, funded by R92 of deposits and R8 of capital. It is solvent (R100 > R92).
R30 of deposits are withdrawn. The bank must sell loans quickly at 80 cents on the rand: to raise R30 it sells loans with a book value of R37.5, a loss of R7.5.
Capital falls from R8 to R0.5. Another round of withdrawals and fire sales wipes it out completely.
A pure liquidity run has made a solvent bank insolvent – a self-fulfilling prophecy: the fear of failure causes the actions that produce failure. Only a lender of last resort, lending against the loans so they need not be sold, breaks the chain.
How panic and insolvency are linked
Panic → insolvency: to meet withdrawals the bank sells long-term loans and illiquid assets immediately at fire-sale discounts (buyers know the seller is desperate). The losses erode equity.
Insolvency → panic: once creditors discover losses, nobody wants to leave money in a bank that cannot repay everybody, and the first to withdraw is paid in full.
Debt deflation (systemic): forced asset sales push prices down, which lowers the value of the same assets on other banks’ balance sheets, erodes their equity and forces them to sell too – a downward spiral that turns one bank’s trouble into a system-wide crisis.
Solvency cannot be observed during a run. Bank assets are loans whose value is private information, so neither depositors nor regulators can tell in real time whether a bank under pressure is solvent. This is why runs often become self-fulfilling.
The two risks that cause failure, and who handles each
A bank earns its margin by borrowing short at low rates and lending long at higher rates (net interest margin = interest earned on long-term assets – interest paid on short-term liabilities – bad debt; e.g. 9% – 5% – 1.5% bad debts = 2.5%). This exposes it to two risks:
Liquidity (refinancing) risk: short-term funding may not be renewed when it matures, and long-term loans cannot be liquidated instantly. The central bank handles this as lender of last resort. Bagehot’s rule: lend freely, against good collateral, at a penalty rate, to solvent banks in a panic. The SARB provides intraday and overnight liquidity against collateral at the repo rate and has an emergency LLR role (Emergency Liquidity Assistance, ELA). It should not lend to insolvent banks: that would be a bail-out with taxpayers’ money.
Credit risk: borrowers default. Banks must charge for expected losses in their loan pricing; capital is the backstop for unexpected losses. If defaults exceed the capital buffer, assets fall below liabilities and the bank is insolvent.
Model answer: What is the difference between solvency and liquidity? True or false: a bank cannot fail if its assets exceed its liabilities.
Solvency concerns the stock of value: is the fair value of what the bank owns greater than what it owes, so that equity is positive? It is lost through credit losses, market write-downs or fraud. Liquidity concerns timing: can the bank pay what is due today from cash, central bank balances or assets that can be sold or pledged at once? It is lost through sudden withdrawals or failure to roll over wholesale funding. The two are different and not strongly related, but linked in a crisis through fire sales.
False – a bank can fail even if assets exceed liabilities. Because banks borrow short and lend long, a run can exhaust liquid assets before the loans mature. The bank must then sell assets at fire-sale prices, creating losses that cause insolvency, or the regulator intervenes because it cannot meet its obligations (Saambou). The remedies differ: solvency problems need capital, bail-in or resolution; liquidity problems need LLR support.
Exam focus: the difference between solvency and liquidity is a favourite final-exam question; 2023 Q5.3 (VBS: solvency first, then liquidity); 2023 Q5.2 (reserves protect against liquidity problems, capital against solvency problems).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 4 – Bank failure > What causes bank failure: the consensus
x:
Correia, Luck and Verner (2024) studied over a century of US bank failures to see whether failures are driven by panics or by weak fundamentals. Their findings form the consensus view:
Insolvency is the ultimate cause. Runs are rarely purely random panics; a run usually reveals hidden insolvency.
Runs matter, but poor fundamentals usually come first. Failing banks show deteriorating asset quality and weak capital before the run.
Asset quality is the key predictor – non-performing loans (loans on which borrowers have stopped paying) and unacknowledged losses (e.g. US subprime losses in the 2008 global financial crisis, GFC). This supports Basel’s focus on risk-weighted assets.
Weak governance contributes materially – dominant CEOs who overrule risk committees, weak underwriting (the process of assessing and approving loans) and aggressive accounting (reporting profits or valuing loans optimistically to hide losses).
Capital matters – banks with lower capital ratios are more vulnerable to runs when bad news emerges; a thick equity cushion reassures creditors.
Model answer: Critically assess the consensus. Can regulatory slowness or policy errors cause or accelerate bank failure?
Yes – the consensus is useful but incomplete. It was written by Federal Reserve economists, so it naturally emphasises what banks did wrong (bad assets, weak management, thin capital) rather than the supervisor’s own role. Regulators can contribute:
Slow or late action: failing to detect deteriorating assets or fraud lets losses grow (VBS; SVB, where the supervisor did not challenge an obvious unhedged exposure).
Withholding liquidity from solvent banks: in 2002 Saambou was solvent but was placed in curatorship instead of receiving SARB liquidity. This signalled that small banks were unsafe, the panic spread to BOE, and BOE’s deposits had to be guaranteed a month later. Regulatory failure played a major role in the 2002 small-bank crisis.
Poor communication: news that a bank has asked for help can start the run (Northern Rock).
Regulatory design: rules can encourage risk (zero risk weights on sovereign debt, later addressed by the leverage ratio; lighter rules for US banks below $250bn, which applied to SVB).
Conclusion: weak fundamentals usually start the process, but the regulator’s speed, tools and credibility decide whether a weak or merely illiquid bank survives.
Exam focus: 2021 MCQ – weak management was the primary cause of VBS’s failure (not Saambou, which was a liquidity run; not Great Depression banks, which fell to runs and contagion; not Investec, which did not fail).

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 4 – Bank failure > Bank runs: game theory and Diamond–Dybvig (1983)
x:
Game theory studies choices where the best choice depends on what others do. The Diamond–Dybvig model (Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig, 1983) shows why runs can happen even when nothing is wrong with the bank: a run is a rational coordination failure caused by two features:
Maturity transformation – deposits are liquid claims, but the money is invested in long-term illiquid assets that lose value if liquidated early.
Sequential service constraint – the bank pays withdrawals first-come, first-served until it runs out.
The bank exists because depositors want a liquid claim (they may need cash early) while the long-term investment earns more. The same liquidity that makes deposits attractive makes a run possible.
Worked example: the two-depositor game
Two depositors, A and B, each deposit R100. The bank invests in a long-term asset paying R150 per depositor if held to maturity (T = 2) but only R80 per depositor (R160 in total) if liquidated early (T = 1). If A withdraws early she is paid R100 in full, which forces liquidation and leaves only R60 for B.
Payoffs (A ; B), in rand
B waits (T = 2) | B withdraws (T = 1)
A waits (T = 2) | (150 ; 150)good equilibrium, Pareto optimal | (60 ; 100)
A withdraws (T = 1) | (100 ; 60) | (80 ; 80)bank-run equilibrium
If A expects B to wait, A’s best response is to wait (150 > 100). If A expects B to withdraw, A’s best response is to withdraw (80 > 60). B faces the same choices.
There are therefore two Nash equilibria: (wait, wait) = (150, 150) and (withdraw, withdraw) = (80, 80). A Nash equilibrium is a set of choices in which nobody can do better by changing only their own choice. Pareto optimal means no one can be made better off without making someone worse off; (150, 150) is best for both.
Which equilibrium occurs depends on expectations, not on the bank’s solvency. Once panic starts, withdrawing is individually rational even though everyone ends up worse off.
Withdrawing is sometimes called the “dominant” strategy; strictly it is the best response only if the other depositor is expected to withdraw, so neither action is dominant. The (80, 80) cell is the average of being first (R100) and last (R60) in the queue, since the R160 is shared under the sequential service rule.
Model answer: True or false – a depositor who joins a bank run despite repeated official assurances that the bank is safe is necessarily behaving irrationally.
False. Running can be the rational individual choice:
Sequential service: deposits are paid first-come, first-served. If you believe others will withdraw, the bank may run out before it reaches you, so the best response to a run is to run – even if you believe the bank is sound. Your decision depends on what you expect others to do.
Assurances do not protect access: even if balances are eventually repaid in full, money may be frozen during curatorship or resolution for weeks or months (Saambou depositors waited up to six months). Deposit insurance protects the amount (up to a limit), not immediate access.
Asymmetric cost: withdrawing costs little (a queue or a few taps on an app); staying risks losing access to savings. Withdrawing is cheap insurance.
Northern Rock: the run continued after the UK Chancellor and the Governor of the Bank of England guaranteed all deposits, for exactly these reasons.
Individually rational behaviour producing a collectively bad outcome is a coordination failure. That is why authorities rely on credible backstops – fast-paying deposit insurance and a lender of last resort – rather than words alone. (Deposit insurance, CODI and moral hazard: see Part 3.)

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 4 – Bank failure > International cases
x:
Each case: background · cause · what happened · lesson.
Bank of East Asia, Hong Kong (24 September 2008) – a run that was not a failure
Background | Hong Kong bank at the height of the GFC, days after Lehman Brothers collapsed (15 September 2008), when confidence in banks was low.
Cause | Malicious rumours (text messages and internet) that the bank was in severe distress.
What happened | Retail depositors queued at branches. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA, the de facto central bank) immediately provided emergency liquidity and publicly stated the bank was sound. The bank was solvent; the panic passed.
Lesson | Not a bank failure. A run on a solvent bank that central bank liquidity stabilises without a takeover is not failure. The LLR worked as designed: the run was met with cash, so no fire sale occurred.
“It’s a Wonderful Life” (film set in the Great Depression) – anatomy of a run
Background | A small Building & Loan (a mutual savings institution that lends savings as home loans), run by George Bailey; a competing monopoly banker, Mr Potter.
Cause | Rumours that the institution is struggling cause a loss of confidence.
What happened | Depositors demand their cash at once. Bailey explains that the money is not in the vault but in their neighbours’ houses: the deposits have been lent out as home loans. Potter offers to buy depositors’ claims at 50 cents on the rand.
Lesson | A run starts with loss of confidence; maturity and liquidity transformation mean the money cannot be paid out at once; competitors benefit by buying assets at fire-sale prices.
Model answer: What is happening in the film, why is the bank at risk, how were deposits transformed into loans, and how would the competition benefit from a failure?
What is happening: a bank run. It starts with a loss of confidence, not an actual loss, and feeds on itself: each person who sees the queue fears the money will run out and joins it.
Why at risk: deposits are payable on demand but invested in long-term mortgages, and only a little cash is held. If many depositors demand cash at once the institution cannot pay, even though each loan is sound and it may be solvent – a liquidity failure caused by the maturity mismatch.
Deposits transformed into loans: the depositors’ money was lent to neighbours to build homes – maturity and liquidity transformation (short, liquid claims turned into long, illiquid assets). This is the bank’s economic function, but it creates the vulnerability.
Competition benefits: Potter offers 50 cents on the rand. If the Building & Loan fails, a competitor obtains its performing mortgage book and customers at a fire-sale price (and a monopoly); depositors who sell in panic lose half their savings. (Saambou’s loan books were later sold to African Bank and FirstRand at similar discounts.)
Northern Rock, UK (2007) – wholesale liquidity failure
Background | A fast-growing UK mortgage bank funded mainly by wholesale markets (borrowing from institutions and investors) rather than retail deposits from households. It originated mortgages, pooled them in securitisation vehicles (entities that buy loan pools and issue bonds backed by the repayments) and issued short-term paper such as 3-month commercial paper (short-term IOUs that must be rolled over at maturity).
Cause | In August 2007, as US subprime defaults surfaced, wholesale money markets froze: investors stopped buying bank and securitised paper because they could not tell where the losses lay. Northern Rock could not renew its funding, despite a good-quality mortgage book.
What happened | News that it had asked the Bank of England for emergency support caused queues outside branches in September 2007 – the first UK bank run in over 100 years. The run continued even after the Chancellor and the Governor guaranteed all deposits. It was nationalised in February 2008 and its mortgage book later split and sold. It is not clear that it was ever insolvent.
Lesson | Wholesale funding is fragile; a liquidity crisis can cause failure without proven insolvency; running despite official assurances is rational.
Why wholesale funding is more run-prone than retail deposits: wholesale lenders are large, professional, uninsured and fast – they withdraw in a day simply by not renewing. Retail deposits are sticky and usually insured. A model built on rolling over 3-month paper breaks the moment the market closes.
Basel III response: the NSFR (Net Stable Funding Ratio) limits the use of short-term wholesale funding for long-term assets.
Learnings: (1) solvency and liquidity are different – a bank can be solvent but illiquid (Northern Rock, Saambou) or insolvent but liquid for a while – yet they are linked through fire sales; (2) Northern Rock had physical queues, but with mobile banking and social media runs now happen at warp speed (millions moved in seconds; SVB lost $42bn in a day).
Nigerian banking crisis (2009–2011) – asset quality, fraud and a bad bank
Background | A banking system heavily concentrated in oil and gas lending, in an economy dependent on oil.
Cause | A sharp fall in oil prices exposed bad loans, insider fraud and reckless underwriting: large unsecured loans to related parties (directors, shareholders and their companies) with no expectation of repayment – for example a bank CEO who borrowed hundreds of millions of naira from her own bank to buy luxury property in Paris.
