What happened | The Central Bank of Nigeria created AMCON (Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria), a state-backed bad bank. Non-performing loans were transferred from troubled banks to AMCON at a discount; AMCON focused on recovery (collecting, restructuring, selling collateral). It was funded by a levy on surviving banks.
Lesson | Failure driven by asset quality, fraud and weak governance; a bad-bank structure can resolve a systemic crisis without crashing the financial sector.
Why a bad bank works: doubtful loans make a bank untrustworthy, so nobody funds it. Removing them leaves a clean bank that can be funded again, while the bad bank holds assets without a fire-sale deadline and recovers more than a forced sale would.
Who pays: the transfer discount puts the loss on the troubled banks’ shareholders; the levy spreads the remainder across the industry rather than onto taxpayers (moral hazard remains).
Barings Bank, UK (1995) – operational risk and insolvency
Background | A 230-year-old London merchant bank (advising, financing and trading rather than mass retail deposit-taking), with a Singapore subsidiary trading on SIMEX (a derivatives exchange).
Cause | Rogue trader Nick Leeson controlled both trading (front office) and settlement (back office, which records and checks trades) – a collapse of internal controls: operational risk (loss from failed internal processes, people or systems) and governance failure.
What happened | He took unhedged speculative positions in Nikkei 225 futures and Japanese interest rates, hid losses in an unauthorised error account (88888), doubled down and requested funds from London for margin calls. Losses of £827 million exceeded Barings’ capital. The bank was declared insolvent and sold to ING for £1, with ING taking over its liabilities.
Lesson | Trading losses on derivatives caused insolvency. Segregate duties and control positions. Futures are leveraged (a small deposit controls a large exposure), and doubling down on a losing bet magnifies the final loss.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 4 – Bank failure > South African bank failures
x:
In the late 1990s South Africa had over 46 registered banks (commercial and mutual; a mutual bank is owned by its members/depositors, not shareholders, and regulated under a lighter Act). After the 2002 small-bank crisis and later failures, the sector consolidated into an oligopoly: the Big Four (Standard Bank, FirstRand/FNB, Absa, Nedbank) plus Capitec and Investec, with virtually no mid-tier banks left.
Orthodox view: a concentrated system of large, well-capitalised banks is more stable – economies of scale, diversified loan books, franchise value (future profits owners will not want to risk) and easier supervision.
Heterodox view (e.g. Richard Werner): extreme concentration inhibits growth. SMEs, which drive employment, have thin track records and little collateral, so big banks’ standardised credit-scoring rejects them; many small local banks that know their customers provide an alternative (China replaced a single state mono-bank with thousands of local credit co-operatives and regional banks). The 2002 crisis removed exactly this tier, so “was consolidation good for South Africa?” has two defensible answers.
Each case below: background · what happened · immediate vs underlying cause · regulator’s role · outcome · lesson. The immediate cause is how the failure surfaced (almost always a liquidity crisis); the underlying cause is why the bank was fragile in the first place.
Saambou Bank (2002) – a solvent bank killed by a liquidity run
Background. Saambou was the 7th largest bank (about 2.3% of system deposits; R15 billion of assets), focused on middle-income personal loans, mortgages and micro-lending (small, short-term, high-interest unsecured loans – no collateral – to lower-income workers). Many micro-loans were repaid by payroll deduction codes (the state, as employer, paid instalments straight to the lender), which made them look almost risk-free; when government suspended the codes in 2000/2001 that protection vanished and defaults rose across the industry.
What happened.
June–December 2001: the rand collapsed to about R13/$; the SARB raised interest rates sharply to defend the currency, squeezing indebted retail borrowers.
January 2002: Absa announced a R1.045 billion write-down at its micro-lending subsidiary Unifer. Market anxiety shifted to Saambou because of its similar loan book (common exposure).
Wednesday 6 February 2002: Saambou’s share price fell 46% intraday (closed down 23%). Deposit outflows totalled R2.9 billion (about 19.2% of deposits) over five weeks, as institutional treasurers refused to roll over short-term deposits.
9 February 2002: placed under curatorship by the Minister of Finance, Trevor Manuel (section 69, Banks Act 1990).
The source report gives the rand as R4.00/$ in June 2001; that starting level looks too low, so quote only the end point (about R13/$ in December 2001).
Causes.
Immediate: a sudden wholesale liquidity run – large institutions withdrew short-term money en masse.
Underlying: extreme reliance on short-term, unrated wholesale deposits from institutional investors (e.g. Sanlam, corporate treasuries) rather than sticky retail savings (“unrated” = no rating agency had assessed it, so investors relied on reputation alone), combined with concentration in unsecured micro-lending. The fatal flaw was the funding structure, not insolvency. The bank was solvent.
Warning signs: the Unifer write-down (read across to Saambou’s similar book); the rand collapse and rate hikes; suspended payroll deduction codes and rising micro-loan defaults; the share-price collapse; the unrated, short-term wholesale funding base.
Regulator’s role. The SARB refused Emergency Liquidity Assistance (ELA) – central bank lending to a bank that is illiquid but believed solvent, against collateral at a penalty rate – even though its own statement said: “The Reserve Bank has no reason to believe that Saambou is insolvent.”
Model answer: What was the possible role of the regulator in the Saambou failure? If Saambou was solvent, why was there no lender-of-last-resort support?
Saambou was never insolvent and, under the LLR doctrine, should have received emergency liquidity. Only the central bank can create unlimited liquidity, so only it can stop a run on a solvent bank.
No bank can pay all its deposits at once (maturity transformation), so every solvent bank depends on central bank support in a panic; no bank withstands a 20% run in five weeks unaided.
Official reasoning: the business model (short-term wholesale funding of risky unsecured loans) was judged fundamentally flawed; ELA would only postpone collapse, put public money at risk and reward a fragile model (moral hazard).
Political economy: media (Noseweek) pointed to Saambou’s image as an “Afrikaner bank” and the Minister’s reluctance to use state funds for it – although over half its clients were black and Nelson Mandela banked there.
The mistake was exposed by BOE: a month later the authorities guaranteed the deposits of the next bank, BOE. Refusing Saambou converted a liquidity problem into a failure, destroyed value through fire sales and signalled that no non-Big-Four bank was safe, triggering contagion. The inconsistency (rescue BOE, not Saambou) fed the loss of confidence.
Outcome. Assets were sold at fire-sale discounts: African Bank bought the R2.8 billion personal-loan book for R1.25 billion (under 45 cents on the rand) and FirstRand bought the R1.4 billion home-loan book for R984 million (roughly doubling its home-loan profits the next year). Value moved from Saambou’s creditors and owners to the buyers. Retail depositors eventually received 100% of their principal, but up to six months late – a real harm to households that needed their savings.
Lesson. Saambou was fundamentally solvent but suffered a severe liquidity run caused by reliance on wholesale funding; the refusal of LLR support was a major regulatory policy error that triggered systemic contagion. Wholesale funding is a bank’s own vulnerability, yet every bank depends on the central bank in a panic.
Model answer: As CEO six months before February 2002 (with perfect hindsight), how would you have kept Saambou out of curatorship? The key problem was liquidity, so:
Build a strong relationship with the SARB and demonstrate solvency, so that emergency liquidity is available when needed.
Arrange committed credit lines with other banks, especially foreign banks, before the crisis (as Investec did before the GFC).
Rely less on flighty wholesale deposits: raise more retail deposits or issue longer-term bonds, reducing the maturity mismatch.
Hold a larger buffer of liquid assets; communicate openly with depositors and the market to limit rumours; reduce concentration in unsecured micro-lending.
BOE Bank (2002) – systemic contagion
Background. BOE (Board of Executors) was the 5th largest bank (about 6.5% of deposits; R47 billion of assets), a respected, roughly 160-year-old Cape institution with a diversified loan book, strong capital and virtually no micro-lending.
What happened. After Saambou’s curatorship, institutional depositors withdrew from all mid-sized and small banks. BOE’s liabilities shrank by R8.5 billion (17.9%) between February and June 2002. On 14 March 2002 the Minister of Finance and the SARB issued a 100% state guarantee on all BOE deposits and provided emergency liquidity. BOE was then merged into Nedcor (Nedbank). Runs spread across about a dozen small banks (including Merrill Lynch SA, TA Bank, Cadiz, FirstCorp, PSG Investment Bank, Brait, Corpcapital, Unibank and Securities Investment Bank).
Causes. Immediate: a contagion-driven wholesale run. Underlying: none in the bank itself – it was sound. As the largest bank below the Big Four it was seen by panicking treasurers as the “next weakest link”.
Contagion is the spread of distress to institutions that are not necessarily weak. Two channels: (1) information – creditors cannot see inside banks, so when one fails they assume similar banks are next and withdraw “just in case”; (2) direct links – interbank exposures pass losses on. In 2002 the information channel dominated: Saambou’s curatorship plus the refusal of ELA told depositors that mid-sized banks would not be rescued.
Regulator’s role. Realising the whole sector was threatened, the authorities did for BOE what they had refused Saambou: guarantee, liquidity and a forced merger. This inconsistency is the core criticism: if BOE needed a guarantee because depositors panicked, Saambou needed ELA for the same reason.
Outcome. Depositors 100% protected; Nedbank acquired BOE.
Closed-system mechanics and flight to quality
South Africa is a closed system: exchange controls limit moving rands abroad and the rand is not used outside the region. Rands withdrawn from one bank must be re-deposited at another domestic bank (or held as banknotes). Contrast Greece in the euro crisis, where deposits could move to German banks, so the Greek system as a whole lost deposits.
Step by step: an institution withdraws R1bn from BOE, so BOE’s deposits and its settlement account at the SARB fall by R1bn; it deposits the R1bn at Standard Bank, whose deposits and settlement balance rise by R1bn. Total deposits and the money supply are unchanged; only their distribution changes. The small bank is drained of liquidity and must sell assets or borrow; the winner is flush with funds.
Deposit runs in South Africa therefore do not reduce aggregate money supply; they reallocate liquidity from small and mid-tier banks to the Big Four. 2002 was a pure flight to quality: over R10 billion moved to the Big Four, whose market share rose from about 48% to over 65%, cementing the oligopoly.
A practical implication: the liquidity a run drains from the weak bank sits in the strong banks, so the system as a whole has the funds – the central bank (or interbank lending) only needs to recycle it back.
Lesson. Contagion can destroy sound banks; the credibility of the lender of last resort is a system-wide public good (once Saambou was abandoned, every similar bank became suspect); policy inconsistency is costly.
African Bank (2014) – slow-motion credit and governance failure
Background. African Bank Limited (subsidiary of the listed holding company ABIL) was a monoline unsecured lender to low- and middle-income borrowers (monoline = essentially one product, so no diversification). With no branch network taking demand deposits, it was funded almost entirely by wholesale debt: about R22 billion of bonds held by asset managers and money market funds (MMFs – unit trusts investing in very short-term debt and promising a stable R1.00 per unit).
What happened. Rapid expansion of unsecured lending; non-performing loans (NPLs) hidden by aggressive accounting (restructuring or re-ageing loans so they are not counted as overdue, delaying provisions); the acquisition of furniture retailer Ellerines at the market peak, using bank debt to fund store credit. From 2012 there was a two-year slide in the share price and growing difficulty rolling over bonds at reasonable yields. On 10 August 2014 SARB Governor Gill Marcus announced curatorship.
Causes. Immediate: a funding liquidity freeze – maturing bonds could not be rolled over. Underlying: bad investments – rapid unsecured loan growth and rising NPLs, understated by aggressive accounting, plus the Ellerines deal – and weak management/governance: a dominant CEO (Leon Kirkinis) and a Chief Risk Officer described by the SARB as unqualified and ineffective (so no independent check on risk).
Why a slow run. Bonds have fixed maturities (3–5 years): bondholders cannot withdraw at an ATM; they can only sell at a falling price or refuse to buy new bonds when old ones mature. The run therefore took the form of a falling share price, rising yields and a struggle to refinance – each maturity date a mini-test of confidence spread over two years (a “slow-motion train smash”, unlike Saambou’s fast run). The regulator had time to see it coming and was criticised for not acting sooner, and by the CEO for acting at all.
Regulator’s role. Curatorship and the first post-GFC statutory bail-in in an emerging market. After the GFC (2007–09), taxpayer bail-outs (the state injecting money) were seen as unacceptable; in a bail-in the bank’s own creditors absorb losses by having claims written down or converted into equity. The bank was split:
African Bank (old)Insolvent, about 10% net capital deficit
↓
Good BankR26 bn performing loans + R10 bn SARB liquidity facilityrelaunched as the new African Bank
Bad BankR17 bn non-performing loansisolated and wound down over time
Good bank / bad bank: the healthy part continues so customers and payments are undisturbed; the toxic part is run off over years, with losses on the old owners and creditors.
10% haircut: senior bondholders and wholesale creditors received 90 cents on the rand in new bonds; 10 cents was converted into equity in the bad bank. “Senior” creditors rank ahead of subordinated debt and shareholders, so their loss was notable. Subordinated debt was written down and shareholders were wiped out.
Money market funds “broke the buck”: over 15 MMFs held African Bank paper; the haircut pushed some funds’ net asset value below R1.00 for the first time in SA history, so managers froze redemptions and wrote down investors’ capital. To prevent a run on the roughly R300 billion unit-trust industry the SARB provided liquidity and market-making support for money-market paper. A bail-in moves losses to creditors, but can transmit them to ordinary savers – a second round of contagion.
Outcome. Depositors did not lose money; the African Bank brand continues in a new legal entity; the old entity’s shareholders lost almost everything.
Model answer: Critically discuss whether African Bank was a bank failure. The answer depends on the definition used.
Insolvency: yes – unsecured-lending losses left a capital deficit of about 10%; bondholders took a 10% haircut and shareholders received nothing of value from the old entity.
Illiquidity: its ability to sell bonds was shrinking (higher yields, loss of confidence).
Curatorship: yes – the SARB placed it under curatorship and split it into good and bad banks.
Counter-argument: the brand still operates in a new legal entity and depositors lost nothing.
Conclusion: for the old legal entity the failure is real on both the insolvency and curatorship definitions. What remains unclear is whether it would have become insolvent had it not been put under curatorship (the CEO’s argument); there is no clear answer.
Lesson. Wholesale-funded monolines can fail slowly; weak risk governance and accounting discretion hide credit problems; bail-in shifts losses to creditors but can spill into the money market; acting early carries a political cost. For exam answers detail: (1) the good bank / bad bank split, (2) the 10% bail-in haircut on senior bondholders, (3) MMFs breaking the buck.
VBS Mutual Bank (2018) – fraud: solvency first, liquidity second
Background. VBS (formerly Venda Building Society) was a small mutual bank under the Mutual Banks Act 124 of 1993 (lighter capital and governance requirements than the Banks Act 1990). The PA-commissioned investigation, “The Great Bank Heist” (Adv. Terry Motau SC and Werksmans), found that R1.5–2.0 billion was stolen through fraudulent accounting and executive corruption.
What happened. Management attracted large short-term deposits from more than 15 municipalities (Limpopo, Gauteng, North West) with above-market rates and bribes to mayors and CFOs, although the Municipal Finance Management Act (MFMA) restricts municipal deposits to registered commercial banks (public money should go only to the soundest institutions). In 2017 National Treasury reminded municipalities that these deposits were illegal and they demanded their money back. VBS was placed under curatorship on 11 March 2018 and liquidated in November 2018.
Causes.
Immediate: a liquidity collapse – it could not meet withdrawals when the municipalities withdrew.
Underlying: fraud (looting) and weak underwriting and governance. Executives (chairman Tshifiwa Matodzi and CEO Andile Ramavhunga) created fake overdraft accounts and fictitious deposit credits (e.g. R700 million of non-existent cash); bribes and commissions went to mayors, municipal CFOs, the KPMG lead audit partner and politically connected parties; an R8.5 million mortgage was granted to former President Zuma on communal land, which cannot legally be mortgaged. The money was spent on luxury cars, bonuses and helicopters.
Solvency or liquidity first? Solvency first. Looting and loans that would never be repaid made assets worth less than liabilities; the bank stayed liquid for a while on fresh (illegal) municipal deposits. The liquidity crisis came second, when municipalities withdrew, and the SARB placed it under curatorship.
Warning signs (clearly visible to staff inside the bank, as a former VBS risk analyst later described):
Extravagance out of scale: Porsches, luxury property, chartered helicopters; executives paid themselves R40 million in bonuses while the bank was losing money, whereas Discovery Bank paid high bonuses only after earning R400 million profit. When pay and lifestyle do not match a bank’s size and earnings, suspect false accounts.
Above-market rates on volatile, illegal municipal deposits; a short-termist “quick buck” culture; fabricated ledger entries; a compromised auditor.
Whistleblowers matter: Mariette Venter, acting CFO of Capricorn District Municipality, refused to deposit municipal funds in VBS despite political threats and a false suspension.
Regulator’s role. Curatorship, then liquidation. South Africa had no formal deposit insurance in 2018; depositors were guaranteed only up to R100 000 (ad hoc). The regulator’s supervision of a small mutual bank did not catch blatant fraud early. (Deposit insurance today: see Part 3.)
Outcome. Unlike Saambou, retail depositors lost hundreds of millions: rural savers, stokvels and burial societies lost everything above R100 000 – e.g. pensioners and burial stokvels with R500 000+ lost up to R400 000 (80%).
Lesson. Capital ratios are meaningless when the books are fabricated, management is dominant and the auditor is compromised. VBS is the example to cite in essays on bank governance: weak (dishonest) management was the primary cause.
Regal Treasury Bank (2002) – audit integrity
Background: a small niche commercial bank.
What happened: in 2002 the external auditors, Ernst & Young, withdrew their audit opinion (the signed statement that the financial statements give a true and fair view), followed by a wholesale run, curatorship and liquidation.
Causes: Immediate: a liquidity run after the audit scandal. Underlying: severe governance failure and unethical conduct by CEO Jeff Zidel; misstatements and undisclosed related-party transactions (deals between the bank and its own directors or their entities, which can move money to insiders and must be disclosed).
Regulator’s role: curatorship, then liquidation.
Outcome: insolvent after asset adjustments; creditors and depositors suffered partial losses; competing mid-tier banks benefited.
Lesson: depositors and creditors cannot inspect a bank’s books, so they rely on the auditor’s signature as a proxy for trust. Its withdrawal (unprecedented in 2002) was read as a terminal signal and caused an instant run: a bank can fail through information, not only economics.
Ditsobotla Co-operative Bank (2025) – the first case under resolution
Background: Ditsobotla Primary Savings and Credit Co-operative Bank (Lichtenburg, North West). A co-operative bank is member-owned, with members sharing a common bond (same region, association or employer) – the smallest tier of bank. In May 2025 it had 1 452 members and assets of about R8.3 million.
What happened: after repeated PA warnings, on 1 August 2025 the Minister of Finance placed it in resolution; the SARB took control and appointed a resolution practitioner.
Causes: persistent losses, weak governance and failure to meet financial and regulatory requirements despite PA warnings.
Regulator’s role (resolution, not curatorship): member accounts temporarily frozen for assessment; obligations to non-member creditors suspended; depositors paid by CODI up to R100 000 per depositor (principal and interest on qualifying savings, including stokvels); borrowers told their loans remain legally binding.
Lesson: failure does not cancel debts. A borrower’s loan is an asset of the failed bank’s estate, and collecting it is how depositors and CODI are repaid. It also shows deposit insurance working without a taxpayer bail-out.
The bank is sometimes misrecorded as “Sabax” or “Sabla”; the correct name is Ditsobotla.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 4 – Bank failure > Curatorship versus resolution
x:
Following Basel Committee and Financial Stability Board (FSB) post-GFC standards, South Africa replaced curatorship with a statutory resolution framework. The Financial Sector Laws Amendment Act 23 of 2021 (FSLAA) amended the Financial Sector Regulation Act (FSRA, “Twin Peaks”) to make the SARB the resolution authority, repealed the Banks Act curatorship provisions and provided for deposit insurance (CODI). Resolution has applied to bank failures since 1 June 2023. (Twin Peaks: the Prudential Authority inside the SARB supervises soundness; the Financial Sector Conduct Authority, FSCA, supervises how firms treat customers.)
Resolution = the orderly restructuring or wind-down of a failing bank using special statutory powers, so that the failure does not damage the wider system or need a taxpayer bail-out. Tools: bail-in (write down creditors’ claims or convert debt to equity), bridge bank (a temporary entity receiving the good assets and critical deposits so services continue), good bank / bad bank splits and transfers of assets.
Saambou, African Bank, VBS and Regal were handled under curatorship; Ditsobotla under resolution.
Dimension | Old: Curatorship (Banks Act 1990, s 69) | New: Resolution (FSRA as amended by FSLAA 2021; in force 1 June 2023)
Primary objective | Save the individual bank; act in the interests of the bank and its creditors and nurse it back to health. | Safeguard systemic financial stability (public policy); sacrifice the institution if needed to save the system.
Authority | Curator appointed by the Minister of Finance (on the regulator’s recommendation) to run the bank. | SARB as resolution authority, with sweeping statutory powers; appoints a resolution practitioner.
Bail-in powers | Limited; required negotiated agreements or liquidation. | Explicit statutory power to write down debt and convert debt to equity.
Management | Replaces CEO and board; curator runs the bank as a going concern. | Replaces management at once; restructures, splits or liquidates without shareholder consent.
Mechanisms | Curatorship, scheme of arrangement or liquidation. | Bridge bank, good bank / bad bank, bail-in, transfer of assets; depositors paid by CODI.
Example | Saambou, African Bank, VBS | Ditsobotla (2025)
Exam focus: a direct comparison question – stress (1) the primary objective, (2) statutory bail-in powers, (3) sacrificing the institution versus saving the system.

VBS | Liquidity: could not meet withdrawals | Fraud (looting) and weak underwriting and governance
Similarities: all three ended in a liquidity crisis and curatorship; all were small or mid-sized; each had a weakness in funding or governance. Differences: Saambou was solvent, the other two insolvent; the root cause was funding structure (Saambou), credit risk and management (African Bank) and fraud (VBS); the outcome differed (asset sales to other banks; good bank / bad bank with bail-in; liquidation with depositor losses). Pattern: liquidity trouble is the visible symptom; the cause lies in funding structure, asset quality or governance.
Exam focus: 2021 Q4 (immediate and underlying reasons for Saambou, African Bank, VBS; regulator’s role in Saambou); 2019 Q4.5 (managing Saambou differently); 2023 Q5.3 (VBS solvency first). On Saambou always state: fundamentally solvent, failed through a liquidity run caused by wholesale funding, worsened by the refusal of LLR support.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 4 – Bank failure > Silicon Valley Bank (US, March 2023) – interest rate risk and a digital run
x:
Background. SVB (Santa Clara, California) banked venture-capital (VC) firms, tech founders and start-ups. It was a mid-tier niche bank, not a G-SIB, so it faced lighter rules. Its customers were all in one industry, linked by the same investors and social networks; average deposits were far above the insured limit; and it grew extremely fast.
Size comparison (US$ billion)
US$ bn
SVB total assets | 212
South African GDP, 2022 | 405
Standard Bank total assets, 2022 | 144
SVB was about half of South Africa’s GDP ( (212)/(405) ≈ 52%) and about 1.5 times Standard Bank ( (212)/(144) ≈ 1.47): a “mid-tier” US bank is very large by South African standards.
Timeline
When | Event
2020–2021 | COVID deposit glut: VC funding and stimulus flooded tech accounts; deposits roughly tripled (about $60bn to over $180bn). SVB invested heavily in long-dated bonds.
2022 | Inflation; the Fed raised rates from 0.25% to over 4.5%. Bond prices fell. Tech funding dried up and clients drew down deposits. SVB had no Chief Risk Officer for 8 months.
Wed 8 March 2023 | SVB announced it had sold $21bn of bonds at a $1.8bn loss and would raise $1.5bn of new equity.
Thu 9 March | Depositors tried to withdraw about $42bn in one day (over 20% of deposits), with about $100bn more queued for the next business day.
Fri 10 – Sun 12 March | Regulators (the FDIC – US deposit insurer and resolution authority – and the California regulator) closed SVB on 10 March; on 12 March Signature Bank ($110bn) was closed, all depositors of both banks were protected and the Fed announced the BTFP. First Republic failed shortly afterwards.
Correct date: SVB was closed on Friday 10 March 2023; Sunday 12 March was the date of the rescue announcements (some course material gives 12 March as the closure date).
Causes – a chain in which each link made the next fatal
Deposit glut and asset-liability mismatch. SVB could not lend over $120bn of new deposits quickly and well, so it bought long-duration US Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities yielding about 1.5–2.0%. These carry no credit risk but large interest rate risk. Long fixed-rate assets funded by demand deposits = maturity transformation without hedging.
Interest rate shock. When the Fed raised rates to over 4.5%, the market value of old 1.5–2% bonds fell, more so for longer maturities. SVB had a large unhedged exposure (quoted as about $10bn) and had reduced hedges to boost short-term profit. An interest rate swap (pay fixed, receive floating) would have gained as rates rose and offset the bond losses.
Accounting distortion (HTM vs AFS). Securities classified as held-to-maturity (HTM) are carried at cost, so price falls are ignored; available-for-sale (AFS) securities are carried at market value. SVB’s unrecognised HTM losses exceeded $15bn against Tier 1 equity of about $16bn: close to insolvent at fair value while reporting healthy ratios. After the 2018 US deregulation, banks below $250bn did not have to include unrealised securities losses in regulatory capital or meet the full LCR.
Realisation event. HTM hides losses only while the bonds are held. Selling to meet withdrawals crystallises the loss ($1.8bn on $21bn sold) and undermines the HTM treatment of the rest.
Panic equity raise. Announcing a share issue because of a loss signals that the problem is bigger than disclosed and that management has no better option. Issuing shares after a $1.8bn knock was a terrible signal; uninsured depositors concluded they should leave first.
Concentrated, uninsured deposits and run speed. Over 90% of deposits exceeded the $250 000 insurance limit and came from one tight-knit sector. VC investors told portfolio companies (via WhatsApp groups and social media) to withdraw; the run was complete in about 24 hours.
Governance – the main cause. Not hedging a huge, obvious exposure and having no CRO for 8 months are management and board failures; the supervisor also failed to challenge them.
Worked illustration: why a rate rise wrecks a long bond portfolio
A bond portfolio with face value $100bn, bought at yields of about 1.75%, average duration about 6 years. Yields rise about 3 percentage points (to about 4.75%).
% price change ≈ – duration × change in yield = – 6 × 3% ≈ –18%
The portfolio is now worth about $82bn: a paper loss of about $18bn – essentially all of Tier 1 capital of about $16bn (actual figures: over $15bn of unrealised losses).
Why prices fall: a bond’s price is the present value of its fixed coupons; if new bonds pay 4.5%, nobody pays full price for one paying 1.75%. The longer the duration, the bigger the fall.
Under HTM accounting none of this appears in profit or regulatory capital, but the loss becomes real the moment the bank must sell: a $42bn withdrawal cannot be paid with bonds worth 18% less than the books say.
The $21bn of bonds sold came from the AFS book, while the $15bn unrealised loss sat in the HTM book; the quoted $10bn unhedged exposure is not reconciled with the $15bn loss. The core point stands: forced sales turn hidden paper losses into realised losses.
Warning signs (all visible in published information)
Deposits tripled in two years and were put into long-duration bonds – very fast growth outpaces controls.
Unhedged interest rate exposure; unrealised losses (over $15bn) close to Tier 1 capital (about $16bn).
Funding concentration: one industry, over 90% uninsured, all connected and with the same incentive to run.
Weak risk governance: no CRO for 8 months.
Management signals under stress: bond sales at a loss followed by a rushed equity raise.
Regulator response
The FDIC closed SVB; Signature Bank (heavy crypto deposits) also failed; First Republic needed a $30bn deposit injection from large banks and was then acquired by JPMorgan Chase. A systemic risk exception protected all depositors of SVB and Signature in full, including above $250 000.
The Fed created the Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP): banks could borrow for up to one year against government bonds valued at par (face value), not market value, with no haircut. A normal central bank loan is against market value minus a haircut. Banks could meet withdrawals without selling, so unrealised losses stayed unrealised.
The BTFP is a subsidy to bank shareholders: the Fed took the interest rate risk that belonged to shareholders. If rates stay high, the bonds remain worth less than par and the central bank bears the gap; if rates fall, shareholders keep the gain. It also reinforces moral hazard: unhedged rate bets get rescued.
Outcome and lessons
SVB, Signature and First Republic failed within weeks – a regional-bank contagion that needed an unusual central bank programme to stop. SVB failed in about 24 hours once the run started: a digital, social-media-speed run.
Model answer: How could the SVB failure have been prevented? Assess slower rate rises, hedging and regulation, full deposit guarantees and better governance.
Slower rate rises – partly. Rapid hikes (0.25% to over 4.5% in about a year) wobble bank balance sheets, so central banks should weigh financial-stability (macroprudential) effects as well as inflation. But the rate path is set for inflation, not for one bank, and a bank should survive a predictable rate cycle: a contributing factor, not the root cause.
Hedging and regulation – yes. The exposure was obvious and measurable; a swap or shorter-duration investments would have capped it. Two failures: the bank’s governance (no CRO, hedges removed for profit) and supervision (the regulator did not challenge the exposure; the 2018 deregulation put banks below $250bn under lighter rules). The regulator was also asleep on the job.
Full deposit guarantee – limited. With over 90% uninsured, a full guarantee would have removed the incentive to run (and was granted after the event). But an ex ante blanket guarantee removes depositor discipline and increases moral hazard, and it is not strictly needed: services such as IntraFi/CDARS already split a $10m deposit into forty $250 000 deposits at different banks for full cover. The limit alone neither explains nor cures the problem.
Better governance – the main answer. The mismatch, missing hedges, missing risk officer and the panic equity raise were all management and board decisions. Regulation can require capital but cannot make management competent. Ranking: governance first, supervision second, rate policy and insurance design third.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 4 – Bank failure > Credit Suisse (Switzerland, March 2023) – a decade-long loss of trust
x:
Background. A Swiss universal bank (investment banking plus commercial banking and wealth management) and a G-SIB (Global Systemically Important Bank – one of about 30 banks the FSB judges so large and interconnected that failure could damage the global system; they carry an extra capital surcharge and are “too big to fail”). One of Switzerland’s two big banks (with UBS); total assets about $732bn (2022), over $500bn at resolution. Regulator: FINMA; central bank: SNB. By contrast, Standard Bank ranks only about 300th–400th globally: it is a D-SIB (domestic systemically important bank) – too important for South Africa, so the SARB would not allow its uncontrolled failure.
Contrast with SVB: SVB was a fast run driven by interest rate risk; Credit Suisse was a slow, decade-long destruction of trust driven by culture and governance – primarily a governance story.
Timeline of scandals and collapse
When | Event
2013–2016 | Mozambique “tuna bonds”: over $2bn of secret loans to state-owned companies (ostensibly for tuna fishing and maritime security), hidden from the IMF; hundreds of millions diverted as bribes; Mozambique defaulted. A former Mozambican minister fled to South Africa, leading to an extradition fight in SA courts.
2019 | Spying scandal: private detectives followed departing executive Iqbal Khan; the COO resigned and CEO Tidjane Thiam resigned in 2020.
2020 | Luckin Coffee: lead underwriter of the IPO of a Chinese coffee chain that had fabricated over $300m of sales – reputational damage and litigation.
March 2021 | Greensill: about $10bn of supply-chain finance funds marketed to clients froze when Greensill collapsed. Archegos: the family office’s leveraged total-return-swap bets collapsed; Credit Suisse lost about $5.5bn, the most of any prime broker.
Oct 2022 | A journalist speculated failure was imminent; viral social-media rumours; clients withdrew CHF 138bn in Q4 2022. Share price down 60% in 2022.
15 March 2023 | Saudi National Bank, the largest shareholder, ruled out more capital; shares fell 30%. The SNB provided an emergency liquidity facility of CHF 50bn, but outflows exceeded CHF 10bn a day.
18–19 March 2023 | Weekend deal: UBS acquired Credit Suisse.
Correct figure: the SNB facility was CHF 50bn (about $54bn); the slide shows CHF 15bn. Either way it did little to comfort depositors.
Credit Suisse market capitalisation (US$ billion) – the long demise
2017 | 2018 | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 17 Mar 2023 | 19 Mar 2023
Market cap | 45 | 28 | 33 | 32 | 23 | 12 | 8.5 | 3.2
Market capitalisation (share price × number of shares) is a forward-looking measure of trust, unlike backward-looking regulatory ratios. The almost linear decline from $45bn to $3.2bn shows confidence ebbing away for years; SVB’s share price, by contrast, was fine until the week of failure.
Causes
Culture and governance: repeated scandals showing weak risk management and control, a pursuit of investment-banking profit with inadequate checks, rapid turnover of CEOs and risk chiefs, and (in 2023) admitted “material weaknesses” in internal controls over financial reporting.
Losses and reputation: Archegos ($5.5bn), Greensill, and restructuring costs of $4–6bn eroded earnings and trust; wealthy private-banking clients – the core franchise – left.
Loss of confidence, not of regulatory capital: capital and liquidity ratios stayed above Basel III requirements to the end. It was a “competence run”: clients and counterparties left because they no longer trusted management, amplified by social media.
Warning signs
A decade-long fall in market value ($45bn to $12bn by end-2022) and a 60% share-price fall in 2022.
Repeated scandals and control failures every year or two; financial-reporting weaknesses.
Public speculation, viral rumours and heavy outflows (CHF 138bn in Q4 2022).
Not a warning sign: capital and leverage ratios. Credit Suisse sat in the middle of the G-SIB peer group on the leverage ratio ( (Tier1)/(total exposure) ) over 2009–2018. Impending failure cannot be identified from capital or leverage ratios alone.
Regulator response: the four options
Option | Assessment
Insolvency / winding up | Rejected: closing a G-SIB with over $500bn of assets could freeze interbank settlement and spread like Lehman Brothers in 2008.
Nationalisation | Rejected: the government did not want a bank of that size on the public balance sheet.
Basel III resolution plan (“living will”) with bail-in | Rejected: the plan (a document setting out how the bank could be wound down without taxpayer money, with shareholders and bondholders absorbing losses) proved unworkable during a fast panic.
Takeover by UBS | Selected: fast (one weekend), private owner, no public ownership.
Outcome
UBS paid CHF 3bn ($3.2bn) in UBS shares (about CHF 0.76 per share against CHF 1.86 the previous Friday; a year earlier the bank was worth about CHF 20bn).
The Swiss government guaranteed losses up to CHF 9bn after UBS absorbs the first CHF 5bn, plus liquidity backstops of about CHF 100bn.
FINMA wrote CHF 16bn ($17bn) of AT1 bonds down to zero, while shareholders received CHF 3bn of UBS stock. AT1 bonds (contingent convertibles, CoCos) are perpetual bonds counting as Tier 1 capital; they pay a high coupon but are converted to equity or written off if capital falls below a trigger or the regulator declares the bank non-viable. They were created after 2008 so that investors, not taxpayers, bear losses.
Depositors lost nothing. The enlarged UBS has assets of about 160% of Swiss GDP.
Lessons
Capital hierarchy inverted. The normal order of loss absorption is ordinary equity, then preference shares, then AT1/Tier 2 hybrids, then unsecured debt, then secured debt. Here AT1 holders were wiped out while shareholders kept something. FINMA relied on emergency powers and on the AT1 terms allowing a write-down when extraordinary state support was given, to complete the merger over one weekend. AT1 bonds were immediately repriced as riskier (higher future coupons; Australia is phasing them out), and AT1 holders sued and won in a lower Swiss court. In a crisis, regulatory discretion can override the pecking order markets expected.
Resolution plans mean little if not implementable – the living will was set aside.
“Too big to fail” becomes “too big to save”: the merged UBS is so large the Swiss state could struggle to absorb its distress.
Basel III capital and liquidity bought time but could not prevent failure: a bank can meet every minimum and still fail through loss of confidence. Capital protects against losses; only confidence and a lender of last resort protect against runs.
Forecasting Credit Suisse: the November 2022 exam questions
Four months before the collapse a final-exam question presented Credit Suisse as follows: a universal bank and G-SIB; secret loans to fund Mozambican fishing and associated bribes; social-media rumours of collapse; share price down 60% in 2022; yet apparently strong numbers – Tier 1 ratio 13.5% (minimum 6%), 20% of total assets of $732bn held in cash, LCR 191% (minimum 100%), restructuring costs of $4–6bn. On regulatory metrics it looked sound; its market value said otherwise. Ratios measure the buffer, not whether people still trust the bank.
Model answer Q1 [3]: Which past South African failure is most like this? Give a similarity and a dissimilarity.
African Bank (2014) (Saambou is a partial parallel).
Similarity: a long, visible erosion of market confidence and a falling share price before intervention – African Bank’s two-year slide, Credit Suisse’s decade of scandals and 60% fall. In both the problem was governance and credibility, not the headline capital number, and in both the regulator intervened before balance-sheet insolvency was formally established, imposing losses on investors (African Bank’s 10% senior haircut; Credit Suisse’s AT1 write-off) while protecting depositors.
Dissimilarity: size and systemic importance. Credit Suisse is a G-SIB with about $732bn of assets and thousands of global counterparties, so the state must act; African Bank and Saambou were domestic mid-tier lenders (about 2% of SA banking assets), so the SARB could let them fail in a controlled way.
Model answer Q2 [4]: Should depositors in Credit Suisse be worried? Probably not (and they lost nothing).
Too big to fail: as a G-SIB its disorderly failure would trigger global contagion, so the authorities would protect depositors by rescue, forced merger or guarantee.
Loss-absorbing layers: depositors rank above shareholders and AT1, Tier 2 and other debt; a 13.5% Tier 1 ratio is a thick cushion.
Liquidity: 20% of assets in cash and an LCR of 191%, with the SNB as lender of last resort behind it.
Caveat: possible inconvenience (frozen access, delays), and uninsured wholesale depositors have no legal guarantee – but the realistic expectation is no loss.
Model answer Q3 [2]: Should shareholders be worried? Yes. Shareholders are the first-loss layer (residual claimants): in a failure or resolution equity absorbs losses first and is heavily diluted or wiped out, so that owners rather than taxpayers bear the cost. The 60% share-price fall shows the market expected this. (In the actual outcome shareholders received CHF 3bn of UBS shares, a fraction of former value; AT1 holders, who should have been worried most of all, were wiped out.)
Model answer Q4 [4]: Why would Citibank analysts say this is not like Bear Stearns in the GFC? Bear Stearns (US investment bank, rescued by JPMorgan with Fed support in March 2008):
Bear Stearns was an acute liquidity and solvency crisis: funded overwhelmingly by short-term wholesale funding (overnight repo) and holding illiquid, falling subprime securities; when lenders refused to roll over, it ran out of cash in days, in a systemic crash with interbank lending frozen.
Credit Suisse had strong buffers: 13.5% Tier 1, 20% of assets in cash, LCR 191% – products of Basel III that Bear Stearns never had; the wider system was healthy.
Different problem: Credit Suisse’s distress was idiosyncratic (scandals, governance decay, loss of trust), not a market-wide collapse in asset values.
Hence “inconvenient and unprofitable, but not on the brink” – a view that proved too optimistic, because lost trust can drain liquidity faster than any buffer is designed to cover.

h: Bank Regulation & Failure > Part 4 – Bank failure > Forecasting bank failure and applying the lessons
x:
Studying failures changes the viewpoint from customer or investor to that of a central bank supervisor (is this bank sound?) or a corporate treasury manager (where do I park the company’s cash, and which counterparties can I trust?). Crises follow predictable structural patterns – a balance-sheet mismatch, a governance breakdown and a loss of confidence interacting – so a trained analyst can spot trouble months before formal insolvency, as the Credit Suisse exam question showed.
Warning-sign checklist
Warning sign | Why it matters | Cases
Funding concentration and short-term wholesale reliance | Large, uninsured, short-term, concentrated funding leaves in hours. | Saambou, African Bank, Northern Rock, SVB
Very fast growth | Outpaces controls; money is deployed in whatever is available. | SVB, African Bank
Asset concentration / mismatch | One product, one sector or long unhedged bonds; one shock hits everything. | African Bank, Saambou, Nigeria, SVB
Falling share price and market value; rising funding cost | Forward-looking loss of trust; a slow run is under way. | African Bank, Credit Suisse
Weak governance | Dominant CEO, weak or missing risk officer, scandals, related-party lending. | African Bank, VBS, Regal, SVB, CS, Barings
Aggressive accounting and audit problems | Hidden NPLs, HTM losses, fabricated entries, withdrawn audit opinion. | African Bank, SVB, VBS, Regal
Pay and lifestyle out of scale with earnings | Suggests the accounts are false. | VBS
Above-market rates on deposits | The bank cannot raise funds normally; an unsustainable model. | VBS
Distress signals from management | Asset sales at a loss, emergency equity raises, requests for central bank help. | SVB, Northern Rock
Read-across from a peer | Similar banks are hit when one reveals losses (contagion). | Unifer → Saambou → BOE
Capital and liquidity ratios alone do not forecast failure: Credit Suisse met every minimum (13.5% Tier 1, LCR 191%) and SVB reported healthy ratios.
Applying the knowledge
As a treasury manager: preserve the company’s cash – limit exposure to weak banks, spread deposits across banks, monitor counterparties against the checklist. Nobody wants to be the treasurer whose $20 million sits in a foreign bank when it fails.
As a regulator: act on the process (deteriorating soundness, unsustainable model, lost confidence) before formal insolvency; provide liquidity to solvent banks consistently; use resolution tools that impose losses on owners and creditors without spreading contagion.
Analysing an unseen case: use the template – background, timeline, immediate vs underlying cause, solvency or liquidity first, warning signs, regulator response, outcome, lessons.
Three conclusions from the failures
The liability side is also risky. Basel focuses mainly on capital for the riskiness of assets (RWA). Failures show that funding that is large, uninsured, short-term and concentrated can vanish in hours. The LCR and NSFR are blunt: SVB was exempt, and Credit Suisse met the LCR at 191% and still failed.
A poor business model or sick culture cannot be fixed with regulation. Rules can prescribe ratios but cannot stop executives cheating, taking unhedged gambles or building a toxic culture; rules are backward-looking and can be gamed.
Too big to fail, and more moral hazard. The G-SIB surcharge was meant to make big banks shrink; instead banks are bigger than before 2008 and small banks fewer. Authorities favour consolidation because large diversified banks fail less often, but this creates too-big-to-fail and too-big-to-save institutions whose creditors lend cheaply and monitor less, encouraging risk-taking. More Credit Suisse-style crises are likely.
Fixing bank governance (Becht, Bolton & Röell)
Misdiagnosis: post-2008 reforms treated the problem as the agency cost of equity (managers not serving shareholders) and aligned pay with shareholders (say-on-pay, deferred options, clawbacks).
Real problem – agency cost of debt (risk-shifting): in a bank funded about 90% by debt and deposits, aligning managers with shareholders encourages gambling, because limited liability puts the downside on creditors, insurers and taxpayers (“gambling for resurrection”). Examples: African Bank’s aggressive unsecured lending; SVB’s unhedged bond bet.
Preventive fixes: (1) pay executives partly in CoCo/AT1 debt, so their pay is lost when debt is hit; (2) give deposit insurers (FDIC, CODI) board or risk-committee representation; (3) give the Chief Risk Officer pay and clout equal to the CEO.

One-page checklist of the most-examined formulas and lists across all four parts.
Item | Method / content
CET1 capital and ratio (min 4.5%; 7% with 2.5% conservation buffer) | Total equity – preference shares – AT1 instruments – goodwill – other intangibles (capitalised software) – deferred tax asset that depends on future profits (only that %) – cash flow hedging reserve. CET1 ratio = (CET1)/(RWA) . Never add Tier 2 sub-debt; never use total assets as denominator.
Tier 1 (min 6%) | Total equity – the same deductions, but keep preference shares and AT1 (Tier 1 = CET1 + AT1). Tier 1 ratio = (Tier1)/(RWA) .
Total capital ratio (min 8% + buffers) | Total equity + Basel III-compliant subordinated debt (Tier 2) + over-provision the regulator disallows – DTA (future-profit part) – software – goodwill; ÷ RWA. Dividend test: can pay only if capital after the dividend still ≥ required % × RWA and cash still ≥ reserve requirement (fail either → no).
RWA | Σ (risk weight × exposure) per asset + off-balance-sheet RWA (+ market and operational risk). Government-related items (cash, government securities, SARB reserve deposits, amounts owed by SARS) 0%; intangibles excluded; apply given weights (e.g. loans 60%, derivatives 120%, investments 100%).
Leverage ratio (min 3%) | (Tier 1)/(total assets) , with total assets after the same deductions (DTA portion, software, goodwill). No risk weights – a backstop against RWA gaming.
LCR (min 100%) | (HQLA)/(net cash outflows over 30 days of stress) , where HQLA = cash + SARB balance + committed SARB facility + unencumbered government bonds. NSFR: (available)/(required stable funding) ≥ 100% (one year).
Cash reserve ratio (SARB method) | (Vault cash + balance / mandatory reserve deposits at SARB) ÷ total liabilities (exclude equity; include off-balance-sheet liabilities if told). Excess = cash held – required % × liabilities.
Maximum SARB repo liquidity | (1) Haircut collateral: (market value)/(adjustment factor) (bucket by residual maturity, e.g. 1–10 years 1.025). (2) Loan + interest = haircut value: X × (1 + r/12 × days/30) = haircut value, so X = (haircut value)/(1+(r)/(12)×(days)/(30)) . (3) Interest = haircut value – X. E.g. (R100m)/(1.025) = R97.561m; X = R97.494m; interest R67 027. Longer bonds get bigger factors because their price is more rate-sensitive (longer duration).
Loan-rate pricing | (1) ROA = ROE × capital ratio (ROE = ROA × 1/capital ratio). (2) Pre-tax ROA = (ROA)/(1-t) . (3) Pre-tax ROA = loan share × X – loan share × bad-debt % – cost of funds + other income – operating costs (all per R1 of assets). (4) Solve for X. Rate rises with: higher credit risk, tax, opex, cash holdings, lower volumes, retained capital; falls with: lower RWA, better property rights/deeds office, lower tax.
Reasons to regulate banks | (1) Important function – payment system, money creation, credit allocation; failure = externalities. (2) Vulnerability – maturity/liquidity transformation, high leverage, runs, contagion. (3) Conflicts of interest – shareholders/management gamble with depositors’ money (agency, information asymmetry, limited liability).
What depositors want | Liquidity (money when demanded), prudent lending (solvency), capital resilience (equity buffer) – to avoid both loss and inconvenience. Management/shareholders want high ROE via leverage and risk – the opposite.
Definitions of failure | Insolvency (L > A; VBS) · illiquidity (cannot pay as due; Saambou) · curatorship/resolution/deregistration (African Bank) · plus breach of minimums, rescue, market loss of confidence. Linked: illiquidity → fire sales → insolvency; insolvency → run; intervention responds to both. Grey on purpose (constructive ambiguity).
Causes of SA failures (immediate / underlying) | Saambou: wholesale run / flighty wholesale funding, micro-lending; solvent; ELA refused. BOE: contagion run / none (sound); guaranteed, merged into Nedbank. African Bank: funding freeze / bad unsecured loans, Ellerines, weak management; bail-in 10%, good/bad bank. VBS: withdrawals / fraud, weak governance; solvency first. Regal: run after audit opinion withdrawn / governance, misstatements. Ditsobotla: persistent losses, governance; resolution, CODI.
Curatorship vs resolution | Curatorship (Banks Act s 69): save the bank; curator; limited bail-in. Resolution (FSRA via FSLAA 2021, from 1 June 2023): financial stability first, may sacrifice the bank; SARB resolution authority; statutory bail-in, bridge bank, good/bad bank; CODI pays depositors.
Key true/false points | Running despite assurances is not irrational (sequential service, frozen access). A solvent bank can fail (liquidity). Yield curve excludes credit risk. LCR stress period is 30 days. Reserves (asset) ≠ capital (funding); reserves protect liquidity, capital protects solvency.
