h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 1 – Risk in banking > Why banks must manage risk
x:
Model answer: Why is it so important for banks to manage risk?
Solvency. A bank that takes on more risk than its capital can absorb goes bankrupt when a shock hits.
Systemic risk. Banks sit at the centre of the financial system. They hold everyone’s deposits and lend to each other through the interbank market, so the failure of one bank can cause a domino effect: other banks lose what they lent to it, depositors lose money and confidence, and the whole system can collapse (as in the 2008 financial crisis). This danger, the collapse of the whole financial system through cascading failures, is systemic risk.
Do not confuse systemic risk with systematic risk, which is market-wide (non-diversifiable) risk measured by beta.
Capital: getting the balance right
The Basel Accord requires banks to hold enough regulatory capital (shareholders’ funds that can absorb losses) to make failure unlikely and protect the system.
Too little capital: the bank becomes insolvent when a shock hits.
Too much capital: inefficient. Capital held in reserve earns nothing, while the bank’s business is to lend and earn a return, so idle capital has an opportunity cost.
This trade-off is why the Basel rules are so detailed: they try to set the right amount of capital for each type of risk (market, credit, operational and liquidity risk).
Concentration matters on both sides of the balance sheet. Diversification (“don’t put all your eggs in one basket”) applies to liabilities too. Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) failed largely because its depositors were concentrated in one sector (venture-capital-backed tech start-ups); when that sector withdrew cash at the same time, the bank collapsed.

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 1 – Risk in banking > The five risks at a glance
x:
A bank faces five main risks. Together they determine its capital (insolvency) risk: the risk that losses wipe out its capital.
Risk | What it is | Where it hits / key example | Main measures and tools
Credit risk | The risk that a borrower or counterparty defaults on its payment obligations (interest and principal). The single most important risk for a bank, because lending is its core business. | Loan book (banking book), bonds, OTC derivatives, guarantees. | Qualitative factors, LPM, logit, Altman Z, term structure of credit risk, loan pricing, RAROC, migration analysis, credit derivatives (Part 2).
Market risk (not examined 2026) | The risk of loss from trading assets and liabilities when market variables (risk factors: interest rates, FX, equity and commodity prices) change. | Trading book; hits trading income (earnings). Example: COVID-19 crash, 2008/9 crisis. | Value-at-Risk (VaR), expected shortfall, back-testing, stress testing, market risk charge.
Interest rate risk | The risk from a mismatch in the maturities / repricing dates of assets and liabilities. One of the market risk factors, but on the banking book. | Net interest income (NII) and the market value of capital. Example: Orange County (borrowing short to invest long). | Repricing gap (ISA vs ISL), refinancing / reinvestment / market value risk, duration, natural and derivative hedges.
Operational risk (not examined 2026) | The risk of loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems, or from external events. | The whole bank. Example: Nick Leeson at Barings, load shedding. | Basel standardised approach, AMA, SMA.
Liquidity risk (not examined 2026) | Asset liquidity risk: being unable to sell an asset at a reasonable price. Funding liquidity risk: being unable to raise cash to meet obligations as they fall due. | Example: a run on deposits forcing fire sales of assets (SVB). | Cost of liquidation (bid-offer spread), liquidity-adjusted VaR, Basel III LCR (30-day stress) and NSFR.
The “market risk” of the trading book and the “market value risk” of the banking book are different things: market value risk is a form of interest rate risk that hits capital (net worth), while market risk hits trading earnings.

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 1 – Risk in banking > Expected loss vs unexpected loss
x:
Expected loss (EL) – the average loss the bank expects to suffer on its loans over time. It is predictable, so it is treated as a normal cost of lending:
EL = PD × LGD × EADPD = probability of default · LGD = loss given default (the share of the exposure lost after recoveries such as collateral) · EAD = exposure at default (the amount owed when default happens)
EL is covered by pricing and provisions: the bank builds it into the interest rate it charges (the credit risk premium φ) and sets aside impairment provisions for it.
Unexpected loss (UL) – losses above the expected level (the bad years, the tail of the loss distribution). These cannot be priced in advance, so they are covered by capital. Absorbing UL is what Basel regulatory capital is for.
UL is not “uncontrollable” and it is not ignored: it is measured (e.g. with PD models, VaR or duration-based capital at risk) and capital is held against it.
Models such as the logit regression estimate PD; they are an input into EL and UL, not the way EL is provided for.
Expected loss → loan pricing (risk premium) + provisions | Unexpected loss → capital

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 2 – Credit risk > What credit risk is
x:
Lending is a core business of banking: banks transform savers’ deposits into loans.
Borrowers have two obligations, due on specific dates: interest payments and repayment of the principal.
Credit risk – the risk of a counterparty defaulting on its payment obligations, i.e. the potential that a borrower or counterparty fails to meet its obligations in accordance with the agreed terms.
Credit risk also comes from instruments other than loans and bonds, such as derivatives and guarantees. An OTC (over-the-counter) swap between two banks carries real default risk if the losing side does not pay; exchange-traded options carry little, because the clearing house requires margin accounts.
Basel I focused almost entirely on credit risk.
Consequences of credit risk
The bank earns zero or only partial interest and may lose all or part of the principal.
Lower profitability, higher insolvency risk, and weaker growth and ability to compete.
Goal of credit risk management: to maximise a bank’s risk-adjusted rate of return by maintaining credit risk exposure within acceptable parameters.

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 2 – Credit risk > Assessing a borrower: qualitative factors
x:
Credit risk models are used to (i) screen and filter out bad loan applicants, (ii) calculate the reserves (capital) needed for future loan losses, and (iii) price default risk on loans and bonds more accurately. Qualitative models use judgement about a list of factors; they are useful but can be subjective. Quantitative models (next section) are less subjective.
Borrower-specific (idiosyncratic) factors
Reputation – the borrower’s borrowing and repayment history and market reputation over the lending relationship. An established firm with a long record of prompt repayment gets better terms than an unknown firm; a history of defaulting signals poor finances or unwillingness to pay. Good reputation → lower premium.
Leverage – the borrower’s existing debt (capital structure, debt/equity). More debt means higher interest obligations and larger prior claims on cash flow, so a higher probability of default. Higher leverage → higher premium.
Volatility of earnings – how much earnings and cash flows swing. Earnings and cash flows are what pay interest and principal. If they are volatile, there is a real chance that in some period they fall below what is needed for debt service, even if the average is comfortable. Strong financials today are only a snapshot; volatility tells you about the bad periods to come. More volatile → higher premium.
Collateral – specific assets pledged that the lender can claim on default. It reduces the loss given default (LGD). Quality and liquidity matter: liquid, good-quality collateral can be sold quickly. Secured / good collateral → lower premium.
Market-specific factors
Business cycle – in a recession default probabilities rise for almost all borrowers (especially cyclical industries such as durable goods, construction and retail), so banks raise premiums and tighten lending standards; in a boom premiums fall. The catch-22: in a recession firms need loans most to survive but banks are least willing to lend; in a boom banks are happy to lend but prosperous firms need it least.
Level of interest rates – high rates usually signal tight monetary policy and a slowing economy, and they raise every borrower’s debt-service burden, so defaults rise. The catch-22: charging a risky borrower a higher rate compensates the bank for default risk, but the higher interest burden itself makes the borrower more likely to default. Above some level, higher rates also attract riskier borrowers (adverse selection), so the bank’s expected return actually falls (the backward-bending loan supply curve).
Worked example: qualitative credit factors (Workshop 3, Q3)
Identify and define the borrower-specific and market-specific factors in a qualitative credit model, and their effect on the risk premium.
Borrower-specific: reputation (lending history: better reputation, lower premium); leverage (debt/equity: higher leverage raises interest obligations and PD, higher premium); volatility of earnings (more volatile earnings make a shortfall against debt payments more likely, higher premium); collateral (assets the lender can claim on default: secured loans lose less, lower premium; quality and liquidity matter).
Market-specific: business cycle (lenders lend less when a recession is forecast; default probabilities rise, especially in cyclical industries, so premiums rise and standards tighten; in an expansion premiums fall); level of interest rates (high rates signal restrictive monetary policy and a slowing economy and raise borrowers’ debt-service burden, so defaults rise and lenders are more reluctant to lend).
Factor | Condition | Effect on risk premium
Reputation | Good, long relationship | ↓
Leverage | Higher | ↑
Earnings volatility | Higher | ↑
Collateral | Secured / high quality | ↓
Business cycle | Recession (expansion) | ↑ (↓)
Interest rate level | High (low) | ↑ (↓)
Worked example: collateral (Workshop 3, Q4)
Why is collateral important to a lender? If the book value of collateral is at least the loan amount, is the lender’s credit risk fully covered?
Why it matters:
It reduces loss given default: the lender can seize and sell it to recover some or all of what is owed.
It gives the lender priority: a secured claim on specific assets ranks ahead of unsecured creditors in bankruptcy or liquidation.
It improves the borrower’s incentives: a borrower who stands to lose pledged assets has more reason to repay and less reason to take excessive risk (less moral hazard), and willingness to post collateral signals confidence in the project (less adverse selection).
So more and better collateral means a lower risk premium. But the risk is not fully covered by book value:
Collateral is worth only its market value, so a loan fully covered at book value may not be covered at market value.
Errors in recording collateral can reduce the lender’s protection.
Collateral values tend to fall when defaults happen: borrowers default in downturns, exactly when asset prices fall, so collateral is worth least when it is needed most.
Seized assets are often sold quickly at fire-sale prices below fair value, especially illiquid assets.
Exam focus: explaining why earnings volatility matters for default risk; naming two borrower-specific and one market-specific factor for a given borrower (e.g. a history of defaulting and a 92% debt ratio).

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 2 – Credit risk > Default models (quantitative credit scoring)
x:
Credit scoring models are quantitative models that use observed borrower characteristics either to (i) calculate a score representing the borrower’s probability of default (PD), or (ii) sort borrowers into default risk classes. The bank picks objective factors for each class of borrower:
Consumer debt: income, assets, age, occupation, location, etc.
Commercial debt: cash flow information and financial ratios (e.g. debt/equity, interest cover).
It then uses statistical techniques to “score” the PD or the default class. The ultimate goal of fitting a model is to find the one that best describes the relationship between default and the explanatory variables, so that each new borrower’s PD can be predicted reliably. That PD is then used to accept or reject the loan, to price it, and as an input into expected and unexpected loss.
Linear probability model (LPM)
Uses past data on borrower characteristics (e.g. financial ratios) to explain repayment on old loans, then applies the same factors to estimate the PD on new loans.
Old loans are split into two groups: those that defaulted (PDi = 1) and those that did not (PDi = 0). A linear regression relates this 0/1 outcome to j explanatory variables Xij.
PD_i=α+j=1nβ_jX_ij+ε βj = estimated importance of variable j in explaining past repayment · Xij = value of variable j for borrower iMultiply each βj by the borrower’s Xij and add them up to get the estimated PDi.
Worked example: LPM
PDi = 0.5(D/E) − 0.0525(S/A), no constant. A potential borrower has leverage D/E = 0.3 and sales/assets S/A = 2.0.
PDi = 0.5(0.3) − 0.0525(2.0) = 0.15 − 0.105 = 0.045 = 4.5% probability of default.
Why a linear regression does not work for binary default data
Default data is binary: each borrower either defaulted (Y = 1) or did not (Y = 0). On a scatter plot of Y against an explanatory variable such as the debt ratio, every point lies on one of two horizontal lines.
A straight line through two horizontal bands of points fits badly; the errors are not normal and do not have constant variance, so the usual regression assumptions fail.
The fitted values (read as PDs) can fall below 0 or above 1 at extreme values of X. A probability outside [0, 1] (e.g. a “PD of 7”) has no meaning. This is the main weakness of the LPM.
The true relationship between X and PD is S-shaped: it flattens as it approaches 0 and 1. In an exam, draw the two bands of points, the straight line breaking out of [0, 1], and an S-shaped logistic curve for contrast.
Economic-cycle bias: the model is re-estimated as new data comes in, but a model estimated on recession data (many defaults) will be biased if used in a boom, and vice versa.
Logit model
The logit (logistic regression) model fixes the LPM’s main flaw. It takes the same kind of linear score Y and passes it through the logistic function, which maps any Y from −∞ to +∞ onto an S-shaped curve between 0 and 1:
PD_i=P(Y)=(1)/(1+exp(-Y)) , where Y=α+jβ_jX_ij+ε exp(Y)=(P(Y))/(1-P(Y)) = the odds ratio: the probability of belonging to one group (default) relative to the probability of not belonging to it.So Y=ln((PD)/(1-PD)) = the log-odds (the “logit”) of default.
Value added over the LPM: the estimated PD is always between 0 and 1, with an S-shaped relationship. It is the model that best fits binary default data.
Meaning of a slope coefficient βj: the change in the logit (log-odds of default) for a one-unit change in that explanatory variable, holding the others constant. It is not the change in PD itself; the effect on PD depends on where on the S-curve the borrower is. A positive β raises the PD, a negative β lowers it.
The β coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood, so a logit model has its own, different coefficients from an LPM on the same data.
Major drawback: it is estimated on historical data, so it assumes the past is an accurate predictor of the future and makes no provision for events outside that history (a financial crisis, an epidemic). Solution: stress testing – run the portfolio through severe but plausible scenarios that the historical data does not contain.
Worked example: logit transformation with the LPM inputs
Y = 0.5(0.3) − 0.0525(2) = 0.045, so PD = (1)/(1+exp(-0.045)) = (1)/(1+0.95600) = (1)/(1.95600) = 51.12%.
This is not comparable with the LPM’s 4.5%. It only demonstrates the transformation: a real logit model estimates its own β coefficients, and with properly estimated betas the PD would be sensible.
Worked example: LPM vs logit (Workshop 3, Q1)
Three ratios are used to evaluate PD: debt/equity (D/E), sales/total assets (S/A) and retained earnings/total assets (RE/A). The applicant has D/E = 1.12, S/A = 1.35, RE/A = 0.37.
(a) LPM: PDi = X1(D/E) + X2(S/A) + X3(RE/A), with X1 = 0.021, X2 = 0.046, X3 = 0.013. Find the PD.
PD = 0.021(1.12) + 0.046(1.35) + 0.013(0.37) = 0.02352 + 0.0621 + 0.00481 = 0.0904, i.e. 9.04%.
(b) Logit: Y = X1(D/E) + X2(S/A) + X3(RE/A), PD = (1)/(1+exp(-Y)) , with X1 = 0.41, X2 = −2.11, X3 = −3.12. Find the PD.
Y = 0.41(1.12) − 2.11(1.35) − 3.12(0.37) = 0.4592 − 2.8485 − 1.1544 = −3.5437.PD = (1)/(1+exp(3.5437)) = (1)/(1+34.59) = (1)/(35.59) = 0.0281, i.e. 2.81%.
(c) Interpret the results. Which model is likely to describe the client’s risk profile more accurately?
The LPM is more prone to error because it can give values outside [0, 1], which are meaningless as probabilities. The logit model restricts PD to between 0 and 1 while still using the whole range of outcomes, so it is likely to give the more accurate description. The two models give very different answers (9.04% vs 2.81%), so here the LPM has probably overstated the client’s probability of default.
Linear discriminant model: the Altman Z-score (1968)
A linear discriminant model (LDM) uses historical data on old loans to classify a new borrower into a high or low default risk class, rather than estimating an exact probability.
Z=1.2X_1+1.4X_2+3.3X_3+0.6X_4+1.0X_5X_1=(net working capital)/(total assets) X_2=(retained earnings)/(total assets) X_3=(EBIT)/(total assets) X_4=(market value of equity)/(book value of total liabilities) X_5=(sales)/(total assets)
Correct labels: X3, X4 and X5 as above (slide labels the last three ratios X1). The weights are fixed parameters from Altman’s original study.
Altman Z-score | Description | Zone | Decision
Z < 1.81 | High default risk firm | Distress zone | Decline the loan
1.81 < Z < 2.99 | Indeterminate default risk firm | Grey zone | Look further (qualitative factors)
Z > 2.99 | Low default risk firm | Safe zone | Lend
The original study was 72% accurate in predicting bankruptcy 2 years before it happened, with a 6% false positive (Type II error) rate.
Worked example: Z-score
X1 = 0.02; X2 = 0.16; X3 = 0.037; X4 = 0.40; X5 = 2.53.
Z = 1.2(0.02) + 1.4(0.16) + 3.3(0.037) + 0.6(0.40) + 1.0(2.53) = 0.024 + 0.224 + 0.1221 + 0.24 + 2.53 = 3.14.
Z > 2.99, so the borrower is in the safe zone (low default risk) and the bank should make the loan.
Worked example: Uthingo Manufacturing (Workshop 3, Q2)
Total assets 500; working capital (current assets − current liabilities) 75; retained earnings 125; EBIT 60; market value of equity 600; total liabilities 300; sales 550. Use the Z-score to evaluate the applicant.
X1 = (75)/(500) = 0.15; X2 = (125)/(500) = 0.25; X3 = (60)/(500) = 0.12; X4 = (600)/(300) = 2.0; X5 = (550)/(500) = 1.1.Z = 1.2(0.15) + 1.4(0.25) + 3.3(0.12) + 0.6(2.0) + 1.0(1.1) = 0.18 + 0.35 + 0.396 + 1.2 + 1.1 = 3.23.Above 2.99 is safe, 1.81–2.99 grey, below 1.81 distress. With 3.23 the firm is in the safe zone, so the loan need not be denied on this basis.
Weaknesses of the Z-score model
It only discriminates between two extremes: default or no default.
Sample dependence: the original study used only 66 firms (33 bankrupt and 33 non-bankrupt US manufacturers).
It uses accounting data, which is backward-looking and can be manipulated.
The weights are fixed and the model is linear, although the true relationships may change over time and may not be linear.
It ignores important hard-to-quantify factors: management quality and governance, and macroeconomic and event risk (pandemics, sanctions, etc.).
Term structure of credit risk approach
A more modern, market-based method: estimate default probabilities from the risk premiums in the current term structure of yields. A corporate yield curve lies above the treasury (government) curve because of default risk; the gap is the default risk spread (corporate yield − treasury yield).
Key assumptions:
The whole yield spread between corporate and treasury bonds of the same maturity is due to default risk only (liquidity, tax and other premia are ignored).
If the borrower defaults, the investor recovers nothing (zero recovery).
Investors are risk-neutral: the risky bond must offer the same expected return as the risk-free bond.
One-year probability of default
If a corporate bond had no default risk it would earn the same as a treasury. With default risk, the expected return on the corporate must equal the risk-free return:
p(1+k)=1+i ⇒ p=(1+i)/(1+k) and probability of default = 1-p p = probability the corporate debt is repaid in full · k = yield on the 1-year zero-coupon corporate bond · i = yield on the 1-year zero-coupon treasury strip (credit-risk-free)
Worked example: one-year default probability
1-year treasury strip i = 2.05%; 1-year zero-coupon corporate bond k = 7.80%.
p = (1.0205)/(1.078) = 0.9467, so the implied probability of default is 1 − 0.9467 = 0.0533 (5.33%).
Correct figure: p = 0.9467 and PD = 5.33% (slide divides by 1.0708 and shows p = 0.953, PD = 0.047). The slide’s own two-year example uses 1.0205 ÷ 1.078, which confirms the correction.
Multi-year (cumulative) probability of default
For a 2- or 3-year loan, estimate a marginal probability of default for each year: the probability of default in year 2 given that the bond did not default in year 1. The year-2 marginal PD (1 − p2) can differ from the year-1 PD (1 − p1).
The probability of surviving both years is p1 × p2, so:
Cumulative probability of default (years 1 and 2): CP=1-(p_1×p_2) For n years: CP=1-(p_1×p_2×⋯×p_n)
Worked example: two-year cumulative default (given marginal PDs)
1 − p1 = 0.05 and 1 − p2 = 0.07. Probability of surviving both years = 0.95 × 0.93 = 0.8835, so the cumulative probability of default = 1 − 0.8835 = 0.1165 (11.65%).
Note that 11.65% is less than 5% + 7% = 12%: the year-2 PD only applies to loans that survived year 1. Never just add the marginal PDs.
Getting the year-2 PD from market prices (forward rates)
To find p2 from the yield curves, first derive the one-year forward rates for year 2 on treasuries and on corporate debt, using (1 + r2)² = (1 + r1)(1 + f1,1):
Treasury forward: 1+f_1,1=((1+i_2)^2)/(1+i_1) Corporate forward: 1+c_1,1=((1+k_2)^2)/(1+k_1) (c1,1 reflects the market’s default expectations for the corporate) p_2(1+c_1,1)=1+f_1,1 ⇒ p_2=(1+f_1,1)/(1+c_1,1) ; year-2 PD = 1 − p2.The same approach gives the expected PD for year 3, and so on.
Worked example: expected default in year 2 and cumulative two-year default
Treasuries: i1 = 2.05%, i2 = 3%. Corporate (grade B): k1 = 7.80%, k2 = 10%.
Treasury forward rate for year 2: 1+f_1,1=(1.03^2)/(1.0205)=(1.0609)/(1.0205)=1.0396 , so f1,1 = 3.96%.
Corporate forward rate for year 2: 1+c_1,1=(1.10^2)/(1.078)=(1.21)/(1.078)=1.1224 , so c1,1 = 12.24%.
Year-2 repayment probability: p_2=(1+f_1,1)/(1+c_1,1)=(1.0396)/(1.1224)=0.9262 , so the expected probability of default in year 2 = 1-0.9262 = 7.38%.
Cumulative default over two years: p_1=(1.0205)/(1.078)=0.9467 , and CP=1-(0.9467×0.9262)=1-0.8768 = 12.32% over the next two years.
Pros and cons of the market-based approach
Advantage: it is forward-looking and based on market expectations, unlike the Z-score’s historical accounting data.
Problems: corporate bonds are not actively traded and prices are not transparent, so the calculation may rest on incorrect prices; and spreads are driven by other factors too (e.g. liquidity), not only default risk, which breaks the key assumption.
Exam focus: LPM vs logit and why linear regression fails for binary data (with a graph), the meaning of the logit slope coefficient, the goal of fitting the model, the drawback of historical models and stress testing as the remedy, Altman zones (e.g. “would you lend at Z = 1.78?”), the term-structure assumption, and one-year and cumulative two-year PD calculations.

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 2 – Credit risk > Pricing a loan
x:
A bank adjusts for a borrower’s credit risk through: the interest rate, any fees, the credit risk premium, the collateral backing the loan, and other non-price terms (especially compensating balances and reserve requirements).
1. Interest rate
Loan rate = BR + φ (BR = base lending rate, φ = credit risk premium)
Example: a R10m loan with BR = 8% and φ = 2% has an interest rate of 8% + 2% = 10%.
Choice of base rate: prime for retail borrowers and for long-term loans to corporate clients; JIBAR (or another interbank rate) for short-term corporate borrowing. Riskier borrowers pay a higher φ.
2. Origination fee
A loan origination fee (of) charged for processing the application raises the contractually promised gross return to of + (BR + φ).
3. Compensating balance
A compensating balance (b) is a part of the loan that the borrower must keep with the bank as a deposit, usually earning little or no interest. The borrower pays interest on the full loan, but the bank only has to fund the part that leaves the bank, so the bank’s return rises. It also acts as a safety net for the bank against default.
Worked example: compensating balance
A R30 000 loan at 10% with an 8% compensating balance. The borrower pays interest of R3 000 but can only use R30 000 × 92% = R27 600.
Effective interest rate = (R3 000)/(R27 600) = 10.87%, or equivalently (10%)/(1-0.08) = 10.87%.
4. Reserve requirement
A portion of a bank’s deposits must be held at the central bank, earning no interest. The SARB reserve requirement ratio (RR) is 2.5%.
Why have it? A liquidity buffer (to settle payments and meet withdrawals), and a monetary policy tool for the SARB to tighten or loosen credit, in addition to changing interest rates.
Effect on pricing: the reserve earns nothing, so the bank grosses up the rate to compensate.
Worked example: reserve requirement
Loan rate 10% (BR 6% + φ 4%) with a 2.5% reserve requirement: interest rate = (BR+φ)/(1-RR) = (0.10)/(0.975) = 10.26%.
Return on assets (ROA) per rand lent: the contractually promised return
1+k=1+(of+(BR+φ))/(1-b(1-RR)) k = contractually promised gross return (ROA) per rand lent · of = origination fee · BR + φ = loan rate · b = compensating balance as a fraction of the loan · RR = reserve requirement
Numerator: what the bank earns per R1 lent (fee + interest).
Denominator: the funds the bank actually gives up per R1 lent. The borrower leaves b on deposit, but the bank must hold RR of that deposit at the SARB, so only b(1 − RR) is truly “given back” to the bank. Net outlay = 1 − b(1 − RR).
If there is no compensating balance (b = 0), the denominator is 1 and k = of + BR + φ: the reserve requirement only enters through the compensating balance.
If a question’s stated loan rate does not equal BR + φ, use BR + φ (as the memo does) and state your assumption.
k is the promised return. If the borrower defaults the actual return is lower, so in practice the expected loss is subtracted in the numerator.
Worked example: ROA per rand lent
Loan rate 10% (BR 6%, φ 4%); origination fee 0.125%; 8% compensating balance held in non-interest-bearing demand deposits; reserves of 2.5% of deposits.
1 + k = 1 + (0.00125+0.06+0.04)/(1-0.08(1-0.025)) = 1 + (0.10125)/(1-0.078) = 1 + (0.10125)/(0.922) = 1.1098, so k = 10.98%.
Interpretation: the fee and the compensating balance (net of the reserves the bank must hold on it) raise the bank’s promised return from the 10% loan rate to 10.98% per rand actually lent.
Worked example: the same loan from the borrower’s side
The borrower can use only 92% of the loan (R92 per R100) because of the 8% compensating balance.
The origination fee is deducted from the proceeds, so usable funds fall to R91.875 per R100.
The 2.5% reserve requirement does not affect the borrower; it is between the bank and the SARB.
True cost to the borrower: R10.125 of interest and fees for about R92 of usable money = (10.125)/(92) = 11.01% (or (10.125)/(91.875) = 11.02%), i.e. about 11%, slightly above the bank’s 10.98% return. The gap is the R0.20 per R100 the bank must hold in reserves (8 × 2.5%).
Exam focus: ROA per rand lent with a fee, compensating balance and reserves (4 marks, examined repeatedly; always interpret the answer), and choosing the loan rate (prime + premium + fee) for a risky corporate borrower.

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 2 – Credit risk > RAROC (risk-adjusted return on capital)
x:
RAROC measures how much a loan earns relative to the economic capital the bank must hold against its risk.
Essential idea: it balances the expected interest and fee income, less the cost of funds, against the loan’s expected risk. (This is the difference from ROA per rand lent, which ignores risk.)
It lets banks compare loans of different risk on a like-for-like basis.
RAROC=(Risk-adjusted net income)/(Economic capital)RAROC=(One-year net income on a loan)/(Loan (asset) risk, or capital at risk)
Using RAROC
Approval benchmark (hurdle rate): approve a loan only if its RAROC is sufficiently higher than the bank’s cost of equity (COE) – the return shareholders require (or the bank’s target ROE).
Pricing tool: if RAROC is below the hurdle, adjust the loan’s terms to make it “profitable” again – usually by raising the credit risk premium (spread) or fees, or by shortening the loan’s duration.
Numerator: one-year net income
Net income = Revenue − (funding cost + operating cost)Revenue = interest income + fees · Funding cost = cost of funds, or the funds transfer price (the internal rate the bank’s treasury charges the lending unit) · Operating cost = cost of originating, servicing and monitoring the loanShort form used in most questions: Net income = (projected spread + fees) × loan amount
Denominator: capital at risk using duration
The capital at risk is the fall in the loan’s market value if its credit quality worsens, i.e. if the loan rate R (base rate + risk premium φ) rises by the expected maximum (worst-case) amount ΔR. The duration model gives:
(ΔLN)/(LN)=-D_LN×(ΔR)/(1+R)=-D_LN^*×ΔR Capital at risk: ΔLN=-D_LN^*×LN×ΔR , with modified duration D^*=(D)/(1+R) LN = loan value · D = (Macaulay) duration of the loan · R = current average rate on bonds in the borrower’s rating class · ΔR = expected maximum change in the loan rate (e.g. from a rise in the credit premium)
Where ΔR comes from: the largest increase in credit risk premiums for bonds in the borrower’s rating class over the past year, at a 99% worst case (e.g. only 1% of the bonds in the class had a bigger increase). The number of bonds in the class is only the sample used to find ΔR; it does not enter the calculation.
Use the size of ΔLN (a positive number) as the denominator.
Worked example: RAROC of a AAA loan
A R1 million loan with duration 2.7 years to a AAA borrower. The expected maximum change in the loan rate due to a change in the credit premium is 1.1%. The current average rate on AAA bonds (R) is 5%. The projected one-year spread is 0.2% and fees are 0.1%. Find the RAROC.
D* = (2.7)/(1.05) = 2.57.
Capital at risk: ΔLN = −2.57 × R1 000 000 × 0.011 = −R28 270 (−R28 286 with D* unrounded). This is the fall in the loan’s market value from a decline in credit quality.
Net income: (0.2% + 0.1%) × R1 000 000 = R3 000.
RAROC = (3 000)/(28 270) = 10.61%.
Worked example: pricing a loan and its RAROC together
This links the loan rate (what the loan earns after fees, compensating balance and reserves) to RAROC (whether that income is enough for the capital the loan puts at risk). R1m loan; base rate (prime) 12%; credit risk premium 2%; origination fee 0.125%; compensating balance b = 10%; reserve requirement RR = 2.5%; the bank’s cost of funds 12%; modified duration D* = 2.41; worst-case rate change ΔR = 4.2% (estimated from about 30 years of rate history at 99% confidence over one year).
Gross income: interest 14% × R1m = R140 000, plus fee 0.125% × R1m = R1 250, so R141 250.
Net funds the bank actually provides: R1m × [1 − b(1 − RR)] = R1m × [1 − 0.10 × 0.975] = R1m × 0.9025 = R902 500.
Funding cost: 12% × R902 500 = R108 300.
One-year net income: R141 250 − R108 300 = R32 950.
Capital at risk: 2.41 × R1m × 0.042 = R101 220.
RAROC = (32 950)/(101 220) = 32.55%.
Decision: against a hurdle rate (cost of equity) of, say, 30%, 32.55% > 30%, so the loan adds value and is approved. If RAROC were below the hurdle, the bank would change the terms, usually by raising the credit risk premium.
Worked example: Zenzele Bank (Workshop 3, Q5)
A R5m loan with duration 4.3 years to a AAA borrower. There are 500 traded AAA bonds; the average AAA rate R = 8%. The largest increase in AAA credit risk premiums over the last year, the 99% worst case, was 1.2% (only 6 of 500 bonds had bigger increases). The projected one-year spread is 0.3% and fees are 0.25% of face value. Find the capital at risk and the RAROC.
Modified duration D* = (D)/(1+R) = (4.3)/(1.08) = 3.98.
Capital at risk: ΔL = −D* × L × ΔR = −3.98 × R5 000 000 × 0.012 = −R238 889. In the 99% worst-case year the loan’s value could fall by about R238 889; this is the capital the bank must hold against it.
One-year net income = (spread + fees) × L = (0.003 + 0.0025) × R5 000 000 = R27 500.
RAROC = (27 500)/(238 889) = 11.51%.
Approve the loan only if 11.51% exceeds the bank’s hurdle rate (cost of equity or target ROE); if not, raise the spread or fees. The 1.2% is the worst-case ΔR because it is the 99th-percentile increase: only 6 of 500 bonds (about 1%) had bigger jumps.
Exam focus: 4-mark RAROC calculations with duration-based capital at risk (examined repeatedly; compare with the hurdle rate and say what to do if it falls short), and an MCQ on the essential idea behind RAROC.

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 2 – Credit risk > Managing credit risk at portfolio level
x:
Beyond screening individual borrowers, banks diversify the loan book by setting concentration limits by borrower (individual / company), sector / industry, and geography / region. A book concentrated in one sector (as SVB’s was in VC-backed tech) is exposed to that sector crashing.
Banks with opposite sector concentrations (e.g. one heavy in manufacturing, another in IT) can also use derivatives to swap sector risk with each other.
Migration analysis and the transition matrix
Migration analysis tracks how borrowers’ credit ratings change over time, so the bank looks at the whole path of credit quality rather than only at whether borrowers default.
The core tool is a rating transition (migration) matrix: the probability that a borrower with a given rating at the start of a period ends it in each rating (including default). It is built from the bank’s own rating history or from rating-agency data.
From / To | AAA | A | BBB | BB | Default
AAA | 92% | 7% | 1% | 0% | 0%
A | 2% | 92% | 5% | 2% | 0%
BBB | 0% | 3% | 88% | 8% | 1%
BB | 0% | 1% | 6% | 85% | 8%
The A row as shown adds up to 101% (2 + 92 + 5 + 2); this is a rounding slip in the source matrix. Each row of a transition matrix should sum to 100%.
Reading it: the main diagonal shows stability (rating unchanged); entries to the right are downgrades (deterioration) and to the left upgrades. Of A-rated borrowers, 2% were upgraded to AAA, 92% stayed A and 5% fell to BBB.
Concentration limits: compare migration patterns across sectors. If downgrades are rising faster in, say, mining or construction than historically or than the rest of the book, the bank can (i) cut or limit lending to that sector, (ii) raise the price, or (iii) tighten lending criteria.
Early warning: a rise in downgrades usually shows up well before defaults, giving the bank time to act. Example: if this year’s A → BBB downgrade rate is 5% against a 1% five-year average, that is a red flag.
Downgrade-to-upgrade ratio (e.g. for A: (5%)/(2%) = 2.5) is a simple way to compare sectors or periods.

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 2 – Credit risk > Managing credit risk with credit derivatives
x:
Banks use credit derivatives to hedge the credit risk on individual loans or bonds, or on whole portfolios: digital default options, credit forwards and credit default swaps (CDS).
Credit derivatives separate the credit risk exposure from the lending itself. The bank keeps the client’s loan unchanged but transfers the risk to another party (e.g. an insurer or investment bank). This is risk sharing: passing part of a loss to someone else.
Digital default options
Binary (digital) options have only two outcomes: a payout occurs only if a specific condition is met at or before expiry.
A digital default option pays a stated amount if a loan defaults. The bank buys (goes long) the option to cover the par value of a loan or loans. On default, the option writer pays the bank the par value of the defaulted loan.
If there is no default, the option expires worthless. The bank’s maximum loss is the premium it paid for the option.
Credit forwards
A credit forward hedges against an increase in the default risk of a loan after the loan rate has been set and the loan issued. (Before the rate is set, the bank could simply price the higher risk into the loan.)
The underlying is the credit yield spread: the difference between the yield on a benchmark bond of the borrower and a comparable government bond. A rise in the spread signals higher default risk and means the bank’s fixed-rate loan has lost value.
The bank sells a credit forward, locking in a forward credit spread φF. The buyer takes on the risk of the spread widening. Modified duration converts the change in spread into a rand amount.
At maturity, with actual spread φT:φT > φF (spread widens, loan loses value): buyer pays the bank (seller) (φT − φF) × D* × AφT < φF (spread narrows, loan gains value): the bank pays the buyer (φF − φT) × D* × AA = notional (size) of the forward · D* = modified duration of the benchmark bond / loan
Spread at end of forward | Credit spread seller (bank) | Credit spread buyer (counterparty)
φT > φF | Receives (φT − φF) × D* × A | Pays (φT − φF) × D* × A
φF > φT | Pays (φF − φT) × D* × A | Receives (φF − φT) × D* × A
The bank’s maximum loss on the forward is limited, reached when φT falls to zero: φF × D* × A. Unlike an option, both sides of a forward can lose: the bank gives away the upside if the spread narrows.
Worked example: spread widening
Modified duration of a BBB bond = 5; contract size A = R10m. The BBB–treasury spread widens from 2% to 3% over the year.
Payment to the seller (bank) = (3% − 2%) × 5 × R10 000 000 = R500 000.
Worked example: hedging a downgrade
A bank lends R5m to an A-rated firm; the loan’s modified duration is 4.5; the A–treasury spread at issue is 2% (φF). Expecting a downgrade, the bank sells a R5m credit spread forward. The borrower is downgraded to BB and the BB–treasury spread is now 5% (φT). Find the change in the loan’s market value and show how the hedge works.
Duration model: ΔL = −L × D* × Δφ = −R5 000 000 × 4.5 × (0.05 − 0.02) = −R675 000.
The forward buyer pays the bank (φT − φF) × D* × A = 0.03 × 4.5 × R5 000 000 = R675 000.
The payout exactly offsets the loss in the loan’s value: a perfect hedge.
Credit default swaps (CDS)
The most commonly traded credit derivative. The buyer of protection (the bank) makes periodic payments (quoted in basis points per year, paid quarterly, semi-annually or annually) to the seller of protection (e.g. an insurance company) until the swap ends or a specified credit event happens.
If the reference entity defaults, settlement is either physical delivery (the bank delivers the defaulted bond or loan and receives its par value) or a cash payment (par minus the recovery value). If there is no default, the seller keeps the premiums and pays nothing.
For the protection seller, a CDS is an unpredictable funding obligation, because the payout depends on someone else defaulting.
Comparing the instruments
Credit forward | Digital default option | CDS
Protects against | A deterioration in credit quality (spread widening), not default itself | Default itself | Default (a credit event)
Payoff | (φT − φF) × D* × A; can be negative for the bank | Fixed, stated amount (e.g. par) on default; zero otherwise | Par (or par − recovery) on the credit event
Upfront / ongoing cost | None, but the bank gives away the gain if the spread narrows | One premium; maximum loss = premium | Periodic premiums until maturity or the credit event
Exam focus: how a credit forward and a digital default option differ in the protection they give (4 marks), and an MCQ on when a credit forward is used (an increase in default risk after the loan rate is set and the loan issued).

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 3 – Interest rate risk > What interest rate risk is
x:
Interest rate risk – the risk that changes in interest rates reduce a bank’s income or its net worth because its assets and liabilities reprice (or mature) at different times. If interest expense rises faster than interest income, profit falls.
Two accounting identities frame the whole topic:
Capital (equity, net worth) = Assets (e.g. loans) − Liabilities (e.g. deposits)Net interest income (NII) = Interest earned on assets − Interest paid on liabilities = Interest income − Interest expense
Remember the bank’s point of view: customer deposits are the bank’s liabilities; loans are its assets.
Interest-sensitive assets (ISA) – assets whose interest rate will be reset (repriced) within a chosen period. Interest-sensitive liabilities (ISL) – liabilities whose rate will be reset within the same period. ISA and ISL are also written RSA and RSL (rate-sensitive assets/liabilities).
The interest rate gap = ISA − ISL.
ISA > ISL (positive gap): the bank loses when rates fall.
ISA < ISL (negative gap): the bank loses when rates rise.
When assets and liabilities are mismatched, interest rate changes expose the bank to three forms of interest rate risk: refinancing risk, reinvestment risk and market value (price) risk. The first two hit income (NII); the third hits capital (net worth).
Worked example: a negative gap and a rate rise
A bank has deposits (ISL) of R1bn that reprice with the market, floating-rate loans (ISA) of R500m that reprice with the market, and fixed-rate loans of R500m that do not reprice. Before the change: deposits cost 3%; all loans earn 7%. Rates then rise by 1%.
Before | After a 1% rise
Interest on ISA (R500m) | 7% → R35m | 8% → R40m
Interest on fixed-rate loans (R500m) | 7% → R35m | 7% → R35m (locked in)
Total interest income | R70m | R75m
Interest on ISL (R1bn) | 3% → R30m | 4% → R40m
NII | R40m | R35m
NII falls by R5m. Check with the gap: gap = R500m − R1bn = −R500m; −R500m × 1% = −R5m. A rate rise reduces NII when the gap is negative.
Model answer: what is the limitation of the gap (ISA vs ISL) as a measure? On its own it only tells you which direction of rate move hurts the bank. It does not tell you how big the loss will be. For the size you need the gap multiplied by the rate change (the repricing model below), or a duration-based measure of the change in market value.

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 3 – Interest rate risk > Refinancing risk
x:
Refinancing risk – the risk that the cost of rolling over (refinancing) maturing liabilities rises above the return still being earned on the assets they fund.
It arises in two linked circumstances:
ISA < ISL (a negative repricing gap): more liabilities than assets reprice in the period. When rates rise, interest expense rises by more than interest income, so NII falls.
Assets have a longer maturity than the liabilities that fund them (long-term assets funded with short-term liabilities). The short liabilities must be refinanced before the assets mature. If rates have risen by then, the bank pays the new, higher rate on its funding while its assets keep earning their old fixed rate. The spread narrows and NII falls.
Refinancing risk = the bank is hurt by rising rates. The Orange County collapse is the classic case of borrowing short to fund long positions.
Worked example: refinancing risk (gap form)
ISA = R20m earning 10%; ISL = R25m costing 7%.
NII = (20 × 0.10) − (25 × 0.07) = R2.0m − R1.75m = R250 000.
Rates rise by 2%: NII = (20 × 0.12) − (25 × 0.09) = R2.4m − R2.25m = R150 000.
NII falls by R100 000 (= gap −R5m × 2%): the cost of refinancing rises more than the return on the assets.
Worked example: refinancing risk (maturity form)
A two-year fixed-rate loan at 10% is funded by a one-year deposit at 9%. Year 1 spread = 10% − 9% = +1%. At the end of year 1 the deposit must be refinanced; rates have risen and the new deposit costs 11%. Year 2 spread = 10% − 11% = −1%. The loan rate is locked, the funding cost is not.

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 3 – Interest rate risk > Reinvestment risk
x:
Reinvestment risk – the risk that the return on funds reinvested when assets mature falls below the cost of the liabilities still funding them.
It arises when ISA > ISL (a positive gap), typically because short-term assets are funded with long-term liabilities. When the assets mature the bank must re-lend at the new market rate while its funding stays at the old fixed cost. If rates fall, interest income drops but interest expense does not, so NII falls.
Worked example: reinvestment risk (gap form)
ISA = R45m earning 10%; ISL = R25m costing 7%.
NII = (45 × 0.10) − (25 × 0.07) = R4.5m − R1.75m = R2 750 000.
Rates fall by 2%: NII = (45 × 0.08) − (25 × 0.05) = R3.6m − R1.25m = R2 350 000.
NII falls by R400 000 (= gap +R20m × −2%): interest income falls by more than interest expense.
Worked example: reinvestment risk (maturity form)
A one-year loan at 10% is funded by a two-year fixed deposit at 9%. Year 1 spread = +1%. At the end of year 1 the loan is repaid and the money must be re-lent; rates have fallen and it can only be lent at 8%. Year 2 spread = 8% − 9% = −1%.
Refinancing vs reinvestment risk at a glance
Refinancing risk | Reinvestment risk
Gap | Negative (ISA < ISL) | Positive (ISA > ISL)
Typical structure | Long assets, short liabilities | Short assets, long liabilities
What has to be rolled over | The liabilities (funding) | The assets (lending)
Hurt by | Rising rates | Falling rates
Helped by | Falling rates | Rising rates
Exam focus: 2020 Section C Q13 (two circumstances that cause refinancing risk, 7 marks) – give both circumstances and the maturity example with the spread turning from +1% to −1%.

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 3 – Interest rate risk > Market value risk
x:
The market (fair) value of any asset or liability is the present value of all its current and future cash flows.
Market value risk – the risk that a change in interest rates changes the market value of the bank’s rate-sensitive assets and liabilities by different amounts, so that capital (net worth) falls.
Rising rates raise the discount rate and reduce market values; falling rates increase them. The longer the duration (the average time until the cash flows are received), the bigger the change.
If assets lose more value than liabilities, capital falls. A large enough fall exposes the bank to economic loss and possibly insolvency.
Model answer: why does an interest rate increase lower the value of interest-bearing assets? The value of a bond or loan is the present value of its fixed future cash flows. A higher interest rate is a higher discount rate, so each future cash flow is worth less today and the price falls. The longer the duration, the bigger the fall.
Market value risk is not the same as market risk. The two are compared at the end of Part 3.

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 3 – Interest rate risk > The repricing model
x:
The repricing model measures the repricing gap: the difference between assets whose interest rates will be repriced over some future period (ISA) and liabilities whose rates will be repriced over that period (ISL). It turns the direction-only gap into a rand figure for the change in NII.
Gaps are calculated for each maturity bucket: 1 day (overnight); more than 1 day to 3 months; more than 3 to 6 months; more than 6 to 12 months; more than 1 year to 5 years; more than 5 years.
Banks report the gap in each bucket by calculating ISA and ISL from their balance sheet, and usually disclose these gaps in their annual reports.
GAPi = ISAi − ISLi (gap in bucket i)ΔNIIi = GAPi × ΔRi (ΔRi = change in the interest rate affecting bucket i)CGAP = cumulative gap = sum of the bucket gaps up to the chosen horizon · ΔNII = CGAP × ΔR
The slide writes ΔNIIi = GAPi × Ri; the last term must be ΔRi, the change in rates.
Worked example: repricing gaps by bucket ($m)
Bucket | (1) Assets (ISA) | (2) Liabilities (ISL) | (3) Gap = (1) − (2) | (4) Cumulative gap
1. One day (overnight) | 20 | 30 | −10 | −10
2. > 1 day – 3 months | 30 | 40 | −10 | −20
3. > 3 – 6 months | 70 | 85 | −15 | −35
4. > 6 – 12 months | 90 | 70 | +20 | −15
5. > 1 – 5 years | 40 | 30 | +10 | −5
6. Over 5 years | 10 | 5 | +5 | 0
Total | 260 | 260
One bucket: the overnight gap is −$10m. If short-term rates (e.g. the repo rate) rise by 1%, the annualised change in NII = −$10m × 0.01 = −$100 000.
One-year cumulative gap (buckets 1–4): CGAP = −10 − 10 − 15 + 20 = −$15m. A 1% rise in rates gives ΔNII = −$15m × 0.01 = −$150 000. The one-year CGAP is the figure managers and regulators watch most, because it shows the exposure of the coming year’s earnings.
By the last bucket the cumulative gap is zero, because total assets equal total liabilities (both $260m). The gaps only show when things reprice.
Positioning the gap for expected rate changes
CGAP positive: ΔNII moves with rates (rates up → NII up). If rates are expected to rise, the bank wants a positive CGAP.
CGAP negative: ΔNII moves against rates (rates up → NII down). If rates are expected to fall, the bank wants a negative CGAP.
What counts as rate-sensitive (one-year horizon)
An item is rate-sensitive if its rate is reset within the horizon, either because it matures and is rolled over at the new rate or because it has a floating rate. Its contractual maturity does not matter.
Interest-sensitive assets (ISA) | Interest-sensitive liabilities (ISL)
Short-term fixed-rate loans that mature soon (e.g. 30-day commercial loans): fixed now, but rolled over at new rates within the year | 3-month certificates of deposit (CDs): mature in 3 months and reprice on rollover
Overdrafts and revolving credit facilities (rates reset frequently) | 6-month commercial paper (unsecured short-term debt), repriced on rollover
Treasury bills (short maturities; reset when rolled over) | 1-year time deposits: repriced at the end of the 1-year horizon
30-year floating-rate mortgages: repriced whenever the repo rate (and so prime) changes, despite the 30-year maturity | Overnight interbank or reserve-bank borrowing, rolled over daily
Not rate-sensitive within one year: fixed-rate loans or bonds maturing after the horizon (e.g. a 2-year fixed loan), long fixed-rate deposits, and equity.
Worked example: one-year repricing gap for a single loan
A bank takes a 1-year fixed deposit of R200 000 and, with R50 000 of equity, funds a 2-year fixed-rate loan of R250 000. Rates fall by 1%.
The 2-year fixed loan does not reprice within 1 year, so ISA = 0. The 1-year deposit does reprice, so ISL = R200 000. Equity pays no interest and is ignored.
CGAP = 0 − 200 000 = −R200 000.
ΔNII = CGAP × ΔR = −200 000 × (−0.01) = +R2 000. NII rises: the deposit reprices at the lower rate while the loan keeps its fixed rate.
Exam focus: 2020 Section C Q6 (repricing gap with a 1-year bucket and ΔNII) and 2019 Section D Q8.3 (365-day repricing gap and ΔNII from a balance sheet). Watch the sign of ΔR and the units of the balance sheet (R million).

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 3 – Interest rate risk > Hedging the gap: natural (on-balance-sheet) hedges
x:
A natural hedge changes the bank’s own assets and liabilities so that the gap in each bucket is closed or reduced. It is the simplest method but it is slow: loan and deposit contracts have to be renegotiated, or old loans and deposits allowed to run off.
Match maturities: fund short-term assets with short-term liabilities (e.g. 3-month loans with 3-month deposits) and long-term assets (e.g. 20-year mortgages) with longer-term deposits or bonds.
Adjust loan structures: offer floating-rate loans when liabilities are floating (so ISA reprices with ISL) and fixed-rate loans when liabilities are fixed (e.g. fixed-term deposits); add rate-adjustment clauses (e.g. link mortgages to prime or JIBAR, the Johannesburg Interbank Average Rate).
Manage the deposit mix: attract longer-term deposits (e.g. 1–3-year fixed deposits) if the bank has many long-term fixed-rate loans, and short-term or floating deposits if it has many short-term loans, by adjusting deposit rates and terms.
Worked example: closing a −R1bn gap on the balance sheet
ISA (0–3 months) = R2bn; ISL (0–3 months) = R3bn; gap = −R1bn. Liabilities reprice faster, so the bank loses if rates rise.
Increase short-term ISA: buy 3-month T-bills funded by selling longer-term securities; shorten loan maturities or move fixed-rate loans to floating (e.g. prime + 2%, which reprices when prime changes); let long-term assets run off and reinvest in short-term assets; offer corporates floating-rate facilities tied to prime.
Reduce short-term ISL: lengthen deposit maturities (pay better rates on 1-year time deposits to draw clients away from 3-month CDs); issue 2–5-year notes or bonds to replace short-term funding; issue medium- or long-term fixed-rate debt and repay interbank borrowing or commercial paper.
Both together: move R500m of fixed-rate loans to floating, so ISA rises to R2.5bn, and replace R500m of short-term deposits with 2-year fixed deposits, so ISL falls to R2.5bn. The 0–3-month gap is now zero and NII in that bucket is protected from rate changes.

h: Risk Management for Banks > Part 3 – Interest rate risk > Hedging the gap: derivatives (off-balance-sheet hedges)
x:
Derivatives hedge the rate exposure without changing the bank’s lending and funding mix, so they are much faster than a natural hedge. The notional (the reference amount on which payments are calculated) is set equal to the size of the gap.
Interest rate swaps – exchange fixed-rate payments for floating-rate payments on a notional amount.
Negative gap (loses when rates rise): pay fixed, receive floating. When rates rise, the floating receipts rise and offset the higher cost of the bank’s repricing liabilities.
Positive gap (loses when rates fall): pay floating, receive fixed. When rates fall, the floating payments fall while the fixed receipts stay the same, which stabilises income.
Interest rate futures – lock in future borrowing or lending rates. With a negative gap and rates likely to rise, the bank sells futures on treasury securities: when rates rise, bond prices fall and the short futures position gains.
Interest rate options:
Cap – pays when the floating rate rises above a strike rate. Payoff = max(floating − strike, 0) × notional. It protects against rising funding costs, so it suits a negative gap.
Floor – pays when the floating rate falls below a strike. Payoff = max(strike − floating, 0) × notional. It protects against falling asset yields, so it suits a positive gap.
Collar – a cap and a floor combined, giving a band of protection.
Worked example: hedging a −R1bn gap with a swap and with a cap
ISA (within 3 months) R2bn; ISL R3bn; gap −R1bn. Rates rise instantly and in parallel by 1%. The swap fixed rate agreed today is 3%; the floating reference rate is 3% before the shock and 4% after it.
No hedge: ΔNII = GAP × ΔR = −R1bn × 0.01 = −R10 000 000.
Swap: the bank pays fixed and receives floating on a notional of R1bn (the size of the gap).Receive floating: 4% × R1bn = R40m. Pay fixed: 3% × R1bn = R30m.Net swap cash flow = (receive floating) − (pay fixed) = R40m − R30m = +R10m, which exactly offsets the R10m fall in NII.
Cap on the floating rate: notional R1bn, strike 3%, premium paid upfront. Payoff = max(4% − 3%, 0) × R1bn = +R10m, which offsets the loss.
Correct direction: with a negative gap the bank receives floating and pays fixed, so the net cash flow is (receive floating) − (pay fixed) = R40m − R30m. The slide writes it as “(receive fixed) − (pay floating)”, which is the wrong way round.
Caps vs swaps
Caps: advantages | Caps: disadvantages
One-sided protection: a cap pays only when rates rise above the strike, so the bank keeps the benefit if rates fall. A swap would have negative value if rates fell instead.Flexibility: the bank chooses the strike and the notional to match its risk appetite. | Upfront premium (or periodic premiums for a series of caplets): a cost whether or not the cap pays out.Basis risk: the index rate in the cap (e.g. JIBAR, SOFR, LIBOR) may not move exactly like the rates on the bank’s own assets and liabilities.
Worked example (Workshop 3, Q6): hedging a bond position with a forward
Awethu Bank holds a 15-year bond, R10m par value, priced at R104 per R100 (yield to maturity 7%, duration 8 years), and plans to sell it in two months. Its analyst expects rates to rise to 8% by then; most of the market expects no change, so two-month forwards on 15-year bonds are available at R104. What hedge should the bank take? Show that it protects the bank if rates rise by 1%.
Market value of the position = R10m × 1.04 = R10 400 000.
Expected change in value if rates rise 1%: ΔP = −D × P × (Δy)/(1+y) = −8 × R10 400 000 × ( (0.01)/(1.07) ) = −R777 570. The price falls from 104 to 96.2243 per R100 face value.
Hedge: sell a two-month forward contract on R10m face value of 15-year bonds at 104. This locks in today’s price for the sale.
If rates rise 1%, the bank loses R777 570 on the bond. It closes the forward by buying bonds at 96.2243 and delivering them at 104: gain = (104-96.2243)/(100) × R10m = R777 570, which offsets the loss. (With futures, the bank would close out by buying a futures contract of the same maturity and amount.)
The same R777 570 follows from the forward payoff form: (change in rate) × D* × A = 0.01 × ( (8)/(1.07) ) × R10 400 000, where D* = (D)/(1+y) is modified duration and A the position value.

x:
The names are similar, but they are different risks. Market risk itself is not examined in 2026, but knowing how it differs from market value risk (which is examined) is.
Market risk | Market value risk
Which book | Trading book (positions held for short-term trading profit) | Banking book (rate-sensitive loans, deposits, bonds held to maturity)
What drives it | Any market variable: share prices, interest rates, FX, commodity prices, volatility, market liquidity | Interest rates only (it is a form of interest rate risk)
What it hits | Trading income, so earnings directly | The present value of assets and liabilities, so capital (net worth) directly
Example | A trader buys 10 000 shares expecting a rise and sells a week later; the price falls | A 30-year fixed-rate mortgage held to maturity loses present value when rates rise
Worked example (Workshop 3, Q7): distinguish market risk from market value risk
Market risk affects assets in the trading portfolio and is driven by changes in market conditions: asset prices, interest rates, market volatility and market liquidity. It affects trading income, so it hits the bank’s earnings directly.
Market value risk is a form of interest rate risk on rate-sensitive assets and liabilities in the banking book (loans, deposits). It is driven by interest rate changes only, and it directly affects the bank’s capital (net worth).
Exam focus: 2020 Section C Q18 (two differences between market risk and market value risk).

Topic | Formula / key point
2026 exam scope | Examined: credit risk (default models, Z-score, term-structure PD, loan pricing, RAROC, migration analysis, credit derivatives), interest rate risk (refinancing/reinvestment, market value risk, repricing gap, hedging), EL vs UL, and the workshop questions. Not examined: market risk, liquidity risk and operational risk. Given in the paper: formulas, Z-score coefficients and X definitions (you calculate the ratios from the financials), the forward-rate formula, the LPM regression.
Why linear regression fails (LPM) | Default data is binary (0/1): points lie on two horizontal lines. A straight line fits badly and its fitted PDs can fall below 0 or above 1. LPM: PDi = α + ΣβjXij.
Logit model | PD = (1)/(1+exp(-Y)) , Y = α + ΣβjXij; S-shaped, PD always in [0, 1]. Slope coefficient = change in the log-odds ln[PD/(1−PD)] for a one-unit change in X, not the change in PD. Goal: reliable PD for each borrower. Drawback: built on past data → solution: stress testing.
Altman Z-score | Z = 1.2X1 + 1.4X2 + 3.3X3 + 0.6X4 + 1.0X5 (WC/TA, RE/TA, EBIT/TA, MVE/TL, Sales/TA). < 1.81 distress; 1.81–2.99 grey; > 2.99 safe. Weaknesses: only default/no default, small sample, backward-looking accounting data, ignores management and macro risk.
Term-structure PD | Assumes the whole spread is default risk. p1 = (1+i)/(1+k) ; PD = 1 − p. Year 2: forwards 1 + f = ((1+i_2)^2)/(1+i_1) and 1 + c = ((1+k_2)^2)/(1+k_1) ; p2 = (1+f)/(1+c) . Cumulative PD = 1 − p1p2.
ROA per rand lent | 1 + k = 1 + (of+(BR+φ))/(1-b(1-RR)) ; of = fee, b = compensating balance, RR = reserve requirement. Reserves only matter when there is a compensating balance.
RAROC | RAROC = (one-year net income)/(capital at risk) . Net income = (spread + fees) × L. Capital at risk ΔL = −D × L × (ΔR)/(1+R) (ΔR = worst-case, e.g. 99th-percentile, rise in rates). Approve if RAROC > hurdle (cost of equity); otherwise raise the premium.
Credit forward vs digital option | Credit forward: bank sells it; pays out (φT − φF) × D* × A when the spread widens, i.e. hedges an increase in default risk after the loan is made; bank pays if spread narrows. Digital default option: bank buys it for a premium; pays a fixed amount (par) only on default; max loss = premium.
Repricing gap and ΔNII | GAP = ISA − ISL per bucket; ΔNII = CGAP × ΔR. Only items repricing within the horizon count (a 2-year fixed loan is not rate-sensitive in a 1-year bucket). Positive CGAP gains when rates rise; negative CGAP gains when rates fall.
Refinancing vs reinvestment risk | Refinancing: ISA < ISL, long assets funded short; hurt by rising rates. Reinvestment: ISA > ISL, short assets funded long; hurt by falling rates. Use the 10%/9%/11% (or 8%) spread example.
Hedging the gap | Negative gap: pay fixed, receive floating swap, buy a cap, or sell futures. Positive gap: pay floating, receive fixed, or buy a floor. Notional = gap size.
Market vs market value risk | Market risk: trading book, any market variable, hits earnings. Market value risk: banking book, interest rates only, hits capital (net worth).
EL vs UL | Expected loss (EL = PD × LGD × EAD) is a cost of lending, covered by pricing (the risk premium in the loan rate) and provisions. Unexpected loss is covered by capital, not provisions (it is not “uncontrollable”).
